Atomic Structure: Senior Secondary · Subatomic particlesexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons.

Theory

Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Protons have charge +1 and neutrons have charge 0 in the nucleus; electrons have charge -1 and occupy the surrounding electron cloud. Protons and neutrons are much more massive than electrons. Worked case: a neutral carbon-12 atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons. Interpretation and limits: Do not say neutrons have no mass; they have no electrical charge. Application: Subatomic particles explain ions, isotopes, electricity and nuclear reactions.

Worked case

a neutral carbon-12 atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons.

Relationship

neutral atom: protons = electrons

Correction / limitation

Do not say neutrons have no mass; they have no electrical charge.

Application

Subatomic particles explain ions, isotopes, electricity and nuclear reactions.

Assessment prompt

Which particle determines an element's atomic number?

Case walkthrough

  2. neutral atom: protons = electrons
  3. Protons have charge +1 and neutrons have charge 0 in the nucleus
  4. electrons have charge -1 and occupy the surrounding electron cloud.
  5. Protons and neutrons are much more massive than electrons.
  6. Do not say neutrons have no mass; they have no electrical charge.
Atomic Structure: Senior Secondary · Atomic number and mass numberexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus.

Theory

Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus. It is written Z and uniquely identifies an element. Changing the number of electrons makes an ion, but changing the proton count makes a different element. It is a whole number written A. Electrons contribute so little mass that they are not counted in the mass number. Worked case: every oxygen atom has Z = 8, so it contains 8 protons. Example: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23. Interpretation and limits: Atomic number is not the number of neutrons or the total number of particles. Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table. Application: Atomic number organizes the modern periodic table and identifies elements in analysis. Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers.

Worked case

every oxygen atom has Z = 8, so it contains 8 protons. Example: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23.

Relationship

Z = number of protons A = Z + N

Correction / limitation

Atomic number is not the number of neutrons or the total number of particles. Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table.

Application

Atomic number organizes the modern periodic table and identifies elements in analysis. Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers.

  4. It is written Z and uniquely identifies an element.
  5. Changing the number of electrons makes an ion, but changing the proton count makes a different element.
  6. It is a whole number written A.
Atomic Structure: Senior Secondary · Isotopes and ionsexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers. Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons.

Theory

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers. Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons. They have similar chemical behavior because they have the same electron arrangement, but their masses and nuclear stability can differ. They may be atoms or ions of different elements. Their sizes can differ because nuclei with more protons attract the shared number of electrons more strongly. Worked case: carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively. Example: Ne, Na+ and F- each have 10 electrons and are isoelectronic. Interpretation and limits: Isotopes are not different elements because their atomic numbers are the same. Isoelectronic does not mean chemically identical; nuclear charge and element identity still differ. Application: Isotopes are used in medical imaging, cancer treatment, dating and chemical tracing. Electron counting helps predict ion sizes, bonding and stable ion formation.

Worked case

carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively. Example: Ne, Na+ and F- each have 10 electrons and are isoelectronic.

Relationship

same Z, different A electrons = atomic number - positive charge + negative charge

Correction / limitation

Isotopes are not different elements because their atomic numbers are the same. Isoelectronic does not mean chemically identical; nuclear charge and element identity still differ.

Application

Isotopes are used in medical imaging, cancer treatment, dating and chemical tracing. Electron counting helps predict ion sizes, bonding and stable ion formation.

Atomic Structure: Senior Secondary · Bohr’s atomic modelexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

The Bohr model places electrons in fixed, quantized energy levels around the nucleus.

Theory

The Bohr model places electrons in fixed, quantized energy levels around the nucleus. An electron absorbs energy to move higher and emits a photon when it returns to a lower level. The model explains hydrogen's line spectrum well. Worked case: an excited hydrogen electron dropping to a lower level releases light with energy equal to the difference between the levels. Interpretation and limits: Bohr paths are a useful school model, not literal planetary orbits for all atoms. Application: Energy-level ideas help explain flame colors, spectra and electronic transitions.

Worked case

an excited hydrogen electron dropping to a lower level releases light with energy equal to the difference between the levels.

Relationship

photon energy = higher level energy - lower level energy

Correction / limitation

Bohr paths are a useful school model, not literal planetary orbits for all atoms.

Application

Energy-level ideas help explain flame colors, spectra and electronic transitions.

Atomic Structure: Senior Secondary · Quantum numbers and orbitalsexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom. An orbital is a three-dimensional probability region that can hold at most two electrons.

Theory

Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom. An orbital is a three-dimensional probability region that can hold at most two electrons. The principal number n identifies shell and energy, l identifies subshell shape, ml identifies orbital orientation, and ms identifies spin. Only allowed combinations describe possible electron states. Orbitals are not fixed paths. The s subshell has one orbital, p has three, d has five and f has seven; their shapes and orientations affect bonding. Worked case: an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2. Example: the three 2p orbitals have equal energy in an isolated atom and together can hold six electrons. Interpretation and limits: Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n. Do not confuse an orbital with a shell; a shell contains one or more subshells and many orbitals. Application: Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior. Orbital shapes explain bond direction, molecular geometry, spectra and periodic trends.

Worked case

an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2. Example: the three 2p orbitals have equal energy in an isolated atom and together can hold six electrons.

Relationship

n = 1,2,...; l = 0 to n-1; ml = -l to +l; ms = +/-1/2 maximum electrons in a subshell = 2(2l + 1)

Correction / limitation

Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n. Do not confuse an orbital with a shell; a shell contains one or more subshells and many orbitals.

Application

Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior. Orbital shapes explain bond direction, molecular geometry, spectra and periodic trends.

  5. The principal number n identifies shell and energy, l identifies subshell shape, ml identifies orbital orientation, and ms identifies spin.
  6. Only allowed combinations describe possible electron states.
Periodic Table and Trends · Periods, groups and blocksexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table. Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table. p-Block elements have valence configuration ns2np1-6 and span metals, metalloids, non-metals and noble gases.

Theory

Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table. Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table. p-Block elements have valence configuration ns2np1-6 and span metals, metalloids, non-metals and noble gases. Main-group elements in one group have similar valence-electron patterns and therefore often show similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied main electron shells, while properties change gradually from left to right. Group chemistry depends on both valence-electron count and the changing importance of d/f shielding and relativistic effects. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute. Worked case: lithium, sodium and potassium are Group 1 metals and commonly form +1 ions. Example: sodium through argon lie in Period 3 and have electrons occupying three main shells. Example: Across a period, increasing effective nuclear charge generally reduces size and increases non-metallic character. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result. Interpretation and limits: Elements in a group are similar, not identical; reactivity can change down the group. Elements in the same period do not usually have similar chemical properties. Do not answer p-Block electronic configuration and group trends from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion. Application: Groups help predict ion charges, formulas and reaction patterns. Period position helps predict electron arrangement and trends across the table. p-Block electronic configuration and group trends supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.

Example: Across a period, increasing effective nuclear charge generally reduces size and increases non-metallic character. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Elements in a group are similar, not identical; reactivity can change down the group. Elements in the same period do not usually have similar chemical properties. Do not answer p-Block electronic configuration and group trends from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.

Application

Period position helps predict electron arrangement and trends across the table. p-Block electronic configuration and group trends supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.

Periodic Table and Trends · Electronic configurationexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: in a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, Zn is oxidized at the anode and Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode. Electrons flow through the wire from Zn to Cu while the salt bridge maintains charge balance.

Concept

Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals.

Theory

Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals. Electrons are placed in available low-energy states while obeying Aufbau filling, Hund's rule and the Pauli principle. Valence electrons largely control chemical behavior. Worked case: oxygen has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4; its six valence electrons explain its common valency of two. Interpretation and limits: Do not exceed subshell capacities: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14 electrons. Application: Configurations predict ion formation, bonding, magnetism and an element's position in the periodic table.

Worked case

oxygen has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4; its six valence electrons explain its common valency of two.

Relationship

total superscripts in a neutral atom = atomic number

Correction / limitation

Do not exceed subshell capacities: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14 electrons.

Application

Configurations predict ion formation, bonding, magnetism and an element's position in the periodic table.

  5. Valence electrons largely control chemical behavior.

Concept

Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group because effective nuclear charge and shell number change.

Theory

Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group because effective nuclear charge and shell number change. Covalent, metallic and van der Waals radii are defined differently; ionic size also depends on charge and coordination. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion. Application: Atomic and ionic radii trends supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.

Chemical Bonding: Senior Secondary · Ionic bondingexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: CH₄ has four bonding domains around carbon and no lone pairs. The domains point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles close to 109.5°. The symmetric molecule is non-polar overall.

Concept

An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

Theory

An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Electron transfer commonly creates cations and anions, which assemble into a three-dimensional lattice rather than separate pairs. Strong attractions give high melting points. Worked case: sodium loses one electron to form Na+, chlorine gains it to form Cl-, and the ions form an NaCl lattice. Interpretation and limits: Do not describe an ionic bond as a shared electron pair or NaCl as a single isolated molecule. Application: Ionic materials are used in salts, ceramics, electrolytes, batteries and fertilizers.

Worked case

sodium loses one electron to form Na+, chlorine gains it to form Cl-, and the ions form an NaCl lattice.

Relationship

electrostatic attraction increases with ionic charge and decreases with distance

Correction / limitation

Do not describe an ionic bond as a shared electron pair or NaCl as a single isolated molecule.

Application

Ionic materials are used in salts, ceramics, electrolytes, batteries and fertilizers.

  4. Strong attractions give high melting points.

Chemical Bonding: Senior Secondary · Covalent bondingexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: CH₄ has four bonding domains around carbon and no lone pairs. The domains point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles close to 109.5°. The symmetric molecule is non-polar overall.

Concept

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

Theory

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Shared electron density attracts both nuclei. Single, double and triple bonds differ in shared pairs, length and strength. Worked case: in H2, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duet. Interpretation and limits: Sharing is not always perfectly equal; electronegativity differences can make a covalent bond polar. Application: Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids.

Worked case

Relationship

bond order: single < double < triple

Correction / limitation

Sharing is not always perfectly equal; electronegativity differences can make a covalent bond polar.

Application

Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids.

Chemical Bonding: Senior Secondary · Metallic bondingexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: CH₄ has four bonding domains around carbon and no lone pairs. The domains point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles close to 109.5°. The symmetric molecule is non-polar overall.

Concept

Metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal cores and delocalized valence electrons.

Theory

Metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal cores and delocalized valence electrons. The mobile electron cloud extends through the solid, explaining electrical and thermal conductivity, lustre and the ability of layers to slide without shattering. Worked case: copper conducts because delocalized electrons move through its lattice when a potential difference is applied. Interpretation and limits: Metallic bonding is not a collection of separate molecules or fixed electron pairs between two atoms. Application: Metallic bonding underpins wires, alloys, structural metals and electronic contacts.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Application

Metallic bonding underpins wires, alloys, structural metals and electronic contacts.

Concept

A state of matter is a physical form determined by particle arrangement, motion and attraction.

Theory

A state of matter is a physical form determined by particle arrangement, motion and attraction. The familiar states are solid, liquid and gas. Plasma occurs at very high energy, while a Bose-Einstein condensate forms near absolute zero. Worked case: ice, liquid water and water vapour are the same substance in three states; heating changes particle motion without changing H2O into a new substance. Interpretation and limits: A state change does not automatically create a new substance. Application: Controlling states of matter is essential in refrigeration, cooking, metal casting and gas storage.

Concept

Gas laws describe relationships among pressure, volume, temperature and amount.

Theory

Gas laws describe relationships among pressure, volume, temperature and amount. Boyle's law applies at constant temperature, Charles's law at constant pressure and Avogadro's law at fixed temperature and pressure. Temperature must be absolute. Worked case: at constant temperature, compressing a gas from 2.0 L to 1.0 L doubles its pressure because P1V1 = P2V2. Interpretation and limits: Never substitute Celsius temperature directly into gas-law ratios; convert it to kelvin. Application: Gas laws guide tyres, syringes, weather balloons, breathing and gas storage.

Concept

Van der Waals forces are weak attractions between atoms or molecules caused by permanent or temporary dipoles. A hydrogen bond is a strong intermolecular attraction involving H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F.

Theory

Van der Waals forces are weak attractions between atoms or molecules caused by permanent or temporary dipoles. A hydrogen bond is a strong intermolecular attraction involving H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F. They include London dispersion forces in all particles and dipole-dipole attractions in polar molecules. Their combined effect grows with polarizability and contact area. The highly polar X-H bond exposes a partially positive hydrogen that attracts an electronegative atom on the same or another molecule. Worked case: iodine is solid at room temperature because its large electron clouds produce stronger dispersion forces than those in chlorine. Example: hydrogen bonds between water molecules raise water's boiling point compared with similarly sized molecules. Interpretation and limits: Weak individually does not mean unimportant; many attractions together can strongly affect properties. A hydrogen bond is not the covalent O-H or N-H bond inside the molecule. Application: These forces influence boiling points, liquefaction, molecular recognition and adhesion. Hydrogen bonding controls water properties, DNA pairing, protein shape and material solubility.

Concept

A phase diagram maps which physical phases are stable at different temperatures and pressures.

Theory

A phase diagram maps which physical phases are stable at different temperatures and pressures. Coexistence curves mark conditions where two phases are in equilibrium. The triple point joins three-phase equilibrium, while the critical point ends the liquid-vapour coexistence curve. Worked case: At pressures below water's triple-point pressure, heating ice cannot produce an equilibrium liquid-water phase; it passes toward vapour by sublimation. At ordinary atmospheric pressure, heating ice instead crosses a melting boundary before boiling. Interpretation and limits: Do not read a phase change from temperature alone without checking the pressure on the diagram. Application: Phase diagrams guide freeze-drying, refrigeration and control of material-processing conditions.

Concept

A crystal lattice is a regular three-dimensional array of repeating points representing particle positions. A unit cell is the smallest repeating volume that reproduces a crystal lattice by translation.

Theory

A crystal lattice is a regular three-dimensional array of repeating points representing particle positions. A unit cell is the smallest repeating volume that reproduces a crystal lattice by translation. A unit cell is the smallest repeating portion. Lattice arrangement and bonding control density, cleavage, strength and other bulk properties. Atoms at corners, faces, edges and inside contribute fractional or whole counts to one cell. Geometry relates cell dimensions to density. Worked case: in rock salt, Na+ and Cl- occupy alternating positions in a cubic repeating structure. Example: a simple cubic cell has eight corner atoms, each shared by eight cells, giving 8 x 1/8 = 1 atom per unit cell. Interpretation and limits: A lattice point represents an equivalent environment, not necessarily one single atom. Do not count every drawn corner atom as fully belonging to one unit cell. Application: Crystal lattices are central to minerals, semiconductors, salts and pharmaceutical solids. Unit-cell analysis reveals crystal density, composition, packing and diffraction patterns.

Concept

A functional group is an atom or group that gives an organic compound its characteristic reactions and naming suffix or prefix.

Theory

A functional group is an atom or group that gives an organic compound its characteristic reactions and naming suffix or prefix. Class 10 groups include halo (-X), alcohol (-OH), aldehyde (-CHO), ketone (>C=O) and carboxylic acid (-COOH). The carbon skeleton determines the parent name, while the principal group determines suffix and numbering. Worked case: CH3CH2OH is an alcohol, CH3CHO an aldehyde, CH3COCH3 a ketone and CH3COOH a carboxylic acid. Interpretation and limits: Do not identify every oxygen-containing compound as an alcohol; locate the exact bonding pattern of the functional group. Application: Functional groups organise fuels, solvents, flavours, medicines, polymers and biological molecules into predictable reaction families.

Concept

A balanced chemical equation contains equal numbers of every type of atom on the reactant and product sides.

Theory

A balanced chemical equation contains equal numbers of every type of atom on the reactant and product sides. Write correct formulae first, count atoms, adjust whole-number coefficients and reduce them to the smallest ratio. Coefficients multiply complete formula units; subscripts belong to substance identities and must not be altered during balancing. Worked case: For Al + O2 -> Al2O3, balance aluminium and oxygen to obtain 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3, then verify four Al and six O atoms on each side. Interpretation and limits: Never change a subscript such as H2O into H2O2 to balance atoms; that changes water into a different substance. Application: Balanced equations support quantitative reaction calculations, manufacturing yields and pollution accounting.

Concept

A combination reaction forms one main product from two or more reactants. A decomposition reaction breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances.

Theory

A combination reaction forms one main product from two or more reactants. A decomposition reaction breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances. Atoms are rearranged into a more complex product while total atoms and mass remain conserved. Energy from heat, light or electricity is often needed to break bonds in the reactant. Worked case: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO combines magnesium and oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Example: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 when limestone is strongly heated. Interpretation and limits: A reaction with several products is not a simple combination reaction. Melting is not decomposition because it forms no new substance. Application: Combination reactions occur in material manufacture, corrosion and synthesis. Decomposition is used to make lime, extract substances and analyze compounds.

Worked case

2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO combines magnesium and oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Example: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 when limestone is strongly heated.

Relationship

A + B -> AB AB -> A + B

Correction / limitation

A reaction with several products is not a simple combination reaction. Melting is not decomposition because it forms no new substance.

Application

Combination reactions occur in material manufacture, corrosion and synthesis. Decomposition is used to make lime, extract substances and analyze compounds.

  5. Energy from heat, light or electricity is often needed to break bonds in the reactant.
  6. A reaction with several products is not a simple combination reaction. Melting is not decomposition because it forms no new substance.
Reaction Equations and Redox · Displacement and precipitation reactionsexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element in a compound. A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid when ions from aqueous solutions combine.

Theory

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element in a compound. A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid when ions from aqueous solutions combine. The reactivity series predicts whether the replacement will occur and electron transfer is often involved. Double-displacement reactions exchange ions, but a reaction is driven only when a precipitate, gas or weakly ionised product forms. The net ionic equation removes spectator ions and shows the species responsible for the visible solid. Worked case: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu because zinc is more reactive than copper. Example: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s)↓ + 2KNO3(aq) gives a yellow lead-iodide precipitate. Interpretation and limits: A less reactive metal cannot normally displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution. Do not call every double-displacement mixture a precipitation reaction; first check whether an insoluble product actually forms. Application: Displacement reactions are used in metal extraction, batteries and reactivity tests. Precipitation is used in ion identification, water treatment, pigment preparation and removal of contaminants.

Correction / limitation

A less reactive metal cannot normally displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution. Do not call every double-displacement mixture a precipitation reaction; first check whether an insoluble product actually forms.

Concept

Dynamic equilibrium occurs when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a closed system.

Theory

Dynamic equilibrium occurs when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a closed system. Macroscopic concentrations remain constant even though both reactions continue microscopically. Equilibrium can be reached from either direction. Worked case: in N2O4(g) <-> 2NO2(g), molecules continue interconverting while the colour and concentrations remain constant at equilibrium. Interpretation and limits: Equilibrium does not mean reactions stop or that reactant and product concentrations are equal. Application: Dynamic equilibrium controls industrial synthesis, gas binding, solubility and acid-base systems.

in N2O4(g) <-> 2NO2(g), molecules continue interconverting while the colour and concentrations remain constant at equilibrium.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Equilibrium does not mean reactions stop or that reactant and product concentrations are equal.

Application

Dynamic equilibrium controls industrial synthesis, gas binding, solubility and acid-base systems.

Concept

Le Chatelier's principle predicts how an equilibrium responds to a disturbance.

Le Chatelier's principle predicts how an equilibrium responds to a disturbance. The system shifts in the direction that partly opposes a concentration, pressure or temperature change. A catalyst speeds approach but does not shift equilibrium. Worked case: increasing pressure in N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3 shifts equilibrium toward ammonia because that side has fewer gas moles. Interpretation and limits: Do not say a catalyst changes K or equilibrium yield; it accelerates both directions. Application: The principle guides ammonia manufacture, gas reactions, buffers and product recovery.

Concept

Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a stated amount of solvent at specified conditions. Concentration expresses how much solute is present relative to a defined amount of solution or solvent.

Theory

Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a stated amount of solvent at specified conditions. Concentration expresses how much solute is present relative to a defined amount of solution or solvent. It depends on solute-solvent interactions, temperature and, for gases, pressure. A saturated solution is in dynamic equilibrium with undissolved solute. Different units suit different purposes, including mass percent, molarity, molality, mole fraction and ppm. Worked case: if at most 36 g NaCl dissolves in 100 g water at a temperature, adding 40 g leaves about 4 g undissolved. Example: dissolving 5 g salt to make 100 g solution gives a mass percentage of 5%. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse dissolving rate with solubility; stirring speeds dissolving but may not change the final maximum. Always identify whether the denominator is solution, solvent, volume or mass. Application: Solubility guides crystallization, medicines, water treatment and formulation. Concentration controls medicine doses, reaction rates, product quality and pollution limits.

Concept

A buffer resists large pH changes when small amounts of acid or base are added. Volumetric analysis determines analyte amount from the accurately measured volume of a standardized reagent.

Theory

A buffer resists large pH changes when small amounts of acid or base are added. Volumetric analysis determines analyte amount from the accurately measured volume of a standardized reagent. It commonly contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, which consume added OH- and H3O+ respectively. Buffer capacity is limited. Determines analyte amount from the accurately measured volume of a standardized reagent. Worked case: an ethanoic acid/ethanoate buffer uses CH3COOH to neutralize added OH- and CH3COO- to consume added H3O+. At equivalence, 25.00 mL of 0.1000 M HCl requires 25.00 mL of 0.1000 M NaOH. Interpretation and limits: A buffer does not keep pH perfectly fixed and fails when too much acid or base is added. The indicator endpoint is an observed signal and may not coincide exactly with the stoichiometric equivalence point. Application: Buffers stabilize blood, medicines, foods, fermentation and analytical solutions. A standardized titrant determines an unknown solution amount from measured endpoint volume and the reaction stoichiometry.

Kinetics and Electrochemistry · Collision theory and activation energyexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield.

Concept

Collision theory explains reaction rate through collision frequency, sufficient energy and suitable molecular orientation. Activation energy is the minimum energy barrier between reactants and the transition-state region.

Theory

Collision theory explains reaction rate through collision frequency, sufficient energy and suitable molecular orientation. Activation energy is the minimum energy barrier between reactants and the transition-state region. Only collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy and an effective orientation produce products. The Arrhenius factor exp(-Ea/RT) estimates the energetic fraction, while the pre-exponential factor includes collision frequency and orientation. Raising temperature increases the high-energy fraction strongly. A larger barrier gives a smaller rate constant at the same temperature. Catalysts speed reactions by providing a pathway with lower activation energy. Worked case: two molecules may collide often but react slowly when Ea is high or their reactive sites do not meet. A catalyst supplies another pathway with lower Ea, increasing effective collisions without changing DeltaG° or K. Example: heating increases the fraction of molecules above Ea, so more collisions can cross the barrier and the reaction accelerates. Interpretation and limits: Do not say every collision causes reaction or that a catalyst increases the energy of colliding molecules. Activation energy is not the reaction enthalpy; it controls rate rather than overall energy difference. Application: Collision theory helps engineers choose temperature, catalysts and mixing conditions for safe and efficient reactors. Barrier control is crucial in combustion, enzymes, food preservation and industrial safety.

Relationship

Theory

Kinetic catalysis increases reaction rate through an alternative lower-energy mechanism. Reaction mechanisms describe elementary bond-making and bond-breaking steps consistent with kinetics, stereochemistry and isotope evidence. A catalyst participates in elementary steps but is regenerated overall. It accelerates forward and reverse processes without changing deltaG, K or equilibrium composition. Describe elementary bond-making and bond-breaking steps consistent with kinetics, stereochemistry and isotope evidence. Worked case: MnO2 accelerates H2O2 decomposition by lowering the pathway barrier and remains chemically regenerated overall. Interpretation and limits: A catalyst does not increase equilibrium yield or make a thermodynamically impossible process favorable. An overall balanced equation does not prove that the reaction occurs in one elementary collision. Application: Catalysis enables lower-temperature manufacturing, emission control and enzyme-driven life chemistry. Mechanistic comparisons explain why changing substrate, nucleophile or solvent alters organic product distribution.

Example: in a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, Zn is oxidized at the anode and Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode. Electrons flow through the wire from Zn to Cu while the salt bridge maintains charge balance.

Concept

A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work. Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction.

Theory

A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work. Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction. Oxidation occurs at the anode, reduction at the cathode, electrons travel through the wire and ions through the electrolyte or salt bridge maintain charge balance. The power supply pushes electrons, while ions migrate to electrodes. Deposited or released amount is proportional to charge passed. Worked case: in a Daniell cell, Zn oxidizes at the anode and Cu2+ reduces at the cathode; electrons flow from Zn to Cu. Example: passing 193000 C through Cu2+ solution supplies 2 mol electrons and ideally deposits 1 mol copper. Interpretation and limits: Oxidation is always at the anode and reduction at the cathode; do not rely only on electrode signs. Electrode signs differ from a galvanic cell, but oxidation remains at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Application: Galvanic-cell principles underpin batteries, sensors and corrosion measurements. Electrolysis is used for plating, metal refining, chemical manufacture and hydrogen production.

Concept

A thermodynamic system is the part of the universe selected for study.

Theory

A thermodynamic system is the part of the universe selected for study. An open system exchanges matter and energy, a closed system exchanges energy but not matter, and an isolated system exchanges neither. The chosen boundary determines which transfers are counted. Worked case: hot water in an open beaker is an open system; a sealed bottle is approximately closed, while an ideal insulated sealed flask approaches an isolated system. Interpretation and limits: Do not classify a system from its container alone; identify whether both matter and energy can cross the boundary. Application: Defining the system correctly is essential in engines, reactors, calorimeters and biological energy balances.

Worked case

hot water in an open beaker is an open system; a sealed bottle is approximately closed, while an ideal insulated sealed flask approaches an isolated system.

Relationship

universe = system + surroundings

Correction / limitation

Do not classify a system from its container alone; identify whether both matter and energy can cross the boundary.

Application

Defining the system correctly is essential in engines, reactors, calorimeters and biological energy balances.

The surroundings are everything outside the system that can interact with it.

Theory

The surroundings are everything outside the system that can interact with it. Energy or matter crossing the boundary appears with opposite accounting in system and surroundings. Interpretation and limits: Do not call only the immediate container the surroundings; the definition includes everything outside the selected boundary. Application: Surroundings accounting supports calorimetry, thermal management and environmental energy analysis.

Concept

Thermodynamic work is organized energy transfer caused by a force acting through a distance.

Theory

Thermodynamic work is organized energy transfer caused by a force acting through a distance. For pressure-volume work with the chemistry sign convention, expansion against external pressure gives negative work on the system; compression gives positive work. Worked case: a gas expanding by 2.0 L against 100 kPa does w = -Pext deltaV = -200 J because 1 kPa L equals 1 J. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse work done by the system with work done on the system; state the sign convention before calculating. Application: Pressure-volume work describes pistons, engines, compressors and expanding reaction gases.

Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of a system.

Interpretation and limits: Do not omit the sign of work or assume internal energy depends only on temperature for every system. Concept

Enthalpy is the state function H = U + PV, useful for constant-pressure processes.

Theory

Enthalpy is the state function H = U + PV, useful for constant-pressure processes. At constant pressure with only pressure-volume work, the enthalpy change equals heat absorbed by the system. Negative deltaH is exothermic and positive deltaH is endothermic. Worked case: combustion releasing 890 kJ per mole has deltaH = -890 kJ mol-1; the negative sign records heat leaving the system. Interpretation and limits: Do not drop the sign of deltaH or describe exothermic products as having more enthalpy than reactants. Application: Enthalpy data support fuel comparison, process heating, food energy and reaction design.

Concept

Calorimetry determines heat transfer from measured temperature changes.

Theory

Calorimetry determines heat transfer from measured temperature changes. An insulated calorimeter uses conservation of energy: heat lost by the reaction equals heat gained by the calorimeter and contents, after accounting for heat capacity. Concept

Bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a specified gas-phase bond.

Theory

Bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a specified gas-phase bond. Average bond enthalpies estimate reaction enthalpy by comparing bonds broken with bonds formed. Breaking requires energy; forming releases energy. Worked case: for H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, estimate deltaH = D(H-H) + D(Cl-Cl) - 2D(H-Cl). State the sign convention, substitute consistent units, and interpret the numerical result chemically. Interpretation and limits: Do not add bond-forming energies as positive; formation lowers energy and is subtracted in the estimate. Application: Bond enthalpies estimate fuel energies, reaction feasibility and bond strengths.

Concept

A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess Law to ionic-solid formation.

Theory

A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess Law to ionic-solid formation. Worked case: a NaCl cycle links sodium sublimation, chlorine bond dissociation, sodium ionization, chlorine electron gain and NaCl lattice formation. Previous worked example

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: at a fixed temperature, xA = 0.40, pA° = 100 kPa, xB = 0.60 and pB° = 50 kPa. ptotal = 0.40(100) + 0.60(50) = 70 kPa. A measured value above 70 kPa indicates positive deviation. Key check: after solving Ideal and non-ideal solutions, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law throughout the composition range; non-ideal solutions show positive or negative deviations because unlike-molecule attractions differ from like-molecule attractions.

Theory

Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law throughout the composition range; non-ideal solutions show positive or negative deviations because unlike-molecule attractions differ from like-molecule attractions. For an ideal binary solution, each partial vapour pressure is pi = xi pi° and the total is their sum. DeltaHmix and DeltaVmix are zero. Weaker A-B attractions produce positive deviation, higher vapour pressure and often a minimum-boiling azeotrope; stronger A-B attractions produce negative deviation and may form a maximum-boiling azeotrope. Worked case: at a fixed temperature, xA = 0.40, pA° = 100 kPa, xB = 0.60 and pB° = 50 kPa. ptotal = 0.40(100) + 0.60(50) = 70 kPa. A measured value above 70 kPa indicates positive deviation. Interpretation and limits: Do not label a solution ideal merely because both components are liquids; compare the measured vapour pressure and mixing effects with Raoult's-law predictions. Application: Vapour-pressure diagrams and azeotropes determine whether industrial liquid mixtures can be separated by ordinary fractional distillation.

Worked case

at a fixed temperature, xA = 0.40, pA° = 100 kPa, xB = 0.60 and pB° = 50 kPa. ptotal = 0.40(100) + 0.60(50) = 70 kPa. A measured value above 70 kPa indicates positive deviation.

Relationship

pi = xi pi°; ptotal = sum(pi); ideal: DeltaHmix = 0 and DeltaVmix = 0

Correction / limitation

Do not label a solution ideal merely because both components are liquids; compare the measured vapour pressure and mixing effects with Raoult's-law predictions.

Application

Vapour-pressure diagrams and azeotropes determine whether industrial liquid mixtures can be separated by ordinary fractional distillation.

Solutions: Senior Secondary · Abnormal molar mass and van't Hoff factorexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: 0.10 mol CaCl2 in 1.0 kg water gives depression in freezing point 0.465 K when Kf = 1.86 K kg mol-1. i = 0.465/(1.86 x 0.10) = 2.50; alpha = (2.50 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 0.75. Key check: after solving Abnormal molar mass and van't Hoff factor, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Solute association or dissociation changes the number of dissolved particles, producing an apparent molar mass different from the true value.

Theory

Solute association or dissociation changes the number of dissolved particles, producing an apparent molar mass different from the true value. The van't Hoff factor i is the observed colligative property divided by the value expected for a non-electrolyte. Dissociation normally gives i greater than one; association gives i less than one. For dissociation into nu particles, i = 1 + alpha(nu - 1); for n-mer association, i = 1 - alpha(1 - 1/n). Worked case: 0.10 mol CaCl2 in 1.0 kg water gives depression in freezing point 0.465 K when Kf = 1.86 K kg mol-1. i = 0.465/(1.86 x 0.10) = 2.50; alpha = (2.50 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 0.75. Interpretation and limits: Do not automatically use the integer number of ions as i; incomplete dissociation and ion pairing make experimental i non-integral. Application: Van't Hoff corrections improve molar-mass determination and electrolyte formulation in pharmaceuticals, antifreeze and physiological solutions.

Worked case

0.10 mol CaCl2 in 1.0 kg water gives depression in freezing point 0.465 K when Kf = 1.86 K kg mol-1. i = 0.465/(1.86 x 0.10) = 2.50; alpha = (2.50 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 0.75.

Relationship

i = observed colligative property / calculated value; DeltaTf = i Kf m

Correction / limitation

Do not automatically use the integer number of ions as i; incomplete dissociation and ion pairing make experimental i non-integral.

Application

Van't Hoff corrections improve molar-mass determination and electrolyte formulation in pharmaceuticals, antifreeze and physiological solutions.

Dynamic equilibrium occurs when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a closed system.

Theory

Dynamic equilibrium occurs when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a closed system. Macroscopic concentrations remain constant even though both reactions continue microscopically. Concept

Le Chatelier's principle predicts how an equilibrium responds to a disturbance.

Concept

Reaction order is the exponent of a concentration term in a rate law; overall order is the exponent sum.

Theory

Reaction order is the exponent of a concentration term in a rate law; overall order is the exponent sum. Order is measured experimentally and may be zero, fractional or negative. It determines rate sensitivity and integrated-law units. Worked case: rate = k[A][B]^2 is first order in A, second order in B and third order overall. Interpretation and limits: Order is not the same as a balanced coefficient or molecularity. Application: Reaction order helps predict concentration-time behavior and select kinetic models.

overall order = sum of concentration exponents

Correction / limitation

Order is not the same as a balanced coefficient or molecularity.

Application

Concept

Molecularity is the number of reacting particles in one elementary step.

Theory

Molecularity is the number of reacting particles in one elementary step. An elementary step may be unimolecular, bimolecular or rarely termolecular. Molecularity is always a positive integer and is defined for a step, not a complex overall reaction. Worked case: A + B -> products as one elementary collision is bimolecular and has step rate proportional to [A][B]. Interpretation and limits: Do not assign molecularity to an overall multistep equation or confuse it with experimentally observed order. Application: Molecularity connects proposed mechanisms with elementary-step rate laws.

Worked case

A + B -> products as one elementary collision is bimolecular and has step rate proportional to [A][B].

Relationship

molecularity = particles participating in an elementary step

Correction / limitation

Do not assign molecularity to an overall multistep equation or confuse it with experimentally observed order.

Application

Molecularity connects proposed mechanisms with elementary-step rate laws.

Previous worked example

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: a first-order reactant falls from 0.800 M to 0.200 M in 40.0 min. k = (2.303/40.0) log(0.800/0.200) = 0.0347 min-1. Key check: after solving Integrated rate equations, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Integrated rate laws connect reactant concentration with time and allow reaction order and rate constants to be extracted from experimental data.

Theory

Integrated rate laws connect reactant concentration with time and allow reaction order and rate constants to be extracted from experimental data. For a zero-order reaction, [A]t = [A]0 - kt and [A] versus t is linear. For first order, ln[A]t = ln[A]0 - kt and ln[A] versus t is linear. The slope is -k, with units mol L-1 s-1 for zero order and s-1 for first order. Worked case: a first-order reactant falls from 0.800 M to 0.200 M in 40.0 min. k = (2.303/40.0) log(0.800/0.200) = 0.0347 min-1. Interpretation and limits: Do not identify order from the balanced equation; order is determined experimentally from the rate law or the correct linear concentration-time plot. Application: Integrated laws predict shelf life, drug degradation, pollutant decay and the time required for industrial conversion.

Worked case

a first-order reactant falls from 0.800 M to 0.200 M in 40.0 min. k = (2.303/40.0) log(0.800/0.200) = 0.0347 min-1.

Relationship

zero: [A]t=[A]0-kt; first: k=(2.303/t)log([A]0/[A]t)

Correction / limitation

Do not identify order from the balanced equation; order is determined experimentally from the rate law or the correct linear concentration-time plot.

Application

Integrated laws predict shelf life, drug degradation, pollutant decay and the time required for industrial conversion.

  2. zero: [A]t=[A]0-kt; first: k=(2.303/t)log([A]0/[A]t)
  3. For a zero-order reaction, [A]t = [A]0 - kt and [A] versus t is linear.
  4. For first order, ln[A]t = ln[A]0 - kt and ln[A] versus t is linear.
  5. The slope is -k, with units mol L-1 s-1 for zero order and s-1 for first order.
  6. Do not identify order from the balanced equation; order is determined experimentally from the rate law or the correct linear concentration-time plot.

Previous worked example

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: if a first-order process has k = 2.31 x 10^-3 s-1, t1/2 = 0.693/k = 300 s. After three half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)^3 = 1/8. Key check: after solving Half-life of reactions, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Half-life is the time required for a reactant concentration to fall to half its current value, and its concentration dependence reveals reaction order.

Theory

Half-life is the time required for a reactant concentration to fall to half its current value, and its concentration dependence reveals reaction order. For zero order, t1/2 = [A]0/(2k), so half-life decreases as the initial concentration decreases. For first order, t1/2 = ln2/k and is independent of initial concentration. Successive first-order halvings therefore take equal times. Worked case: if a first-order process has k = 2.31 x 10^-3 s-1, t1/2 = 0.693/k = 300 s. After three half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)^3 = 1/8. Interpretation and limits: Do not apply the radioactive or first-order half-life formula to a zero-order reaction without first establishing the reaction order. Application: Half-life calculations guide pharmaceutical expiry, radiotracer use, environmental persistence and reaction scheduling.

Worked case

if a first-order process has k = 2.31 x 10^-3 s-1, t1/2 = 0.693/k = 300 s. After three half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)^3 = 1/8.

Relationship

zero: t1/2=[A]0/(2k); first: t1/2=0.693/k

Correction / limitation

Do not apply the radioactive or first-order half-life formula to a zero-order reaction without first establishing the reaction order.

Application

Half-life calculations guide pharmaceutical expiry, radiotracer use, environmental persistence and reaction scheduling.

  3. zero: t1/2=[A]0/(2k); first: t1/2=0.693/k
  4. For zero order, t1/2 = [A]0/(2k), so half-life decreases as the initial concentration decreases.
  5. For first order, t1/2 = ln2/k and is independent of initial concentration.
  6. Successive first-order halvings therefore take equal times.

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Key check: after solving Collision theory, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Collision theory explains reaction rate through collision frequency, sufficient energy and suitable molecular orientation.

Theory

Collision theory explains reaction rate through collision frequency, sufficient energy and suitable molecular orientation. Only collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy and an effective orientation produce products. The Arrhenius factor exp(-Ea/RT) estimates the energetic fraction, while the pre-exponential factor includes collision frequency and orientation. Raising temperature increases the high-energy fraction strongly. Worked case: two molecules may collide often but react slowly when Ea is high or their reactive sites do not meet. A catalyst supplies another pathway with lower Ea, increasing effective collisions without changing DeltaG° or K. Interpretation and limits: Do not say every collision causes reaction or that a catalyst increases the energy of colliding molecules. Application: Collision theory helps engineers choose temperature, catalysts and mixing conditions for safe and efficient reactors.

Worked case

two molecules may collide often but react slowly when Ea is high or their reactive sites do not meet. A catalyst supplies another pathway with lower Ea, increasing effective collisions without changing DeltaG° or K.

Relationship

k = A exp(-Ea/RT); effective collision = sufficient energy + correct orientation

Correction / limitation

Do not say every collision causes reaction or that a catalyst increases the energy of colliding molecules.

Application

Collision theory helps engineers choose temperature, catalysts and mixing conditions for safe and efficient reactors.

Concept

The Arrhenius equation describes how the rate constant changes with temperature and activation energy.

Theory

The Arrhenius equation describes how the rate constant changes with temperature and activation energy. A is the pre-exponential factor and exp(-Ea/RT) represents the fraction of suitably energetic events. A plot of ln k against 1/T has slope -Ea/R. Worked case: rate constants at two temperatures can give Ea from ln(k2/k1) = -Ea/R(1/T2 - 1/T1). Interpretation and limits: Use kelvin temperature and consistent energy units for Ea and R. Application: Arrhenius analysis predicts shelf life, process rates and temperature sensitivity.

Relationship

k = A exp(-Ea/RT)

Correction / limitation

Use kelvin temperature and consistent energy units for Ea and R.

Application

Arrhenius analysis predicts shelf life, process rates and temperature sensitivity.

Concept

Activation energy is the minimum energy barrier between reactants and the transition-state region.

Theory

Activation energy is the minimum energy barrier between reactants and the transition-state region. A larger barrier gives a smaller rate constant at the same temperature. Catalysts speed reactions by providing a pathway with lower activation energy. Worked case: heating increases the fraction of molecules above Ea, so more collisions can cross the barrier and the reaction accelerates. Interpretation and limits: Activation energy is not the reaction enthalpy; it controls rate rather than overall energy difference. Application: Barrier control is crucial in combustion, enzymes, food preservation and industrial safety.

heating increases the fraction of molecules above Ea, so more collisions can cross the barrier and the reaction accelerates.

Relationship

higher Ea at fixed T -> smaller k

Correction / limitation

Activation energy is not the reaction enthalpy; it controls rate rather than overall energy difference.

Application

Barrier control is crucial in combustion, enzymes, food preservation and industrial safety.

Concept

Kinetic catalysis increases reaction rate through an alternative lower-energy mechanism.

Theory

Kinetic catalysis increases reaction rate through an alternative lower-energy mechanism. A catalyst participates in elementary steps but is regenerated overall. It accelerates forward and reverse processes without changing deltaG, K or equilibrium composition. Worked case: MnO2 accelerates H2O2 decomposition by lowering the pathway barrier and remains chemically regenerated overall. Interpretation and limits: A catalyst does not increase equilibrium yield or make a thermodynamically impossible process favorable. Application: Catalysis enables lower-temperature manufacturing, emission control and enzyme-driven life chemistry.

Relationship

catalyst -> alternative pathway with lower activation energy

Correction / limitation

A catalyst does not increase equilibrium yield or make a thermodynamically impossible process favorable.

Application

Catalysis enables lower-temperature manufacturing, emission control and enzyme-driven life chemistry.

Concept

A redox reaction transfers electrons through simultaneous oxidation and reduction.

Theory

A redox reaction transfers electrons through simultaneous oxidation and reduction. Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain. Half-reactions balance atoms, charge and transferred electrons. Worked case: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu; zinc loses two electrons and copper(II) gains the same two electrons. Interpretation and limits: Do not change subscripts to balance redox equations; use coefficients and balance charge explicitly. Application: Redox chemistry powers cells, corrosion, electrolysis, metallurgy and biological respiration.

Concept

A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work.

Theory

A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work. Oxidation occurs at the anode, reduction at the cathode, electrons travel through the wire and ions through the electrolyte or salt bridge maintain charge balance. Worked case: in a Daniell cell, Zn oxidizes at the anode and Cu2+ reduces at the cathode; electrons flow from Zn to Cu. Interpretation and limits: Oxidation is always at the anode and reduction at the cathode; do not rely only on electrode signs. Application: Galvanic-cell principles underpin batteries, sensors and corrosion measurements.

Relationship

Ecell = Ecathode - Eanode

Correction / limitation

Application

Galvanic-cell principles underpin batteries, sensors and corrosion measurements.

Concept

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction.

Theory

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction. The power supply pushes electrons, while ions migrate to electrodes. Deposited or released amount is proportional to charge passed. Worked case: passing 193000 C through Cu2+ solution supplies 2 mol electrons and ideally deposits 1 mol copper. Interpretation and limits: Electrode signs differ from a galvanic cell, but oxidation remains at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Application: Electrolysis is used for plating, metal refining, chemical manufacture and hydrogen production.

Concept

The Nernst equation gives electrode or cell potential under nonstandard conditions.

Theory

The Nernst equation gives electrode or cell potential under nonstandard conditions. Potential depends logarithmically on reaction quotient and approaches zero at equilibrium for the full cell. Temperature and electron count must be specified. Worked case: at 298 K, E = Estandard - (0.05916/n)log Q; increasing product activity lowers E for the written cell reaction. Interpretation and limits: Construct Q from the balanced cell reaction and omit pure solids and liquids. Application: The Nernst equation supports concentration sensors, batteries, pH electrodes and equilibrium calculations.

Concept

Electromotive force is the maximum potential difference of a cell when essentially no current flows.

Theory

Electromotive force is the maximum potential difference of a cell when essentially no current flows. Positive Ecell for the written reaction indicates a spontaneous galvanic process under those conditions and connects directly with Gibbs free energy. Worked case: if Ecathode = +0.34 V and Eanode reduction potential = -0.76 V, Ecell = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V. Interpretation and limits: EMF is a voltage, not a mechanical force, and standard potentials are not multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients. Application: EMF determines battery voltage, sensor response and available electrical work.

Electrochemistry · Electrolytic conductivityexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: a solution has R = 250 ohm in a cell with cell constant 1.25 cm-1. G = 0.00400 S and kappa = 0.00400 x 1.25 = 5.00 x 10^-3 S cm-1. Key check: after solving Electrolytic conductivity, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Conductivity measures the ability of an electrolyte solution to carry current through moving ions; it depends on ion concentration, charge and mobility.

Theory

Conductivity measures the ability of an electrolyte solution to carry current through moving ions; it depends on ion concentration, charge and mobility. Resistance R is measured between electrodes. Conductance G = 1/R, while conductivity kappa = G(l/A), where l/A is the cell constant. Conductivity usually decreases on dilution because fewer ions occupy each unit volume, even though individual ions may move more freely. Worked case: a solution has R = 250 ohm in a cell with cell constant 1.25 cm-1. G = 0.00400 S and kappa = 0.00400 x 1.25 = 5.00 x 10^-3 S cm-1. Interpretation and limits: Do not use conductance and conductivity as synonyms: conductance depends on cell geometry, whereas conductivity is a property of the solution at a stated temperature. Application: Conductivity measurements monitor water purity, salinity, ionic reactions, batteries and industrial process streams.

Worked case

a solution has R = 250 ohm in a cell with cell constant 1.25 cm-1. G = 0.00400 S and kappa = 0.00400 x 1.25 = 5.00 x 10^-3 S cm-1.

Relationship

G = 1/R; kappa = G x cell constant; cell constant = l/A

Correction / limitation

Do not use conductance and conductivity as synonyms: conductance depends on cell geometry, whereas conductivity is a property of the solution at a stated temperature.

Application

Conductivity measurements monitor water purity, salinity, ionic reactions, batteries and industrial process streams.

  3. G = 1/R; kappa = G x cell constant; cell constant = l/A
  4. Resistance R is measured between electrodes.
  5. Conductance G = 1/R, while conductivity kappa = G(l/A), where l/A is the cell constant.
  6. Conductivity usually decreases on dilution because fewer ions occupy each unit volume, even though individual ions may move more freely.
Electrochemistry · Molar conductivity and Kohlrausch lawexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: Lambda°m(CH3COOH) = Lambda°m(HCl) + Lambda°m(CH3COONa) - Lambda°m(NaCl). Using 426.0, 91.0 and 126.4 S cm2 mol-1 gives 390.6 S cm2 mol-1. Key check: after solving Molar conductivity and Kohlrausch law, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Molar conductivity is the conductance contribution of the ions produced by one mole of electrolyte and approaches a limiting value at infinite dilution.

Theory

Molar conductivity is the conductance contribution of the ions produced by one mole of electrolyte and approaches a limiting value at infinite dilution. Lambda_m = kappa x 1000/C when kappa is in S cm-1 and C is in mol L-1. Strong electrolytes rise gradually on dilution; weak electrolytes rise sharply as ionisation increases. Kohlrausch's law states that at infinite dilution each ion contributes independently, allowing limiting values for weak electrolytes to be assembled from strong-electrolyte data. Worked case: Lambda°m(CH3COOH) = Lambda°m(HCl) + Lambda°m(CH3COONa) - Lambda°m(NaCl). Using 426.0, 91.0 and 126.4 S cm2 mol-1 gives 390.6 S cm2 mol-1. Interpretation and limits: Do not extrapolate weak-electrolyte data as a straight line or forget to use compatible concentration and conductivity units. Application: Kohlrausch's law supports weak-electrolyte dissociation constants, sparingly soluble salt solubilities and electrolyte quality control.

Worked case

Lambda°m(CH3COOH) = Lambda°m(HCl) + Lambda°m(CH3COONa) - Lambda°m(NaCl). Using 426.0, 91.0 and 126.4 S cm2 mol-1 gives 390.6 S cm2 mol-1.

Relationship

Lambda_m = kappa x 1000/C; Kohlrausch: Lambda°m = sum(nu_i lambda°_i)

Correction / limitation

Do not extrapolate weak-electrolyte data as a straight line or forget to use compatible concentration and conductivity units.

Application

Kohlrausch's law supports weak-electrolyte dissociation constants, sparingly soluble salt solubilities and electrolyte quality control.

Concept

Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

Theory

Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers. Protons have charge +1 and neutrons have charge 0 in the nucleus; electrons have charge -1 and occupy the surrounding electron cloud. Protons and neutrons are much more massive than electrons. They have similar chemical behavior because they have the same electron arrangement, but their masses and nuclear stability can differ. Worked case: a neutral carbon-12 atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons. Example: carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively. Interpretation and limits: Do not say neutrons have no mass; they have no electrical charge. Isotopes are not different elements because their atomic numbers are the same. Application: Subatomic particles explain ions, isotopes, electricity and nuclear reactions. Isotopes are used in medical imaging, cancer treatment, dating and chemical tracing.

Concept

Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus. Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.

Theory

Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus. Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. It is a whole number written A. Electrons contribute so little mass that they are not counted in the mass number. It is written Z and uniquely identifies an element. Changing the number of electrons makes an ion, but changing the proton count makes a different element. Worked case: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23. Example: every oxygen atom has Z = 8, so it contains 8 protons. Interpretation and limits: Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table. Atomic number is not the number of neutrons or the total number of particles. Application: Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers. Atomic number organizes the modern periodic table and identifies elements in analysis.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table. Atomic number is not the number of neutrons or the total number of particles.

Application

Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers. Atomic number organizes the modern periodic table and identifies elements in analysis.

Concept

Nuclear stability depends on neutron-to-proton balance, pairing and binding energy rather than ordinary chemical bonding.

Theory

Nuclear stability depends on neutron-to-proton balance, pairing and binding energy rather than ordinary chemical bonding. Nuclides outside stable combinations can undergo radioactive transformation. A larger neutron number does not automatically make a nucleus more stable, and chemical oxidation state is not a nuclear stability test. Worked case: Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons and is stable. Carbon-14 has six protons and eight neutrons and undergoes beta-minus decay to nitrogen-14, conserving nucleon number and charge when the emitted particles are included. Interpretation and limits: Isotopes of the same element can have very different nuclear stability despite similar chemical behaviour. Application: Radiocarbon dating uses the decay of carbon-14 rather than any change in ordinary carbon bonding.

Worked case

Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons and is stable. Carbon-14 has six protons and eight neutrons and undergoes beta-minus decay to nitrogen-14, conserving nucleon number and charge when the emitted particles are included.

Correction / limitation

Concept

A nuclear equation tracks changes in nuclides and emitted particles while conserving mass number and charge.

Theory

A nuclear equation tracks changes in nuclides and emitted particles while conserving mass number and charge. Write both mass number A and atomic number Z for every nuclear species. An alpha particle contributes A = 4 and Z = 2, while a beta-minus electron contributes A = 0 and Z = -1. Worked case: For 238U alpha decay, subtract four from 238 and two from 92 to obtain 234Th. The equation is 238U -> 234Th + 4He, with 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2. Interpretation and limits: Do not balance a nuclear equation using only element symbols; nucleon number and charge must both balance. Application: Balanced decay equations identify daughter nuclides and support interpretation of decay chains.

Worked case

For 238U alpha decay, subtract four from 238 and two from 92 to obtain 234Th. The equation is 238U -> 234Th + 4He, with 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2.

sum of A and sum of Z are conserved

Correction / limitation

Do not balance a nuclear equation using only element symbols; nucleon number and charge must both balance.

Application

Balanced decay equations identify daughter nuclides and support interpretation of decay chains.

Concept

Mass defect is the difference between the summed masses of separated nucleons and the bound nucleus.

Theory

Mass defect is the difference between the summed masses of separated nucleons and the bound nucleus. The missing rest mass corresponds to nuclear binding energy. Nuclear masses and atomic masses require consistent accounting for electrons when used in a calculation. Worked case: A nucleus with a mass defect of 0.0100 u has a binding energy of 0.0100 x 931.5 = 9.315 MeV. The positive binding energy is the energy required to separate that nucleus into its nucleons. Interpretation and limits: A mass defect is not an error in the balance, and u must be converted consistently before using SI energy units. Application: Mass measurements permit quantitative comparisons of nuclear binding and reaction energy release.

Worked case: If a nucleus with 12 nucleons has total binding energy 92 MeV, its binding energy per nucleon is 92/12 = 7.67 MeV. Compare that quotient rather than 92 MeV alone with another nucleus. Application: Binding-energy comparisons explain why certain fission and fusion reactions release energy.

Concept

An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of elements in a compound. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each type of atom in one molecule.

Theory

An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of elements in a compound. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each type of atom in one molecule. Convert each element's mass or percentage to moles, divide by the smallest amount and scale to whole numbers. It is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found by comparing molar mass with empirical-formula mass. Worked case: 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O gives mole ratio about 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is CH2O. Example: CH2O has empirical mass 30 g/mol; if the compound's molar mass is 180 g/mol, n = 6 and the formula is C6H12O6. Interpretation and limits: Do not use mass ratios directly as subscripts; convert each mass to moles first. The multiplier n must be a positive whole number within experimental uncertainty. Application: Empirical formulas help identify unknown substances from composition data. Molecular formulas support substance identification, structure determination and reaction calculations.

40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O gives mole ratio about 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is CH2O. Example: CH2O has empirical mass 30 g/mol; if the compound's molar mass is 180 g/mol, n = 6 and the formula is C6H12O6.

Relationship

empirical subscripts = simplest mole ratio molecular formula = (empirical formula)n; n = molar mass / empirical mass

Correction / limitation

Do not use mass ratios directly as subscripts; convert each mass to moles first. The multiplier n must be a positive whole number within experimental uncertainty.

Application

Concept

Molarity is the number of moles of solute per litre of solution. Molality is the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Mole fraction is the fraction of total moles contributed by one component.

Theory

Molarity is the number of moles of solute per litre of solution. Molality is the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Mole fraction is the fraction of total moles contributed by one component. Because solution volume changes with temperature, molarity is temperature dependent. Volumetric glassware is used to prepare accurate molar solutions. It depends on mass rather than volume and therefore does not change with temperature. It is useful for colligative properties. It is dimensionless, lies between zero and one, and all component mole fractions sum to one. Worked case: 0.50 mol NaCl made up to 2.00 L of solution has molarity 0.250 mol/L. Identify the given quantities or particles, apply the relationship, and check units and chemical meaning. Example: 0.20 mol glucose dissolved in 0.50 kg water gives molality 0.40 mol/kg. Example: a mixture of 2 mol ethanol and 3 mol water has ethanol mole fraction 2/(2+3) = 0.40. Interpretation and limits: Use final solution volume, not the initial solvent volume, and convert millilitres to litres. The denominator is mass of solvent, not mass of the whole solution. Use moles rather than masses directly, and include every component in the total. Application: Molarity is used in reaction calculations, titrations and laboratory preparation. Molality is used for boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and precise thermal work. Mole fraction is used in gas mixtures, vapour-liquid equilibrium and solution thermodynamics.

0.50 mol NaCl made up to 2.00 L of solution has molarity 0.250 mol/L. Identify the given quantities or particles, apply the relationship, and check units and chemical meaning. Example: 0.20 mol glucose dissolved in 0.50 kg water gives molality 0.40 mol/kg. Example: a mixture of 2 mol ethanol and 3 mol water has ethanol mole fraction 2/(2+3) = 0.40.

Relationship

M = moles of solute / litres of solution m = moles of solute / kilograms of solvent xi = ni / total moles; sum xi = 1

Correction / limitation

Use final solution volume, not the initial solvent volume, and convert millilitres to litres. The denominator is mass of solvent, not mass of the whole solution. Use moles rather than masses directly, and include every component in the total.

Application

Molarity is used in reaction calculations, titrations and laboratory preparation. Molality is used for boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and precise thermal work. Mole fraction is used in gas mixtures, vapour-liquid equilibrium and solution thermodynamics.
