Concept

Equivalent mass is molar mass divided by the reaction-specific number of transferable charges or reacting equivalents.

Theory

Equivalent mass is molar mass divided by the reaction-specific number of transferable charges or reacting equivalents. The n-factor depends on the stated reaction. An acid's equivalent mass cannot be assigned without specifying how many protons react in that process. Worked case: For complete neutralisation of both protons of H2SO4, equivalent mass = 98/2 = 49 g per equivalent. If only one proton is neutralised in the stated reaction, the corresponding value is 98 g per equivalent. Interpretation and limits: The n-factor is not always the number of hydrogen atoms written in a formula. Application: Reaction-specific equivalents simplify stoichiometric comparison in acid-base and redox titration calculations.

Worked case

For complete neutralisation of both protons of H2SO4, equivalent mass = 98/2 = 49 g per equivalent. If only one proton is neutralised in the stated reaction, the corresponding value is 98 g per equivalent.

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: if [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹, pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3. Concept

The photoelectric effect ejects electrons from a material when photon energy exceeds its work function.

Theory

The photoelectric effect ejects electrons from a material when photon energy exceeds its work function. Increasing intensity supplies more photons but does not compensate for photon energy below threshold. Above threshold, the maximum electron kinetic energy depends on frequency. Worked case: If a photon carries 5.0 eV and the work function is 2.0 eV, the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy is 3.0 eV. A 1.5 eV photon cannot eject an electron from that surface regardless of beam intensity in this model. Interpretation and limits: Brightness is not the same as photon frequency, and threshold energy must be exceeded. Application: Photoelectron measurements connect electronic binding energies with incident photon energies.

Worked case

Relationship

Kmax = h nu - work function

Correction / limitation

Brightness is not the same as photon frequency, and threshold energy must be exceeded.

Application

Photoelectron measurements connect electronic binding energies with incident photon energies.

Concept

A particle with momentum p has de Broglie wavelength h/p.

Theory

A particle with momentum p has de Broglie wavelength h/p. Matter-wave wavelength decreases as momentum increases. The nonrelativistic substitution p = mv is valid only when the particle speed is sufficiently below the speed of light. Worked case: If an electron's momentum doubles, its de Broglie wavelength halves because h is constant. A particle with p = 6.626 x 10^-24 kg m/s has wavelength 1.00 x 10^-10 m. Interpretation and limits: Do not use a light-wave speed in p = mv for an electron, or confuse momentum with kinetic energy. Application: Electron diffraction uses matter-wave wavelengths comparable to atomic spacings.

Worked case

Correction / limitation

Do not use a light-wave speed in p = mv for an electron, or confuse momentum with kinetic energy.

Application

Concept

Position and momentum cannot simultaneously have arbitrarily narrow distributions in a quantum state.

Theory

Position and momentum cannot simultaneously have arbitrarily narrow distributions in a quantum state. The relation concerns intrinsic quantum spreads, not merely poor measuring instruments. Position-momentum uncertainty must be distinguished from uncertainty in macroscopic instrument readings. Worked case: An electron localized to a smaller spatial region requires a broader spread of momentum components. Halving a position uncertainty requires the lower bound on momentum uncertainty to double. Interpretation and limits: An improved microscope does not remove the intrinsic position-momentum uncertainty relation. Application: Quantum confinement links localization of electrons to increased kinetic-energy scales.

Worked case

An electron localized to a smaller spatial region requires a broader spread of momentum components. Halving a position uncertainty requires the lower bound on momentum uncertainty to double.

Relationship

Delta x Delta p >= hbar/2

Correction / limitation

An improved microscope does not remove the intrinsic position-momentum uncertainty relation.

Application

Quantum confinement links localization of electrons to increased kinetic-energy scales.

Concept

An orbital is a three-dimensional probability region that can hold at most two electrons. Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom.

Theory

An orbital is a three-dimensional probability region that can hold at most two electrons. Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom. Orbitals are not fixed paths. The s subshell has one orbital, p has three, d has five and f has seven; their shapes and orientations affect bonding. The principal number n identifies shell and energy, l identifies subshell shape, ml identifies orbital orientation, and ms identifies spin. Only allowed combinations describe possible electron states. Worked case: the three 2p orbitals have equal energy in an isolated atom and together can hold six electrons. Example: an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse an orbital with a shell; a shell contains one or more subshells and many orbitals. Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n. Application: Orbital shapes explain bond direction, molecular geometry, spectra and periodic trends. Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior.

Worked case

the three 2p orbitals have equal energy in an isolated atom and together can hold six electrons. Example: an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2.

Relationship

maximum electrons in a subshell = 2(2l + 1) n = 1,2,...; l = 0 to n-1; ml = -l to +l; ms = +/-1/2

Correction / limitation

Do not confuse an orbital with a shell; a shell contains one or more subshells and many orbitals. Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n.

Application

Orbital shapes explain bond direction, molecular geometry, spectra and periodic trends. Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior.

Concept

Hybridization is a model that mixes atomic orbitals on one atom into directed bonding orbitals.

Theory

Hybridization is a model that mixes atomic orbitals on one atom into directed bonding orbitals. Common sets are sp for two domains, sp2 for three and sp3 for four. The model connects Lewis structures with sigma-bond geometry. Worked case: carbon in methane is described as sp3 hybridized, giving four equivalent orbitals directed tetrahedrally. Interpretation and limits: Hybridization is a bonding model, not a physical stirring of orbitals, and pi bonds use unhybridized orbitals. Application: Hybridization helps explain geometry, bond angles and multiple bonding in organic molecules.

Worked case

carbon in methane is described as sp3 hybridized, giving four equivalent orbitals directed tetrahedrally.

Relationship

steric number 2 -> sp; 3 -> sp2; 4 -> sp3

Correction / limitation

Hybridization is a bonding model, not a physical stirring of orbitals, and pi bonds use unhybridized orbitals.

Application

Hybridization helps explain geometry, bond angles and multiple bonding in organic molecules.

Previous worked example

The domains point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles close to 109.5°. The symmetric molecule is non-polar overall. Key check: after solving Bond order and magnetism, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Molecular orbital occupancy determines bond order and whether a molecule has unpaired electrons.

Theory

Molecular orbital occupancy determines bond order and whether a molecule has unpaired electrons. Bond order counts the difference between bonding and antibonding electrons divided by two. Paramagnetism requires unpaired electrons, not simply an odd atomic number somewhere in a formula. Worked case: In O2, two electrons occupy separate degenerate pi-star orbitals. The molecular orbital count gives bond order 2 and two unpaired electrons, so O2 is paramagnetic despite having a double bond. Interpretation and limits: A Lewis double-bond drawing by itself does not describe the observed magnetic behaviour of O2. Application: Magnetic measurements help test molecular orbital descriptions of small molecules.

Worked case

In O2, two electrons occupy separate degenerate pi-star orbitals. The molecular orbital count gives bond order 2 and two unpaired electrons, so O2 is paramagnetic despite having a double bond.

Relationship

bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons)/2

Correction / limitation

A Lewis double-bond drawing by itself does not describe the observed magnetic behaviour of O2.

Application

Magnetic measurements help test molecular orbital descriptions of small molecules.

Concept

A small highly charged cation can polarize a large polarizable anion and increase covalent character.

Theory

A small highly charged cation can polarize a large polarizable anion and increase covalent character. Polarizing power increases with cation charge density, while anion polarizability tends to increase with size. These are qualitative trends rather than an equation assigning an exact covalent percentage. Worked case: Comparing anhydrous AlCl3 with NaCl, Al3+ has much greater polarizing power than Na+. Greater distortion of chloride electron density helps explain the stronger covalent character of AlCl3. Interpretation and limits: Formal ionic charges do not guarantee purely ionic bonding, and the rules do not predict an exact melting point. Application: Polarization arguments help explain bonding trends across metal halides.

Worked case

Comparing anhydrous AlCl3 with NaCl, Al3+ has much greater polarizing power than Na+. Greater distortion of chloride electron density helps explain the stronger covalent character of AlCl3.

Relationship

small highly charged cation + polarizable anion -> increased covalent character

Correction / limitation

Formal ionic charges do not guarantee purely ionic bonding, and the rules do not predict an exact melting point.

Application

Polarization arguments help explain bonding trends across metal halides.

Concept

Hydrides contain hydrogen bonded to other elements, with bonding ranging from ionic to covalent and metallic.

Theory

Hydrides contain hydrogen bonded to other elements, with bonding ranging from ionic to covalent and metallic. Saline hydrides such as sodium hydride behave as strong proton acceptors, whereas molecular hydrides have element-dependent structures and reactivity. The name hydride does not identify one universal reaction type. Worked case: NaH reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide and hydrogen: NaH + H2O -> NaOH + H2. This reflects hydride-ion protonation, not a hydrogen-bonding interaction between two neutral molecules. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse hydride bonding with intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Application: Hydrides are used as reagents and as components of hydrogen-related materials.

Concept

Certain diagonally adjacent elements in the periodic table show similarities because opposing size and charge trends partly compensate.

Theory

Certain diagonally adjacent elements in the periodic table show similarities because opposing size and charge trends partly compensate. Lithium and magnesium are a common comparison. Similar charge-density effects can produce similarities in compound behaviour even though the elements belong to different groups. Worked case: Lithium carbonate and magnesium carbonate decompose on heating, unlike the more thermally stable carbonates of the heavier alkali metals under comparable conditions. This is one example of a diagonal relationship, not identical chemistry in every reaction. Interpretation and limits: A diagonal relationship does not place lithium and magnesium in the same group or give them identical valence electrons. Application: Comparing related compounds reveals where simple group trends require qualification.

Concept

The uses of sodium and calcium compounds depend on the identities of the ions and the chemical reactions they undergo.

Theory

The uses of sodium and calcium compounds depend on the identities of the ions and the chemical reactions they undergo. Sodium carbonate is a basic salt used in glass manufacture; calcium carbonate decomposes to calcium oxide on strong heating. Calcium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to form a carbonate precipitate. Worked case: Passing CO2 into limewater forms white CaCO3: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. Excess CO2 can dissolve the precipitate by forming soluble hydrogencarbonate species. Interpretation and limits: Calcium carbonate, calcium oxide and calcium hydroxide are different substances and are not interchangeable formulas. Application: Limestone and lime chemistry connect construction materials, water treatment and industrial processing.

Groups 13 and 14 show changes in bonding and oxidation-state stability down each group. Boron is commonly electron-deficient in its compounds; carbon forms strong multiple bonds. The relative stability of lower oxidation states often increases down the heavier p-block elements because the ns2 pair participates less readily. Worked case: Compare carbon dioxide with lead(II) oxide: carbon commonly displays +4 in CO2, while +2 is especially important for lead. The comparison illustrates an oxidation-state trend rather than a rule that every group-14 compound has the same oxidation state. Interpretation and limits: The group number does not force one oxidation state in every compound. Application: Boron compounds, aluminium materials and silicon-based materials illustrate diverse p-block bonding.

Concept

Halogens are reactive group-17 elements whose atoms commonly gain one electron or share one covalent bond.

Theory

Halogens are reactive group-17 elements whose atoms commonly gain one electron or share one covalent bond. Their elemental oxidizing power generally decreases down the group under comparable aqueous conditions. Halide ions have different properties from the corresponding elemental halogens. Worked case: Chlorine added to aqueous bromide oxidizes Br- to Br2: Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2. Bromine does not similarly displace chloride under ordinary conditions. Interpretation and limits: Chlorine gas and chloride ions are not the same material and do not have the same hazards. Application: Halogen displacement reactions help compare oxidizing strength and identify halide chemistry.

Concept

Noble gases have filled valence shells and generally low chemical reactivity, although heavier members can form compounds.

Theory

Noble gases have filled valence shells and generally low chemical reactivity, although heavier members can form compounds. Closed-shell configurations make electron removal difficult. Xenon compounds show that chemical inertness is relative, especially with strongly oxidizing reactants. Worked case: XeF2 is a real xenon compound with a linear molecular shape. Interpretation and limits: Do not interpret noble-gas classification as proof that all noble gases are chemically incapable of forming compounds. Concept

Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals.

Theory

Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals. Electrons are placed in available low-energy states while obeying Aufbau filling, Hund's rule and the Pauli principle. Valence electrons largely control chemical behavior. Worked case: oxygen has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4; its six valence electrons explain its common valency of two. Interpretation and limits: Do not exceed subshell capacities: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14 electrons. Application: Configurations predict ion formation, bonding, magnetism and an element's position in the periodic table.

Worked case

oxygen has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4; its six valence electrons explain its common valency of two.

Relationship

total superscripts in a neutral atom = atomic number

Correction / limitation

Application

Configurations predict ion formation, bonding, magnetism and an element's position in the periodic table.

Key check: after solving Oxidation states and color, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate are strongly coloured transition-metal oxidants whose products depend on reaction conditions.

Theory

Potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate are strongly coloured transition-metal oxidants whose products depend on reaction conditions. Acidified dichromate, Cr2O7^2-, is reduced from Cr(VI) to green Cr3+; acidified permanganate, MnO4-, is reduced from Mn(VII) to nearly colourless Mn2+. In neutral or weakly alkaline medium permanganate commonly forms brown MnO2. Preparation, colour changes and balanced ionic equations are central board requirements. Worked case: MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O. One mole permanganate oxidises five moles Fe2+ in acid solution and acts as its own indicator in titration. Interpretation and limits: Do not write the same permanganate reduction product for acidic, neutral and strongly alkaline media; the medium controls the manganese product. Application: Dichromate and permanganate chemistry is used in redox analysis, synthesis, water testing and oxidation-process control.

Worked case

MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O. One mole permanganate oxidises five moles Fe2+ in acid solution and acts as its own indicator in titration.

Relationship

Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O; MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O

Correction / limitation

Do not write the same permanganate reduction product for acidic, neutral and strongly alkaline media; the medium controls the manganese product.

Application

Dichromate and permanganate chemistry is used in redox analysis, synthesis, water testing and oxidation-process control.

Concept

Unpaired electrons contribute to paramagnetism, while paired-electron contributions are generally diamagnetic.

Theory

Unpaired electrons contribute to paramagnetism, while paired-electron contributions are generally diamagnetic. For a simple first-row transition-metal ion with largely quenched orbital angular momentum, the spin-only estimate depends on the number n of unpaired electrons. More complete treatments may require orbital and exchange effects. Worked case: High-spin Fe3+ is d5 with five unpaired electrons. Its spin-only magnetic moment is sqrt(5 x 7) = 5.92 Bohr magnetons, whereas a low-spin d6 ion has no unpaired electrons in an octahedral field. Interpretation and limits: Oxidation state alone does not determine spin state; ligand field and geometry also matter. Application: Magnetic susceptibility measurements help distinguish possible electronic configurations of metal complexes.

Worked case

High-spin Fe3+ is d5 with five unpaired electrons. Its spin-only magnetic moment is sqrt(5 x 7) = 5.92 Bohr magnetons, whereas a low-spin d6 ion has no unpaired electrons in an octahedral field.

Relationship

mu spin-only = sqrt(n(n+2)) Bohr magnetons

Correction / limitation

Oxidation state alone does not determine spin state; ligand field and geometry also matter.

Application

Magnetic susceptibility measurements help distinguish possible electronic configurations of metal complexes.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, six CN⁻ ligands contribute −6 overall. Concept

Lanthanoid contraction is the progressive decrease in lanthanoid ionic size associated with increasing nuclear charge and incomplete 4f shielding.

Theory

Lanthanoid contraction is the progressive decrease in lanthanoid ionic size associated with increasing nuclear charge and incomplete 4f shielding. The size trend affects later transition elements and makes some pairs chemically similar. It is not caused by removal of a whole electron shell across the series. Worked case: Zirconium and hafnium have unusually similar radii and chemistry because the intervening lanthanoids contract. Their separation is therefore more difficult than a simple period-based size argument would suggest. Interpretation and limits: Do not predict that hafnium must be much larger than zirconium solely because it is one period lower. Application: The contraction explains similarities that complicate separation of lanthanoids and zirconium-hafnium mixtures.

Worked case

Zirconium and hafnium have unusually similar radii and chemistry because the intervening lanthanoids contract. Their separation is therefore more difficult than a simple period-based size argument would suggest.

Relationship

increasing effective nuclear attraction contracts the 4f series

Correction / limitation

Do not predict that hafnium must be much larger than zirconium solely because it is one period lower.

Application

The contraction explains similarities that complicate separation of lanthanoids and zirconium-hafnium mixtures.

Concept

Actinoids involve filling of 5f-derived states and often show several accessible oxidation states.

Theory

Actinoids involve filling of 5f-derived states and often show several accessible oxidation states. All actinoid elements are radioactive, but their half-lives, chemical behaviour and practical handling requirements differ greatly. The 5f orbitals can participate in bonding more extensively than a simple inner-core picture suggests. Worked case: Uranium occurs in both +4 and +6 oxidation states; the uranyl ion UO2(2+) contains uranium(VI). Changing oxidation state can change solubility and therefore the design of a separation process. Interpretation and limits: Radioactivity does not imply that all actinoids have identical chemistry or identical decay rates. Application: Actinoid redox and coordination chemistry are important in environmental transport and specialized nuclear-material separations.

Worked case

Uranium occurs in both +4 and +6 oxidation states; the uranyl ion UO2(2+) contains uranium(VI). Changing oxidation state can change solubility and therefore the design of a separation process.

Relationship

actinoid chemistry depends strongly on oxidation state and ligand environment

Correction / limitation

Radioactivity does not imply that all actinoids have identical chemistry or identical decay rates.

Application

Actinoid redox and coordination chemistry are important in environmental transport and specialized nuclear-material separations.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, six CN⁻ ligands contribute −6 overall. Concept

Werner distinguished a metal's primary valence from its secondary valence to explain coordination compounds.

Theory

Werner distinguished a metal's primary valence from its secondary valence to explain coordination compounds. Primary valence corresponds to oxidation state, while secondary valence corresponds to coordination number and directed ligand positions. Counterions lie outside the coordination sphere. Worked case: [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 contains a cobalt(III) centre coordinated by six neutral ammonia ligands and three external chloride counterions. Ionization yields one complex cation and three chloride ions. Interpretation and limits: Do not count external chloride counterions as ligands merely because they appear in the formula. Application: Werner's distinction explains conductivity and precipitation evidence for coordination-sphere formulations.

Worked case

[Co(NH3)6]Cl3 contains a cobalt(III) centre coordinated by six neutral ammonia ligands and three external chloride counterions. Ionization yields one complex cation and three chloride ions.

Relationship

oxidation state differs from coordination number

Correction / limitation

Do not count external chloride counterions as ligands merely because they appear in the formula.

Application

Werner's distinction explains conductivity and precipitation evidence for coordination-sphere formulations.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, six CN⁻ ligands contribute −6 overall. Concept

Ligands donate electron pairs to a central atom or ion, and nomenclature identifies ligand identities and the metal's oxidation state.

Theory

Ligands donate electron pairs to a central atom or ion, and nomenclature identifies ligand identities and the metal's oxidation state. Denticity counts donor atoms from one ligand that bind to the metal. Coordination number counts donor atoms attached overall, not the number of separate ligand molecules. Worked case: In [Co(en)3]3+, each ethane-1,2-diamine ligand binds through two nitrogen atoms. Three ligands therefore give coordination number six; neutral en leaves cobalt at oxidation state +3. Interpretation and limits: Three bidentate ligands do not imply coordination number three. Application: Clear complex names and denticity assignments support comparison of structures and metal-binding agents.

Worked case

In [Co(en)3]3+, each ethane-1,2-diamine ligand binds through two nitrogen atoms. Three ligands therefore give coordination number six; neutral en leaves cobalt at oxidation state +3.

Relationship

coordination number = total bound donor atoms

Correction / limitation

Three bidentate ligands do not imply coordination number three.

Application

Clear complex names and denticity assignments support comparison of structures and metal-binding agents.

Concept

Coordination compounds can share a formula but differ in ligand connectivity or spatial arrangement.

Theory

Coordination compounds can share a formula but differ in ligand connectivity or spatial arrangement. Geometrical isomerism concerns positions such as cis and trans; optical isomerism concerns non-superimposable mirror images. Linkage isomers involve ambidentate ligands attaching through different atoms. Worked case: Square-planar [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] has cis and trans forms. In the cis form the chloride ligands occupy adjacent positions, whereas in the trans form they are opposite. Interpretation and limits: Cis and trans compounds have the same formula but need not have the same reactivity or biological effects. Application: Structure-dependent activity makes isomer identification important in coordination and medicinal chemistry.

Worked case

Coordination Compounds · Bonding in metal carbonylsexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: Ni in Ni(CO)4 has oxidation state zero. Nickel contributes 10 valence electrons and four neutral CO ligands donate 8, giving an 18-electron tetrahedral complex. Key check: after solving Bonding in metal carbonyls, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Metal carbonyl bonding is synergic: carbon monoxide donates a lone pair to the metal while the metal back-donates d-electron density into CO antibonding orbitals.

Theory

Metal carbonyl bonding is synergic: carbon monoxide donates a lone pair to the metal while the metal back-donates d-electron density into CO antibonding orbitals. Sigma donation forms M<-CO bonding and pi back-bonding strengthens M-C while weakening C-O. Greater back-donation lowers the C-O stretching frequency. Electron counting explains stable examples such as Ni(CO)4 and Fe(CO)5, while bridging and terminal carbonyls differ structurally and spectroscopically. Worked case: Ni in Ni(CO)4 has oxidation state zero. Nickel contributes 10 valence electrons and four neutral CO ligands donate 8, giving an 18-electron tetrahedral complex. Interpretation and limits: Do not describe the M-C bond as donation in only one direction, and do not assign CO a negative charge in ordinary neutral carbonyl electron counting. Application: Metal carbonyl bonding underlies homogeneous catalysis, metal purification and interpretation of infrared spectra.

Worked case

Ni in Ni(CO)4 has oxidation state zero. Nickel contributes 10 valence electrons and four neutral CO ligands donate 8, giving an 18-electron tetrahedral complex.

Relationship

M <- :CO sigma donation; M(dpi) -> CO(pi*) back-donation; 18-electron count

Correction / limitation

Concept

Theory

Formation constants describe thermodynamic preference for a metal-ligand complex under specified conditions. Thermodynamic stability must be distinguished from substitution rate. Worked case: EDTA binds many metal ions in a 1:1 metal-to-ligand ratio. Concept

Inductive, resonance and hyperconjugative effects redistribute electron density and influence organic reactivity.

Theory

Inductive, resonance and hyperconjugative effects redistribute electron density and influence organic reactivity. The inductive effect is transmitted through sigma bonds, while resonance requires an appropriate conjugated orbital arrangement. These mechanisms should not be used as interchangeable labels. Worked case: The chloroacetate ion is more stabilized than acetate by the electron-withdrawing effect of chlorine through sigma bonds, helping explain why chloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic acid. Interpretation and limits: Do not draw resonance through an intervening saturated atom that breaks conjugation. Application: Electronic effects help compare acid strengths, carbocation stability and substituent-directed reactions.

Concept

A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and a Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton. A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base donates an electron pair.

Theory

A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and a Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton. A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base donates an electron pair. Each acid forms a conjugate base after donating H+, and each base forms a conjugate acid after accepting H+. This broad definition includes reactions without proton transfer, such as bond formation with electron-deficient molecules or metal ions. Worked case: NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-; NH3 accepts H+ and is the base, while water donates H+ and is the acid. Example: BF3 accepts a lone pair from NH3, so BF3 is a Lewis acid and NH3 is a Lewis base. Interpretation and limits: Identify proton transfer, not simply the presence of H or OH in a formula. Do not reverse donor and acceptor: the base donates the electron pair. Application: This theory explains buffers, biological proton transfer and non-hydroxide bases. Lewis theory explains coordination compounds, catalysts and many organic mechanisms.

HX addition generally follows Markovnikov's rule; HBr with peroxide is the important anti-Markovnikov exception. Ozonolysis identifies double-bond positions. Concept

Benzene is prepared by cyclic polymerisation, decarboxylation or reduction routes and characteristically undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution while retaining aromaticity.

Theory

Benzene is prepared by cyclic polymerisation, decarboxylation or reduction routes and characteristically undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution while retaining aromaticity. Nitration uses concentrated HNO3/H2SO4, sulphonation uses fuming H2SO4, halogenation uses FeX3 and Friedel-Crafts reactions use anhydrous AlCl3. Substituents direct later substitution according to electron donation or withdrawal. Addition occurs only under forcing conditions because aromatic stabilisation would be lost. Worked case: C6H6 + HNO3 --conc H2SO4--> C6H5NO2 + H2O. The electrophile is NO2+, generated by the acid mixture. Interpretation and limits: Do not draw benzene as an ordinary isolated triene or predict easy bromine-water decolourisation without a Lewis-acid catalyst. Application: Aromatic substitution produces dyes, pharmaceuticals, polymers and high-volume chemical intermediates.

Worked case

C6H6 + HNO3 --conc H2SO4--> C6H5NO2 + H2O. The electrophile is NO2+, generated by the acid mixture.

Relationship

benzene + E+ -> substituted benzene + H+; 3HCCH -> C6H6

Correction / limitation

Do not draw benzene as an ordinary isolated triene or predict easy bromine-water decolourisation without a Lewis-acid catalyst.

Application

Aromatic substitution produces dyes, pharmaceuticals, polymers and high-volume chemical intermediates.

  4. Nitration uses concentrated HNO3/H2SO4, sulphonation uses fuming H2SO4, halogenation uses FeX3 and Friedel-Crafts reactions use anhydrous AlCl3.

Key check: after solving Haloalkanes, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Haloalkanes are prepared from alcohols or hydrocarbons and undergo nucleophilic substitution, elimination and reactions with metals.

Theory

Haloalkanes are prepared from alcohols or hydrocarbons and undergo nucleophilic substitution, elimination and reactions with metals. Alcohols react with HX, PCl3/PCl5 or SOCl2; SOCl2 is convenient because gaseous by-products escape. SN1 is favoured by stable carbocations, polar protic solvent and tertiary substrates; SN2 is a one-step backside attack favoured by methyl or primary substrates. Alcoholic KOH promotes beta-elimination, while aqueous KOH promotes substitution. Worked case: CH3CH2Br + KOH(aq) -> CH3CH2OH + KBr, whereas CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc), heat -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O. Interpretation and limits: Do not ignore solvent and temperature when choosing substitution versus elimination, and do not assign SN2 to a tertiary carbon without severe steric consequences. Application: Haloalkanes are intermediates for alcohols, nitriles, amines, organometallic reagents and polymers.

Worked case

CH3CH2Br + KOH(aq) -> CH3CH2OH + KBr, whereas CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc), heat -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O.

Relationship

RX + OH- -> ROH + X-; RX + KOH(alc) -> alkene + KX + H2O

Correction / limitation

Do not ignore solvent and temperature when choosing substitution versus elimination, and do not assign SN2 to a tertiary carbon without severe steric consequences.

Application

Haloalkanes are intermediates for alcohols, nitriles, amines, organometallic reagents and polymers.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: propene reacts with HBr by protonation of the double bond followed by bromide attack. Concept

Haloarenes are made by aromatic halogenation or diazonium chemistry and are less reactive toward nucleophilic substitution than haloalkanes because the aryl C-X bond has partial double-bond character.

Theory

Haloarenes are made by aromatic halogenation or diazonium chemistry and are less reactive toward nucleophilic substitution than haloalkanes because the aryl C-X bond has partial double-bond character. Benzene reacts with Cl2/FeCl3 or Br2/FeBr3. Sandmeyer reactions replace an aryl diazonium group by Cl or Br using Cu(I) salts. Resonance, sp2 carbon and bond shortening resist ordinary SN1/SN2 pathways, though strong conditions or electron-withdrawing groups enable substitution. Worked case: C6H5N2+Cl- --CuCl--> C6H5Cl + N2. Chlorobenzene with NaOH at high temperature and pressure gives phenol after acidification. Interpretation and limits: Do not assume chlorobenzene reacts with aqueous hydroxide as readily as chloroethane; aryl and alkyl C-X bonds have different structures. Application: Haloarenes serve as intermediates in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, dyes and specialty polymers.

Worked case

C6H5N2+Cl- --CuCl--> C6H5Cl + N2. Chlorobenzene with NaOH at high temperature and pressure gives phenol after acidification.

Relationship

ArN2+ + CuX -> ArX + N2; ArX + NaOH --high T,P--> ArONa -> ArOH

Correction / limitation

Do not assume chlorobenzene reacts with aqueous hydroxide as readily as chloroethane; aryl and alkyl C-X bonds have different structures.

Application

Haloarenes serve as intermediates in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, dyes and specialty polymers.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: if [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹, pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3. The solution is acidic, and diluting it tenfold ideally raises the pH by about one unit. Key check: after solving Alcohols and phenols, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Phenol is prepared from haloarenes, diazonium salts or cumene and undergoes acidic and strongly activated electrophilic aromatic reactions.

Theory

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Phenol is prepared from haloarenes, diazonium salts or cumene and undergoes acidic and strongly activated electrophilic aromatic reactions. Alkenes hydrate to alcohols; aldehydes and ketones reduce to primary and secondary alcohols. Primary alcohol oxidation gives aldehydes then acids, secondary gives ketones, while tertiary alcohols resist mild oxidation. Concentrated acid causes dehydration, and carboxylic acids give esters reversibly. Phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised, making phenol more acidic than alcohols. The OH group activates ortho and para positions: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, dilute nitric acid gives o- and p-nitrophenols. Kolbe-Schmitt carboxylation gives salicylic acid and Reimer-Tiemann reaction gives salicylaldehyde. Worked case: CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O -> CH3COOH. With ethanoic acid and acid catalyst it forms ethyl ethanoate and water. Example: phenol + 3Br2(aq) -> 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate) + 3HBr; phenol dissolves in NaOH but not in NaHCO3. Interpretation and limits: Do not state that all alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids; the product depends on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary. Do not treat phenol as an ordinary alcohol; resonance changes both its acidity and the reactivity of its aromatic ring. Application: Alcohol reactions support solvents, fuels, antiseptics, fragrances, polymers and pharmaceutical synthesis. Phenol chemistry produces antiseptics, resins, dyes, aspirin precursors and polymer materials.

Worked case

CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O -> CH3COOH. With ethanoic acid and acid catalyst it forms ethyl ethanoate and water. Example: phenol + 3Br2(aq) -> 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate) + 3HBr; phenol dissolves in NaOH but not in NaHCO3.

Relationship

RCH2OH + [O] -> RCHO -> RCOOH; ROH + R'COOH <=> R'COOR + H2O C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O; phenoxide + CO2 -> salicylate

Correction / limitation

Do not state that all alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids; the product depends on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary. Do not treat phenol as an ordinary alcohol; resonance changes both its acidity and the reactivity of its aromatic ring.

Application

Alcohol reactions support solvents, fuels, antiseptics, fragrances, polymers and pharmaceutical synthesis. Phenol chemistry produces antiseptics, resins, dyes, aspirin precursors and polymer materials.

  4. phenol dissolves in NaOH but not in NaHCO3.
  5. RCH2OH + [O] -> RCHO -> RCOOH; ROH + R'COOH <=> R'COOR + H2O C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O; phenoxide + CO2 -> salicylate

Concept

Ethers are prepared by dehydration of alcohols or Williamson synthesis and generally react only under strong cleavage conditions.

Theory

Ethers are prepared by dehydration of alcohols or Williamson synthesis and generally react only under strong cleavage conditions. Williamson synthesis is an SN2 reaction between an alkoxide and a primary alkyl halide; tertiary halides tend to eliminate. Symmetrical ethers can form by intermolecular dehydration of primary alcohols near 413 K. Hot concentrated HI or HBr cleaves C-O bonds, with aryl-alkyl ethers cleaving on the alkyl side. Worked case: C2H5ONa + CH3I -> C2H5OCH3 + NaI. Anisole + HI gives phenol and CH3I rather than iodobenzene. Interpretation and limits: Do not choose a tertiary haloalkane for Williamson synthesis or predict cleavage of the aryl C-O bond in anisole under ordinary HI treatment. Application: Ethers are solvents, anaesthetic-related compounds, fuel additives and intermediates in organic synthesis.

Worked case

C2H5ONa + CH3I -> C2H5OCH3 + NaI. Anisole + HI gives phenol and CH3I rather than iodobenzene.

Relationship

RONa + R'X -> ROR' + NaX; ROR' + HI -> RI + R'OH

Correction / limitation

Do not choose a tertiary haloalkane for Williamson synthesis or predict cleavage of the aryl C-O bond in anisole under ordinary HI treatment.

Application

Ethers are solvents, anaesthetic-related compounds, fuel additives and intermediates in organic synthesis.

Carbonyl compounds are prepared by controlled oxidation or other functional-group conversions and undergo nucleophilic addition, reduction, oxidation and carbon-carbon bond-forming condensations.

Theory

Carbonyl compounds are prepared by controlled oxidation or other functional-group conversions and undergo nucleophilic addition, reduction, oxidation and carbon-carbon bond-forming condensations. Primary alcohols give aldehydes and secondary alcohols give ketones. Aldehydes oxidise readily with Tollens' or Fehling's reagent; ketones usually resist. Both add HCN and bisulphite, reduce to alcohols, and compounds with alpha-hydrogen undergo aldol condensation. Carbonyls lacking alpha-hydrogen may undergo Cannizzaro disproportionation. Worked case: 2CH3CHO --dilute NaOH--> CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO, which on heating loses water to form crotonaldehyde. Ethanal also gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Interpretation and limits: Do not use Tollens' oxidation as a universal ketone test, and check for alpha-hydrogen before choosing aldol versus Cannizzaro reaction. Application: Carbonyl chemistry is central to flavours, fragrances, pharmaceuticals, resins and carbon-carbon bond formation.

Concept

Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides.

Theory

Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides. Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes and hydrolysis of nitriles produce acids. Resonance stabilises carboxylate ions. Acids react with bicarbonate releasing CO2, esterify alcohols reversibly, and decarboxylate as sodium salts with soda lime. Electron-withdrawing substituents increase acidity. Worked case: CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O. CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O with H+ and heat. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst. Application: Carboxylic-acid derivatives occur in medicines, polymers, food preservatives, fats, soaps and fragrances.

Worked case

CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O. CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O with H+ and heat.

RCOOH + ROH <=> RCOOR + H2O; RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3

Correction / limitation

Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: propene reacts with HBr by protonation of the double bond followed by bromide attack. Key check: after solving Amines and Diazonium Salts, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Amines are prepared by reduction, ammonolysis, Gabriel synthesis or Hofmann bromamide degradation and react as bases and nucleophiles. Arenediazonium salts are prepared from primary aromatic amines at low temperature and replace the diazonium group by many substituents or form azo dyes.

Theory

Amines are prepared by reduction, ammonolysis, Gabriel synthesis or Hofmann bromamide degradation and react as bases and nucleophiles. Arenediazonium salts are prepared from primary aromatic amines at low temperature and replace the diazonium group by many substituents or form azo dyes. Nitro compounds, nitriles and amides can be reduced to amines. Gabriel synthesis gives pure primary alkyl amines; Hofmann degradation gives a primary amine with one fewer carbon. Basicity depends on electron donation, resonance, solvation and steric effects. Primary amines react with nitrous acid differently from aromatic primary amines. Aniline is diazotised using NaNO2/HCl at 273-278 K because diazonium salts decompose when warm. Sandmeyer and Gattermann reactions introduce Cl, Br or CN; KI introduces I, warm water gives phenol, hypophosphorous acid gives H, and coupling with activated rings gives coloured azo compounds. Worked case: CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> CH3NH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O. Aniline is less basic than methylamine because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring. Example: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl at 273-278 K -> C6H5N2+Cl- + NaCl + 2H2O; coupling with phenol in alkaline solution gives an orange azo dye. Interpretation and limits: Do not rank amine basicity from inductive effect alone; resonance and aqueous solvation can reverse a simple gas-phase prediction. Do not prepare or store arenediazonium salts at room temperature; maintain 273-278 K and distinguish diazotisation from azo coupling. Application: Amines are building blocks for medicines, dyes, surfactants, polymers and biological molecules. Diazonium chemistry connects aromatic amines with dyes, indicators, pharmaceuticals and diverse substituted aromatic compounds.

Worked case

CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> CH3NH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O. Aniline is less basic than methylamine because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring. Example: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl at 273-278 K -> C6H5N2+Cl- + NaCl + 2H2O; coupling with phenol in alkaline solution gives an orange azo dye.

Relationship

RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> RNH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O ArNH2 + HNO2 + H+ -> ArN2+ + 2H2O; ArN2+ + CuX -> ArX + N2

Correction / limitation

Do not rank amine basicity from inductive effect alone; resonance and aqueous solvation can reverse a simple gas-phase prediction. Do not prepare or store arenediazonium salts at room temperature; maintain 273-278 K and distinguish diazotisation from azo coupling.

Application

Amines are building blocks for medicines, dyes, surfactants, polymers and biological molecules. Diazonium chemistry connects aromatic amines with dyes, indicators, pharmaceuticals and diverse substituted aromatic compounds.

Concept

Carbohydrates include polyhydroxy aldehydes, ketones and substances that yield such units on hydrolysis.

Theory

Carbohydrates include polyhydroxy aldehydes, ketones and substances that yield such units on hydrolysis. Monosaccharides can form cyclic hemiacetals or hemiketals. Glycosidic bonding links sugar units, and the availability of an anomeric centre influences reducing behaviour. Worked case: Glucose commonly exists as cyclic forms in solution, yet an equilibrium small open-chain fraction allows reducing behaviour. Sucrose joins both anomeric centres in its glycosidic bond and is nonreducing under the usual test conditions. Interpretation and limits: A sweet taste does not determine whether a sugar is reducing, and a cyclic drawing does not imply that glucose cannot open. Application: Carbohydrate structure influences food properties, digestion and biological energy storage.

Concept

Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small amounts; water-soluble B and C vitamins differ in storage and deficiency patterns from fat-soluble A, D, E and K.

Theory

Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small amounts; water-soluble B and C vitamins differ in storage and deficiency patterns from fat-soluble A, D, E and K. Water-soluble vitamins are generally not stored extensively and excess is excreted, while fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate. Key board associations include A with vision, B1 with carbohydrate metabolism, C with collagen, D with calcium balance, E with antioxidant protection and K with blood clotting. Deficiency and source must be paired carefully. Worked case: prolonged vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen formation and causes scurvy; vitamin D deficiency reduces mineralisation and causes rickets in children. Interpretation and limits: Do not classify every vitamin as an energy source; vitamins mainly support biochemical processes and excessive fat-soluble vitamin intake can be harmful. Application: Vitamin chemistry guides nutrition, food fortification, clinical diagnosis and stability of pharmaceutical formulations.

Worked case

prolonged vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen formation and causes scurvy; vitamin D deficiency reduces mineralisation and causes rickets in children.

Correction / limitation

Do not classify every vitamin as an energy source; vitamins mainly support biochemical processes and excessive fat-soluble vitamin intake can be harmful.

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: after a meal, increased blood glucose stimulates insulin release. Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, lowering blood glucose; falling glucose then reduces the stimulus through negative feedback. Key check: after solving Hormones, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Hormones are chemical messengers released in small amounts that coordinate metabolism, growth, reproduction and internal balance through specific receptors.

Theory

Hormones are chemical messengers released in small amounts that coordinate metabolism, growth, reproduction and internal balance through specific receptors. Peptide hormones such as insulin bind cell-surface receptors, while steroid hormones derived from cholesterol cross membranes and regulate gene expression through intracellular receptors. Thyroxine is an iodinated amino-acid derivative. Hormone action depends on concentration, receptor selectivity, feedback and controlled secretion. Worked case: after a meal, increased blood glucose stimulates insulin release. Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, lowering blood glucose; falling glucose then reduces the stimulus through negative feedback. Interpretation and limits: Do not treat hormones as enzymes or assume all hormones share one chemical structure and one receptor location. Application: Hormone chemistry supports diabetes care, thyroid diagnosis, reproductive medicine and understanding of endocrine-disrupting chemicals.

Worked case

after a meal, increased blood glucose stimulates insulin release. Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, lowering blood glucose; falling glucose then reduces the stimulus through negative feedback.

Correction / limitation

Do not treat hormones as enzymes or assume all hormones share one chemical structure and one receptor location.

Application

Concept

Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles. Synthetic detergents clean effectively in hard water because their calcium and magnesium salts remain much more soluble than soap scum.

Theory

Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles. Synthetic detergents clean effectively in hard water because their calcium and magnesium salts remain much more soluble than soap scum. Above a suitable concentration in water, tails cluster inward around oily dirt while charged heads face outward. Agitation breaks grease into suspended droplets that can be rinsed away. Soap carboxylate ions react with Ca2+ or Mg2+ to form insoluble scum, wasting soap and reducing lather. Sulfonate or sulfate detergent heads generally avoid this precipitation, though detergent biodegradability and phosphate pollution must be considered. Worked case: When oily cloth is washed with soap, micelles encapsulate oil and keep droplets dispersed instead of redepositing them on the fabric. Example: Soap lathers poorly in hard water until Ca2+/Mg2+ are removed, while a suitable detergent continues forming micelles and cleaning. Interpretation and limits: Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material. Do not claim every detergent is environmentally harmless merely because it works in hard water; composition and biodegradability matter. Application: Micelles enable washing, emulsification and formulation of cleaners and personal-care products. Detergents support domestic and industrial cleaning, while formulation choices affect wastewater and aquatic ecosystems.

Worked case

When oily cloth is washed with soap, micelles encapsulate oil and keep droplets dispersed instead of redepositing them on the fabric. Example: Soap lathers poorly in hard water until Ca2+/Mg2+ are removed, while a suitable detergent continues forming micelles and cleaning.

Relationship

hydrophobic tails -> grease core; hydrophilic COO- heads -> water 2RCOO- + Ca2+ -> (RCOO)2Ca(s) scum

Correction / limitation

Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material. Do not claim every detergent is environmentally harmless merely because it works in hard water; composition and biodegradability matter.

Application

Micelles enable washing, emulsification and formulation of cleaners and personal-care products. Detergents support domestic and industrial cleaning, while formulation choices affect wastewater and aquatic ecosystems.

Concept

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Stoichiometry uses a balanced equation to calculate quantitative relationships between reactants and products.

Theory

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Stoichiometry uses a balanced equation to calculate quantitative relationships between reactants and products. One mole contains Avogadro's number of specified entities. Molar mass converts between amount in moles and measured mass. Coefficients give mole ratios. Convert the known quantity to moles, apply the ratio, then convert to the requested unit. Worked case: 18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O shows that 3.0 mol O2 can react with 6.0 mol H2 to form 6.0 mol H2O. Interpretation and limits: Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Never calculate from an unbalanced equation or treat coefficients as mass ratios. Application: Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. Stoichiometry controls industrial batches, medicine preparation, fuels and laboratory synthesis.

Worked case

18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O shows that 3.0 mol O2 can react with 6.0 mol H2 to form 6.0 mol H2O.

Relationship

moles = mass / molar mass moles wanted = moles known x coefficient wanted / coefficient known

Correction / limitation

Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Never calculate from an unbalanced equation or treat coefficients as mass ratios.

Application

Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. Stoichiometry controls industrial batches, medicine preparation, fuels and laboratory synthesis.

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: 18.0 g of H₂O ÷ 18.0 g mol⁻¹ = 1.00 mol H₂O. This represents about 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, producing 1.00 mol H₂O requires 1.00 mol H₂ and 0.50 mol O₂. Key check: after solving Stoichiometry and limiting reagent, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Stoichiometry uses a balanced equation to calculate quantitative relationships between reactants and products. The limiting reagent is the reactant consumed first and therefore sets the maximum product amount.

Theory

Stoichiometry uses a balanced equation to calculate quantitative relationships between reactants and products. The limiting reagent is the reactant consumed first and therefore sets the maximum product amount. Coefficients give mole ratios. Convert the known quantity to moles, apply the ratio, then convert to the requested unit. Compare each reactant in moles relative to its balanced coefficient. The other reactant is present in excess. Worked case: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O shows that 3.0 mol O2 can react with 6.0 mol H2 to form 6.0 mol H2O. Example: for 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, 3 mol H2 needs 1.5 mol O2; if only 1 mol O2 is available, O2 is limiting. Interpretation and limits: Never calculate from an unbalanced equation or treat coefficients as mass ratios. Do not choose the reactant with the smaller mass without converting to moles and using coefficients. Application: Stoichiometry controls industrial batches, medicine preparation, fuels and laboratory synthesis. Limiting-reagent control reduces waste and predicts output in manufacturing and synthesis.

Worked case

2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O shows that 3.0 mol O2 can react with 6.0 mol H2 to form 6.0 mol H2O. Example: for 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, 3 mol H2 needs 1.5 mol O2; if only 1 mol O2 is available, O2 is limiting.

Relationship

moles wanted = moles known x coefficient wanted / coefficient known smallest value of moles/coefficient identifies the limiting reagent

Correction / limitation

Never calculate from an unbalanced equation or treat coefficients as mass ratios. Do not choose the reactant with the smaller mass without converting to moles and using coefficients.

Application

Stoichiometry controls industrial batches, medicine preparation, fuels and laboratory synthesis. Limiting-reagent control reduces waste and predicts output in manufacturing and synthesis.

Concept

Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom. Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals.

Theory

Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom. Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals. The principal number n identifies shell and energy, l identifies subshell shape, ml identifies orbital orientation, and ms identifies spin. Only allowed combinations describe possible electron states. Electrons are placed in available low-energy states while obeying Aufbau filling, Hund's rule and the Pauli principle. Valence electrons largely control chemical behavior. Worked case: an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2. Example: oxygen has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4; its six valence electrons explain its common valency of two. Interpretation and limits: Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n. Do not exceed subshell capacities: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14 electrons. Application: Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior. Configurations predict ion formation, bonding, magnetism and an element's position in the periodic table.

Worked case

an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2. Example: oxygen has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4; its six valence electrons explain its common valency of two.

Relationship

n = 1,2,...; l = 0 to n-1; ml = -l to +l; ms = +/-1/2 total superscripts in a neutral atom = atomic number

Correction / limitation

Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n. Do not exceed subshell capacities: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14 electrons.

Application

Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior. Configurations predict ion formation, bonding, magnetism and an element's position in the periodic table.

Concept

Hydrogen forms molecular hydrogen, water and several classes of hydrides with different bonding patterns.

Theory

Hydrogen forms molecular hydrogen, water and several classes of hydrides with different bonding patterns. Saline hydrides contain hydride-like hydrogen and can react with water; covalent hydrides and many metallic hydrides behave differently. One hydrogen formula does not define a single reaction class. Worked case: Sodium hydride reacts with water: NaH + H2O -> NaOH + H2. The hydride ion accepts a proton, so the gas originates from combining hydrogen in two different chemical environments. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse hydride H- with a proton H+ or assume all hydrides react like NaH. Application: Hydride chemistry is used in acid-base reactions, synthesis and hydrogen-related materials.

Concept

Gas laws describe relationships among pressure, volume, temperature and amount. A state of matter is a physical form determined by particle arrangement, motion and attraction.

Theory

Gas laws describe relationships among pressure, volume, temperature and amount. A state of matter is a physical form determined by particle arrangement, motion and attraction. Boyle's law applies at constant temperature, Charles's law at constant pressure and Avogadro's law at fixed temperature and pressure. Temperature must be absolute. The familiar states are solid, liquid and gas. Plasma occurs at very high energy, while a Bose-Einstein condensate forms near absolute zero. Worked case: at constant temperature, compressing a gas from 2.0 L to 1.0 L doubles its pressure because P1V1 = P2V2. Example: ice, liquid water and water vapour are the same substance in three states; heating changes particle motion without changing H2O into a new substance. Interpretation and limits: Never substitute Celsius temperature directly into gas-law ratios; convert it to kelvin. A state change does not automatically create a new substance. Application: Gas laws guide tyres, syringes, weather balloons, breathing and gas storage. Controlling states of matter is essential in refrigeration, cooking, metal casting and gas storage.

Worked case

at constant temperature, compressing a gas from 2.0 L to 1.0 L doubles its pressure because P1V1 = P2V2. Example: ice, liquid water and water vapour are the same substance in three states; heating changes particle motion without changing H2O into a new substance.

Relationship

P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 for fixed amount heating or cooling <-> change in particle energy <-> change of state

Correction / limitation

Never substitute Celsius temperature directly into gas-law ratios; convert it to kelvin. A state change does not automatically create a new substance.

Application

Gas laws guide tyres, syringes, weather balloons, breathing and gas storage. Controlling states of matter is essential in refrigeration, cooking, metal casting and gas storage.

Intermediate First Year Physical Chemistry · Thermodynamics at school levelexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Key check: after solving Thermodynamics at school level, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of a system. Enthalpy is the state function H = U + PV, useful for constant-pressure processes.

Theory

Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of a system. Enthalpy is the state function H = U + PV, useful for constant-pressure processes. Its absolute value is usually unknown, but changes can be measured. The first law says energy changes through heat and work and is conserved overall. At constant pressure with only pressure-volume work, the enthalpy change equals heat absorbed by the system. Negative deltaH is exothermic and positive deltaH is endothermic. Worked case: if a system absorbs 300 J of heat and 80 J of work is done on it, deltaU = 300 + 80 = 380 J. Example: combustion releasing 890 kJ per mole has deltaH = -890 kJ mol-1; the negative sign records heat leaving the system. Interpretation and limits: Do not omit the sign of work or assume internal energy depends only on temperature for every system. Do not drop the sign of deltaH or describe exothermic products as having more enthalpy than reactants. Application: Internal-energy balances are used in reactors, engines, batteries and phase-change equipment. Enthalpy data support fuel comparison, process heating, food energy and reaction design.

Worked case

if a system absorbs 300 J of heat and 80 J of work is done on it, deltaU = 300 + 80 = 380 J. Example: combustion releasing 890 kJ per mole has deltaH = -890 kJ mol-1; the negative sign records heat leaving the system.

Relationship

deltaU = q + w H = U + PV; at constant pressure deltaH = qp

Correction / limitation

Do not omit the sign of work or assume internal energy depends only on temperature for every system. Do not drop the sign of deltaH or describe exothermic products as having more enthalpy than reactants.

Application

Internal-energy balances are used in reactors, engines, batteries and phase-change equipment. Enthalpy data support fuel comparison, process heating, food energy and reaction design.

Intermediate First Year Physical Chemistry · Chemical and ionic equilibriumexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Concept

The equilibrium constant relates equilibrium activities or concentrations of products and reactants. Ionic equilibrium describes reversible ionization and ion reactions in solution.

Theory

The equilibrium constant relates equilibrium activities or concentrations of products and reactants. Ionic equilibrium describes reversible ionization and ion reactions in solution. Each term is raised to its stoichiometric coefficient; pure solids and liquids are omitted. K changes with temperature but not with initial composition. Weak acids, weak bases, water and sparingly soluble salts establish equilibria described by Ka, Kb, Kw and Ksp. Worked case: for N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3). State the sign convention, substitute consistent units, and interpret the numerical result chemically. Example: for HA <-> H+ + A-, Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA]; a smaller Ka indicates less ionization under comparable conditions. Interpretation and limits: Use equilibrium values, omit pure solids and liquids, and never include catalysts in the expression. Do not treat weak electrolytes as fully dissociated or ignore charge and mass balance. Application: Equilibrium constants predict yield, dissociation, solubility and acid-base composition. Ionic equilibria determine pH, precipitation, water chemistry and analytical separations.

Worked case

for N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3). State the sign convention, substitute consistent units, and interpret the numerical result chemically. Example: for HA <-> H+ + A-, Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA]; a smaller Ka indicates less ionization under comparable conditions.

Relationship

Kc = product concentrations^coefficients / reactant concentrations^coefficients Kw = [H3O+][OH-]; at 25 C, Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14

Correction / limitation

Use equilibrium values, omit pure solids and liquids, and never include catalysts in the expression. Do not treat weak electrolytes as fully dissociated or ignore charge and mass balance.

Application

Equilibrium constants predict yield, dissociation, solubility and acid-base composition. Ionic equilibria determine pH, precipitation, water chemistry and analytical separations.

Concept

A redox reaction transfers electrons through simultaneous oxidation and reduction.

Theory

A redox reaction transfers electrons through simultaneous oxidation and reduction. Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain. Half-reactions balance atoms, charge and transferred electrons. Worked case: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu; zinc loses two electrons and copper(II) gains the same two electrons. Interpretation and limits: Do not change subscripts to balance redox equations; use coefficients and balance charge explicitly. Application: Redox chemistry powers cells, corrosion, electrolysis, metallurgy and biological respiration.

Worked case

Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu; zinc loses two electrons and copper(II) gains the same two electrons.

Relationship

electrons lost = electrons gained

Correction / limitation

Do not change subscripts to balance redox equations; use coefficients and balance charge explicitly.

Application

Redox chemistry powers cells, corrosion, electrolysis, metallurgy and biological respiration.

Intermediate Second Year Inorganic and Physical · Solutions and Raoult's Lawexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, six CN⁻ ligands contribute −6 overall. Because the complex charge is −4, iron is +2. The metal oxidation state and ligand field are then used to discuss electron count, magnetism and color. Key check: after solving Solutions and Raoult's Law, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law throughout the composition range; non-ideal solutions show positive or negative deviations because unlike-molecule attractions differ from like-molecule attractions.

Theory

Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law throughout the composition range; non-ideal solutions show positive or negative deviations because unlike-molecule attractions differ from like-molecule attractions. For an ideal binary solution, each partial vapour pressure is pi = xi pi° and the total is their sum. DeltaHmix and DeltaVmix are zero. Weaker A-B attractions produce positive deviation, higher vapour pressure and often a minimum-boiling azeotrope; stronger A-B attractions produce negative deviation and may form a maximum-boiling azeotrope. Worked case: at a fixed temperature, xA = 0.40, pA° = 100 kPa, xB = 0.60 and pB° = 50 kPa. ptotal = 0.40(100) + 0.60(50) = 70 kPa. A measured value above 70 kPa indicates positive deviation. Interpretation and limits: Do not label a solution ideal merely because both components are liquids; compare the measured vapour pressure and mixing effects with Raoult's-law predictions. Application: Vapour-pressure diagrams and azeotropes determine whether industrial liquid mixtures can be separated by ordinary fractional distillation.

Worked case

at a fixed temperature, xA = 0.40, pA° = 100 kPa, xB = 0.60 and pB° = 50 kPa. ptotal = 0.40(100) + 0.60(50) = 70 kPa. A measured value above 70 kPa indicates positive deviation.

Relationship

pi = xi pi°; ptotal = sum(pi); ideal: DeltaHmix = 0 and DeltaVmix = 0

Correction / limitation

Do not label a solution ideal merely because both components are liquids; compare the measured vapour pressure and mixing effects with Raoult's-law predictions.

Application

Vapour-pressure diagrams and azeotropes determine whether industrial liquid mixtures can be separated by ordinary fractional distillation.

Concept

Relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure depend on the number of solute particles rather than their chemical identity.

Theory

Relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure depend on the number of solute particles rather than their chemical identity. Select the equation that matches the measurement, convert mass to moles, use kilograms of solvent for molality and kelvin for temperature differences. Include i for association or dissociation. Osmotic pressure is preferred for macromolecules because it can be measured at room temperature using very dilute solutions. Worked case: 1.80 g glucose is dissolved in 100 g water. Moles = 1.80/180 = 0.0100 and m = 0.0100/0.100 = 0.100 mol kg-1. With Kf(water) = 1.86 K kg mol-1, DeltaTf = 0.186 K and the freezing point is -0.186 °C. Interpretation and limits: Do not use grams of solvent where kilograms are required, and do not substitute solution volume into a molality calculation. Application: Colligative calculations are used in molar-mass measurement, IV-fluid design, food preservation and engine coolants.

Concept

Theory

d- and f-block elements show characteristic electron-configuration, oxidation-state and size trends. Transition-metal properties depend on partly filled d-derived states and ligand environment. Lanthanoid size changes and actinoid oxidation-state variability reflect different shielding and orbital participation. Worked case: Fe2+ and Fe3+ have different d-electron counts, while lanthanoid contraction explains the close similarity of zirconium and hafnium sizes. One colour rule cannot account for every d- and f-block compound. Interpretation and limits: Do not assume every d-block ion is coloured or that all f-block elements show identical oxidation states. Application: Electronic trends guide interpretation of complexes, magnetic materials and separation chemistry.

Concept

Metal carbonyl bonding is synergic: carbon monoxide donates a lone pair to the metal while the metal back-donates d-electron density into CO antibonding orbitals. Crystal field theory models electrostatic splitting of metal d orbitals by surrounding ligands.

Theory

Metal carbonyl bonding is synergic: carbon monoxide donates a lone pair to the metal while the metal back-donates d-electron density into CO antibonding orbitals. Crystal field theory models electrostatic splitting of metal d orbitals by surrounding ligands. Sigma donation forms M<-CO bonding and pi back-bonding strengthens M-C while weakening C-O. Greater back-donation lowers the C-O stretching frequency. Electron counting explains stable examples such as Ni(CO)4 and Fe(CO)5, while bridging and terminal carbonyls differ structurally and spectroscopically. Models electrostatic splitting of metal d orbitals by surrounding ligands. Worked case: Ni in Ni(CO)4 has oxidation state zero. Nickel contributes 10 valence electrons and four neutral CO ligands donate 8, giving an 18-electron tetrahedral complex. In an octahedral field, d orbitals split into lower t2g and higher eg sets separated by deltao. Interpretation and limits: Do not describe the M-C bond as donation in only one direction, and do not assign CO a negative charge in ordinary neutral carbonyl electron counting. Ligand-field splitting and electron pairing compete; oxidation state alone does not decide whether a complex is high spin or low spin. Application: Metal carbonyl bonding underlies homogeneous catalysis, metal purification and interpretation of infrared spectra. A simplified electrostatic field explains d-orbital splitting patterns and helps compare possible spin configurations.

Ni in Ni(CO)4 has oxidation state zero. Nickel contributes 10 valence electrons and four neutral CO ligands donate 8, giving an 18-electron tetrahedral complex. In an octahedral field, d orbitals split into lower t2g and higher eg sets separated by deltao.

Relationship

M <- :CO sigma donation; M(dpi) -> CO(pi*) back-donation; 18-electron count CFSEoct = (-0.4 nt2g + 0.6 neg) deltao

Correction / limitation

Do not describe the M-C bond as donation in only one direction, and do not assign CO a negative charge in ordinary neutral carbonyl electron counting. Ligand-field splitting and electron pairing compete; oxidation state alone does not decide whether a complex is high spin or low spin.

Application

Metal carbonyl bonding underlies homogeneous catalysis, metal purification and interpretation of infrared spectra. A simplified electrostatic field explains d-orbital splitting patterns and helps compare possible spin configurations.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: in a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, Zn is oxidized at the anode and Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode. Key check: after solving Electrochemistry cells and Nernst equation, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work. The Nernst equation gives electrode or cell potential under nonstandard conditions.

Theory

A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work. The Nernst equation gives electrode or cell potential under nonstandard conditions. Oxidation occurs at the anode, reduction at the cathode, electrons travel through the wire and ions through the electrolyte or salt bridge maintain charge balance. Potential depends logarithmically on reaction quotient and approaches zero at equilibrium for the full cell. Temperature and electron count must be specified. Worked case: in a Daniell cell, Zn oxidizes at the anode and Cu2+ reduces at the cathode; electrons flow from Zn to Cu. Example: at 298 K, E = Estandard - (0.05916/n)log Q; increasing product activity lowers E for the written cell reaction. Interpretation and limits: Oxidation is always at the anode and reduction at the cathode; do not rely only on electrode signs. Construct Q from the balanced cell reaction and omit pure solids and liquids. Application: Galvanic-cell principles underpin batteries, sensors and corrosion measurements. The Nernst equation supports concentration sensors, batteries, pH electrodes and equilibrium calculations.

Worked case

in a Daniell cell, Zn oxidizes at the anode and Cu2+ reduces at the cathode; electrons flow from Zn to Cu. Example: at 298 K, E = Estandard - (0.05916/n)log Q; increasing product activity lowers E for the written cell reaction.

Relationship

Ecell = Ecathode - Eanode E = Estandard - (RT/nF) ln Q

Correction / limitation

Oxidation is always at the anode and reduction at the cathode; do not rely only on electrode signs. Construct Q from the balanced cell reaction and omit pure solids and liquids.

Application

Galvanic-cell principles underpin batteries, sensors and corrosion measurements. The Nernst equation supports concentration sensors, batteries, pH electrodes and equilibrium calculations.
