Intermediate Second Year Organic and Biomolecules · Haloalkanes and haloarenesexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: propene reacts with HBr by protonation of the double bond followed by bromide attack. Under ordinary ionic conditions, the pathway through the more stable secondary carbocation gives 2-bromopropane as the major product. Key check: after solving Haloalkanes and haloarenes, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Haloalkanes are prepared from alcohols or hydrocarbons and undergo nucleophilic substitution, elimination and reactions with metals. Haloarenes are made by aromatic halogenation or diazonium chemistry and are less reactive toward nucleophilic substitution than haloalkanes because the aryl C-X bond has partial double-bond character.

Theory

Haloalkanes are prepared from alcohols or hydrocarbons and undergo nucleophilic substitution, elimination and reactions with metals. Haloarenes are made by aromatic halogenation or diazonium chemistry and are less reactive toward nucleophilic substitution than haloalkanes because the aryl C-X bond has partial double-bond character. Alcohols react with HX, PCl3/PCl5 or SOCl2; SOCl2 is convenient because gaseous by-products escape. SN1 is favoured by stable carbocations, polar protic solvent and tertiary substrates; SN2 is a one-step backside attack favoured by methyl or primary substrates. Alcoholic KOH promotes beta-elimination, while aqueous KOH promotes substitution. Benzene reacts with Cl2/FeCl3 or Br2/FeBr3. Sandmeyer reactions replace an aryl diazonium group by Cl or Br using Cu(I) salts. Resonance, sp2 carbon and bond shortening resist ordinary SN1/SN2 pathways, though strong conditions or electron-withdrawing groups enable substitution. Worked case: CH3CH2Br + KOH(aq) -> CH3CH2OH + KBr, whereas CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc), heat -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O. Example: C6H5N2+Cl- --CuCl--> C6H5Cl + N2. Chlorobenzene with NaOH at high temperature and pressure gives phenol after acidification. Interpretation and limits: Do not ignore solvent and temperature when choosing substitution versus elimination, and do not assign SN2 to a tertiary carbon without severe steric consequences. Do not assume chlorobenzene reacts with aqueous hydroxide as readily as chloroethane; aryl and alkyl C-X bonds have different structures. Application: Haloalkanes are intermediates for alcohols, nitriles, amines, organometallic reagents and polymers. Haloarenes serve as intermediates in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, dyes and specialty polymers.

Worked case

CH3CH2Br + KOH(aq) -> CH3CH2OH + KBr, whereas CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc), heat -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O. Example: C6H5N2+Cl- --CuCl--> C6H5Cl + N2. Chlorobenzene with NaOH at high temperature and pressure gives phenol after acidification.

Relationship

RX + OH- -> ROH + X-; RX + KOH(alc) -> alkene + KX + H2O ArN2+ + CuX -> ArX + N2; ArX + NaOH --high T,P--> ArONa -> ArOH

Correction / limitation

Do not ignore solvent and temperature when choosing substitution versus elimination, and do not assign SN2 to a tertiary carbon without severe steric consequences. Do not assume chlorobenzene reacts with aqueous hydroxide as readily as chloroethane; aryl and alkyl C-X bonds have different structures.

Application

Haloalkanes are intermediates for alcohols, nitriles, amines, organometallic reagents and polymers. Haloarenes serve as intermediates in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, dyes and specialty polymers.

Concept

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Phenol is prepared from haloarenes, diazonium salts or cumene and undergoes acidic and strongly activated electrophilic aromatic reactions. Ethers are prepared by dehydration of alcohols or Williamson synthesis and generally react only under strong cleavage conditions.

Theory

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Phenol is prepared from haloarenes, diazonium salts or cumene and undergoes acidic and strongly activated electrophilic aromatic reactions. Ethers are prepared by dehydration of alcohols or Williamson synthesis and generally react only under strong cleavage conditions. Alkenes hydrate to alcohols; aldehydes and ketones reduce to primary and secondary alcohols. Primary alcohol oxidation gives aldehydes then acids, secondary gives ketones, while tertiary alcohols resist mild oxidation. Concentrated acid causes dehydration, and carboxylic acids give esters reversibly. Phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised, making phenol more acidic than alcohols. The OH group activates ortho and para positions: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, dilute nitric acid gives o- and p-nitrophenols. Kolbe-Schmitt carboxylation gives salicylic acid and Reimer-Tiemann reaction gives salicylaldehyde. Williamson synthesis is an SN2 reaction between an alkoxide and a primary alkyl halide; tertiary halides tend to eliminate. Symmetrical ethers can form by intermolecular dehydration of primary alcohols near 413 K. Hot concentrated HI or HBr cleaves C-O bonds, with aryl-alkyl ethers cleaving on the alkyl side. Worked case: CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O -> CH3COOH. With ethanoic acid and acid catalyst it forms ethyl ethanoate and water. Example: phenol + 3Br2(aq) -> 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate) + 3HBr; phenol dissolves in NaOH but not in NaHCO3. Example: C2H5ONa + CH3I -> C2H5OCH3 + NaI. Anisole + HI gives phenol and CH3I rather than iodobenzene. Interpretation and limits: Do not state that all alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids; the product depends on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary. Do not treat phenol as an ordinary alcohol; resonance changes both its acidity and the reactivity of its aromatic ring. Do not choose a tertiary haloalkane for Williamson synthesis or predict cleavage of the aryl C-O bond in anisole under ordinary HI treatment. Application: Alcohol reactions support solvents, fuels, antiseptics, fragrances, polymers and pharmaceutical synthesis. Phenol chemistry produces antiseptics, resins, dyes, aspirin precursors and polymer materials. Ethers are solvents, anaesthetic-related compounds, fuel additives and intermediates in organic synthesis.

Anisole + HI gives phenol and CH3I rather than iodobenzene.

Concept

Carbonyl compounds are prepared by controlled oxidation or other functional-group conversions and undergo nucleophilic addition, reduction, oxidation and carbon-carbon bond-forming condensations. Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides.

Theory

Carbonyl compounds are prepared by controlled oxidation or other functional-group conversions and undergo nucleophilic addition, reduction, oxidation and carbon-carbon bond-forming condensations. Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides. Primary alcohols give aldehydes and secondary alcohols give ketones. Aldehydes oxidise readily with Tollens' or Fehling's reagent; ketones usually resist. Both add HCN and bisulphite, reduce to alcohols, and compounds with alpha-hydrogen undergo aldol condensation. Carbonyls lacking alpha-hydrogen may undergo Cannizzaro disproportionation. Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes and hydrolysis of nitriles produce acids. Resonance stabilises carboxylate ions. Acids react with bicarbonate releasing CO2, esterify alcohols reversibly, and decarboxylate as sodium salts with soda lime. Electron-withdrawing substituents increase acidity. Worked case: 2CH3CHO --dilute NaOH--> CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO, which on heating loses water to form crotonaldehyde. Ethanal also gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Example: CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O. CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O with H+ and heat. Interpretation and limits: Do not use Tollens' oxidation as a universal ketone test, and check for alpha-hydrogen before choosing aldol versus Cannizzaro reaction. Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst. Application: Carbonyl chemistry is central to flavours, fragrances, pharmaceuticals, resins and carbon-carbon bond formation. Carboxylic-acid derivatives occur in medicines, polymers, food preservatives, fats, soaps and fragrances.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: propene reacts with HBr by protonation of the double bond followed by bromide attack. Concept

Amines are prepared by reduction, ammonolysis, Gabriel synthesis or Hofmann bromamide degradation and react as bases and nucleophiles. Arenediazonium salts are prepared from primary aromatic amines at low temperature and replace the diazonium group by many substituents or form azo dyes.

Theory

Amines are prepared by reduction, ammonolysis, Gabriel synthesis or Hofmann bromamide degradation and react as bases and nucleophiles. Arenediazonium salts are prepared from primary aromatic amines at low temperature and replace the diazonium group by many substituents or form azo dyes. Nitro compounds, nitriles and amides can be reduced to amines. Gabriel synthesis gives pure primary alkyl amines; Hofmann degradation gives a primary amine with one fewer carbon. Basicity depends on electron donation, resonance, solvation and steric effects. Primary amines react with nitrous acid differently from aromatic primary amines. Aniline is diazotised using NaNO2/HCl at 273-278 K because diazonium salts decompose when warm. Sandmeyer and Gattermann reactions introduce Cl, Br or CN; KI introduces I, warm water gives phenol, hypophosphorous acid gives H, and coupling with activated rings gives coloured azo compounds. Worked case: CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> CH3NH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O. Aniline is less basic than methylamine because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring. Example: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl at 273-278 K -> C6H5N2+Cl- + NaCl + 2H2O; coupling with phenol in alkaline solution gives an orange azo dye. Interpretation and limits: Do not rank amine basicity from inductive effect alone; resonance and aqueous solvation can reverse a simple gas-phase prediction. Do not prepare or store arenediazonium salts at room temperature; maintain 273-278 K and distinguish diazotisation from azo coupling. Application: Amines are building blocks for medicines, dyes, surfactants, polymers and biological molecules. Diazonium chemistry connects aromatic amines with dyes, indicators, pharmaceuticals and diverse substituted aromatic compounds.

Concept

Carbohydrates include polyhydroxy aldehydes, ketones and substances that yield such units on hydrolysis. Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small amounts; water-soluble B and C vitamins differ in storage and deficiency patterns from fat-soluble A, D, E and K. Polymerization joins monomers into macromolecules by chain-growth or step-growth pathways.

Theory

Carbohydrates include polyhydroxy aldehydes, ketones and substances that yield such units on hydrolysis. Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small amounts; water-soluble B and C vitamins differ in storage and deficiency patterns from fat-soluble A, D, E and K. Polymerization joins monomers into macromolecules by chain-growth or step-growth pathways. Monosaccharides can form cyclic hemiacetals or hemiketals. Glycosidic bonding links sugar units, and the availability of an anomeric centre influences reducing behaviour. Water-soluble vitamins are generally not stored extensively and excess is excreted, while fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate. Key board associations include A with vision, B1 with carbohydrate metabolism, C with collagen, D with calcium balance, E with antioxidant protection and K with blood clotting. Deficiency and source must be paired carefully. Worked case: Glucose commonly exists as cyclic forms in solution, yet an equilibrium small open-chain fraction allows reducing behaviour. Sucrose joins both anomeric centres in its glycosidic bond and is nonreducing under the usual test conditions. Example: prolonged vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen formation and causes scurvy; vitamin D deficiency reduces mineralisation and causes rickets in children. Example: Free-radical ethene polymerization uses initiation, propagation and termination to form polyethylene. Interpretation and limits: A sweet taste does not determine whether a sugar is reducing, and a cyclic drawing does not imply that glucose cannot open. Do not classify every vitamin as an energy source; vitamins mainly support biochemical processes and excessive fat-soluble vitamin intake can be harmful. The repeat-unit formula does not specify molecular-mass distribution, branching or tacticity. Application: Carbohydrate structure influences food properties, digestion and biological energy storage. Vitamin chemistry guides nutrition, food fortification, clinical diagnosis and stability of pharmaceutical formulations. Monomer structure and polymerization mechanism determine chain architecture, molecular-mass distribution and material behaviour.

Example: Free-radical ethene polymerization uses initiation, propagation and termination to form polyethylene.

Concept

Systematic salt analysis identifies ions through a planned sequence of selective reactions and confirmatory tests.

Theory

Systematic salt analysis identifies ions through a planned sequence of selective reactions and confirmatory tests. Separation and control of pH or reagent conditions reduce interference. A single precipitate colour is usually insufficient to identify every possible ion in a mixture. Worked case: Adding silver nitrate under appropriate acidified conditions can precipitate chloride as AgCl. Confirmatory behaviour and possible interfering ions must be considered before identifying chloride from cloudiness alone. Interpretation and limits: A precipitate's colour alone is not a complete identification when other ions can produce similar observations. Application: Qualitative analysis develops selective separation and chemical identification skills.

Concept

A chemical preparation combines controlled reaction, isolation, purification and characterization of a target substance.

Theory

A chemical preparation combines controlled reaction, isolation, purification and characterization of a target substance. Reaction yield and product identity answer different questions. Isolation conditions must suit the product's solubility, volatility and stability, and purity requires an appropriate test. Worked case: Prepare a crystalline product, filter it, wash away soluble impurities and dry before weighing. A wet solid gives an artificially high apparent yield, so mass alone cannot establish successful pure-product preparation. Interpretation and limits: Do not count retained solvent or unreacted starting material as pure product. Application: Preparation workflows connect synthetic transformations with reproducible isolation and quality assessment.

isolated yield = dry product amount / theoretical product amount

Do not count retained solvent or unreacted starting material as pure product.

Previous worked example

Worked example focus: define analyte, choose calibration, calculate with units, then report uncertainty. Example: for rate = k[A], doubling [A] doubles the initial rate. If doubling [A] instead makes the rate four times larger, the reaction is second order in A because 2² = 4. Key check: after solving Chemical kinetics and electrochemistry experiments, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Integrated rate laws connect reactant concentration with time and allow reaction order and rate constants to be extracted from experimental data. A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work.

Theory

Integrated rate laws connect reactant concentration with time and allow reaction order and rate constants to be extracted from experimental data. A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work. For a zero-order reaction, [A]t = [A]0 - kt and [A] versus t is linear. For first order, ln[A]t = ln[A]0 - kt and ln[A] versus t is linear. The slope is -k, with units mol L-1 s-1 for zero order and s-1 for first order. Oxidation occurs at the anode, reduction at the cathode, electrons travel through the wire and ions through the electrolyte or salt bridge maintain charge balance. Worked case: a first-order reactant falls from 0.800 M to 0.200 M in 40.0 min. k = (2.303/40.0) log(0.800/0.200) = 0.0347 min-1. Example: in a Daniell cell, Zn oxidizes at the anode and Cu2+ reduces at the cathode; electrons flow from Zn to Cu. Interpretation and limits: Do not identify order from the balanced equation; order is determined experimentally from the rate law or the correct linear concentration-time plot. Oxidation is always at the anode and reduction at the cathode; do not rely only on electrode signs. Application: Integrated laws predict shelf life, drug degradation, pollutant decay and the time required for industrial conversion. Galvanic-cell principles underpin batteries, sensors and corrosion measurements.

Worked case

a first-order reactant falls from 0.800 M to 0.200 M in 40.0 min. k = (2.303/40.0) log(0.800/0.200) = 0.0347 min-1. Example: in a Daniell cell, Zn oxidizes at the anode and Cu2+ reduces at the cathode; electrons flow from Zn to Cu.

Relationship

zero: [A]t=[A]0-kt; first: k=(2.303/t)log([A]0/[A]t) Ecell = Ecathode - Eanode

Correction / limitation

Do not identify order from the balanced equation; order is determined experimentally from the rate law or the correct linear concentration-time plot. Oxidation is always at the anode and reduction at the cathode; do not rely only on electrode signs.

Application

Integrated laws predict shelf life, drug degradation, pollutant decay and the time required for industrial conversion. Galvanic-cell principles underpin batteries, sensors and corrosion measurements.

Interpretation and limits: Particles in a solid are not motionless; they vibrate about fixed positions. Matter Around Us · Bose-Einstein Condensateexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: dilute rubidium atoms cooled with lasers and magnetic traps can overlap into one condensate instead of behaving as separate warm atoms. Key check: after solving Bose-Einstein Condensate, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

A Bose-Einstein condensate is a state formed when certain atoms are cooled extremely close to absolute zero.

Theory

A Bose-Einstein condensate is a state formed when certain atoms are cooled extremely close to absolute zero. At such low temperatures the atoms lose almost all thermal motion and many occupy the same lowest-energy quantum state, behaving like one collective matter wave. Worked case: dilute rubidium atoms cooled with lasers and magnetic traps can overlap into one condensate instead of behaving as separate warm atoms. Interpretation and limits: A Bose-Einstein condensate is not simply a frozen solid; it is a quantum state produced under special laboratory conditions. Application: Scientists use condensates to study quantum behavior, precision sensing and atom interferometry.

Worked case

dilute rubidium atoms cooled with lasers and magnetic traps can overlap into one condensate instead of behaving as separate warm atoms.

Relationship

temperature near 0 K -> many bosons share one quantum state

Correction / limitation

A Bose-Einstein condensate is not simply a frozen solid; it is a quantum state produced under special laboratory conditions.

Application

Scientists use condensates to study quantum behavior, precision sensing and atom interferometry.

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: a balance that reads 0.20 g when empty adds about 0.20 g to every uncorrected mass, creating systematic error. Key check: after solving Errors, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Measurement error is the difference between a measured value and an accepted value.

Theory

Measurement error is the difference between a measured value and an accepted value. Random errors make readings scatter, systematic errors shift them in one direction, and gross errors come from mistakes such as misreading a scale. Worked case: a balance that reads 0.20 g when empty adds about 0.20 g to every uncorrected mass, creating systematic error. Interpretation and limits: Error does not always mean carelessness; every measurement has uncertainty. Application: Understanding errors improves instrument design, calibration and confidence in scientific conclusions.

Worked case

a balance that reads 0.20 g when empty adds about 0.20 g to every uncorrected mass, creating systematic error.

Relationship

absolute error = |measured value - accepted value|

Correction / limitation

Error does not always mean carelessness; every measurement has uncertainty.

Application

Understanding errors improves instrument design, calibration and confidence in scientific conclusions.

Concept

Density is the mass contained in a unit volume of a substance.

Theory

Density is the mass contained in a unit volume of a substance. Density is a characteristic property at a stated temperature and can help identify a material or predict whether it will float. Worked case: a sample of mass 54 g and volume 20 cm3 has density 54/20 = 2.7 g/cm3. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse density with mass; a large object can have more mass but lower density. Application: Density is used to identify materials, test purity and design ships, aircraft and storage systems.

Worked case

a sample of mass 54 g and volume 20 cm3 has density 54/20 = 2.7 g/cm3.

Relationship

density = mass / volume

Correction / limitation

Do not confuse density with mass; a large object can have more mass but lower density.

Application

Density is used to identify materials, test purity and design ships, aircraft and storage systems.

Concept

Temperature measures how hot or cold a system is and is reported using scales such as Celsius and kelvin.

Theory

Temperature measures how hot or cold a system is and is reported using scales such as Celsius and kelvin. Celsius sets water's freezing point near 0 degrees C at standard pressure. Kelvin begins at absolute zero and has no negative values. Worked case: 25 degrees C = 25 + 273.15 = 298.15 K. Interpretation and limits: A temperature of 0 degrees C is not zero particle motion; 0 K is absolute zero. Application: Temperature control is essential in food storage, reactions, medicine and weather observations.

Worked case

25 degrees C = 25 + 273.15 = 298.15 K.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

A temperature of 0 degrees C is not zero particle motion; 0 K is absolute zero.

Application

Temperature control is essential in food storage, reactions, medicine and weather observations.

Laboratory measurements use suitable instruments and careful reading techniques to obtain reliable data.

Laboratory measurements use suitable instruments and careful reading techniques to obtain reliable data. Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: cathode-ray experiments showed that all atoms contain the same negatively charged particle, the electron. Key check: after solving Discovery of atom, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

The atomic idea developed from philosophical proposals into an evidence-based scientific model.

Theory

The atomic idea developed from philosophical proposals into an evidence-based scientific model. Democritus suggested indivisible particles, but later experiments by Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr and others revealed atoms, electrons, nuclei and quantized behavior. Worked case: cathode-ray experiments showed that all atoms contain the same negatively charged particle, the electron. Interpretation and limits: No single scientist discovered the complete modern atom at once. Application: Atomic models explain materials, electricity, spectra, medicines and nuclear energy.

Worked case

Relationship

new evidence -> revised atomic model

Correction / limitation

No single scientist discovered the complete modern atom at once.

Application

Atomic models explain materials, electricity, spectra, medicines and nuclear energy.

Atoms · Dalton theoryexisting authored record

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: water forms with hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a fixed ratio, consistent with atoms combining in simple whole numbers. Key check: after solving Dalton theory, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Dalton proposed that matter consists of atoms and that chemical reactions rearrange them in whole-number ratios.

Theory

Dalton proposed that matter consists of atoms and that chemical reactions rearrange them in whole-number ratios. His theory explained conservation of mass and fixed composition. We now know atoms are divisible and isotopes of one element can have different masses. Worked case: water forms with hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a fixed ratio, consistent with atoms combining in simple whole numbers. Interpretation and limits: Dalton's claim that atoms are indivisible is historically important but not part of the modern model. Application: Dalton's ideas provide the foundation for formulas, equations and stoichiometry.

Worked case

water forms with hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a fixed ratio, consistent with atoms combining in simple whole numbers.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Dalton's claim that atoms are indivisible is historically important but not part of the modern model.

Application

Dalton's ideas provide the foundation for formulas, equations and stoichiometry.

Concept

Thomson's model pictured negative electrons embedded in a diffuse positively charged atom.

Theory

Thomson's model pictured negative electrons embedded in a diffuse positively charged atom. It was proposed after the electron was discovered and explained overall electrical neutrality, but it had no central nucleus. Worked case: the model is often compared to raisins distributed through a pudding, with electrons spread inside positive matter. Interpretation and limits: Do not place a nucleus in Thomson's model; the nucleus was introduced after Rutherford's evidence. Application: The model shows how scientific explanations change when new particles are discovered.

Worked case

the model is often compared to raisins distributed through a pudding, with electrons spread inside positive matter.

Relationship

total positive charge + total negative charge = neutral atom

Correction / limitation

Do not place a nucleus in Thomson's model; the nucleus was introduced after Rutherford's evidence.

Application

The model shows how scientific explanations change when new particles are discovered.

Atoms · Rutherford modelexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Concept

Rutherford's model places nearly all mass and positive charge in a tiny central nucleus.

Theory

Rutherford's model places nearly all mass and positive charge in a tiny central nucleus. Most alpha particles passed through gold foil, showing that atoms are mostly empty space; a few large deflections revealed a small, dense, positive center. Worked case: if positive charge were spread out as Thomson proposed, large-angle alpha-particle deflections would have been extremely unlikely. Interpretation and limits: The nucleus is tiny compared with the whole atom; drawings are not to scale. Application: Scattering methods still reveal structures too small to see directly.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Application

Scattering methods still reveal structures too small to see directly.

Atoms · Bohr modelexisting authored record

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: an excited hydrogen electron dropping to a lower level releases light with energy equal to the difference between the levels. Concept

The Bohr model places electrons in fixed, quantized energy levels around the nucleus.

Theory

The Bohr model places electrons in fixed, quantized energy levels around the nucleus. An electron absorbs energy to move higher and emits a photon when it returns to a lower level. The model explains hydrogen's line spectrum well. Worked case: an excited hydrogen electron dropping to a lower level releases light with energy equal to the difference between the levels. Interpretation and limits: Bohr paths are a useful school model, not literal planetary orbits for all atoms. Application: Energy-level ideas help explain flame colors, spectra and electronic transitions.

Worked case

an excited hydrogen electron dropping to a lower level releases light with energy equal to the difference between the levels.

Relationship

photon energy = higher level energy - lower level energy

Correction / limitation

Bohr paths are a useful school model, not literal planetary orbits for all atoms.

Application

Energy-level ideas help explain flame colors, spectra and electronic transitions.

Concept

The modern atomic model describes electrons with probability regions called orbitals.

Theory

The modern atomic model describes electrons with probability regions called orbitals. Quantum mechanics does not assign an electron a fixed circular path. Orbitals show where an electron is likely to be found and have quantized energies and shapes. Worked case: the lowest-energy electron in hydrogen occupies a spherical 1s orbital, represented as a probability cloud. Interpretation and limits: An orbital is not a solid shell or a track followed by an electron. Concept

Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons.

Theory

Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Protons have charge +1 and neutrons have charge 0 in the nucleus; electrons have charge -1 and occupy the surrounding electron cloud. Protons and neutrons are much more massive than electrons. Worked case: a neutral carbon-12 atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons. Interpretation and limits: Do not say neutrons have no mass; they have no electrical charge. Application: Subatomic particles explain ions, isotopes, electricity and nuclear reactions.

Worked case

a neutral carbon-12 atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Do not say neutrons have no mass; they have no electrical charge.

Application

Subatomic particles explain ions, isotopes, electricity and nuclear reactions.

Atoms · Atomic numberexisting authored record

Concept

Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.

Theory

Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. It is written Z and uniquely identifies an element. Changing the number of electrons makes an ion, but changing the proton count makes a different element. Worked case: every oxygen atom has Z = 8, so it contains 8 protons. Interpretation and limits: Atomic number is not the number of neutrons or the total number of particles. Application: Atomic number organizes the modern periodic table and identifies elements in analysis.

Worked case

every oxygen atom has Z = 8, so it contains 8 protons.

Relationship

Z = number of protons

Correction / limitation

Atomic number is not the number of neutrons or the total number of particles.

Application

Atomic number organizes the modern periodic table and identifies elements in analysis.

Concept

Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus.

Theory

Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus. It is a whole number written A. Electrons contribute so little mass that they are not counted in the mass number. Worked case: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23. Interpretation and limits: Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table. Application: Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers.

Worked case

sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23.

Relationship

A = Z + N

Correction / limitation

Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table.

Application

Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers.

Atoms · Isotopesexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively. Key check: after solving Isotopes, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

Theory

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers. They have similar chemical behavior because they have the same electron arrangement, but their masses and nuclear stability can differ. Worked case: carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively. Interpretation and limits: Isotopes are not different elements because their atomic numbers are the same. Application: Isotopes are used in medical imaging, cancer treatment, dating and chemical tracing.

Worked case

carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.

Relationship

same Z, different A

Correction / limitation

Isotopes are not different elements because their atomic numbers are the same.

Application

Isotopes are used in medical imaging, cancer treatment, dating and chemical tracing.

Concept

Isobars are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number.

Theory

Isobars are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number. They have different proton numbers and therefore different chemical identities, even though the total number of nucleons is equal. Worked case: argon-40 and calcium-40 are isobars: both have A = 40, but their atomic numbers are 18 and 20. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse isobars with isotopes; isotopes belong to the same element. Application: Comparing isobars helps organize nuclear transformations and nuclide notation.

same A, different Z

Correction / limitation

Do not confuse isobars with isotopes; isotopes belong to the same element.

Application

Concept

A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds.

Theory

A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds. Molecules may contain one element, such as O2, or several elements, such as H2O. Ionic compounds form formula units rather than separate molecules. Worked case: one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom. Interpretation and limits: Do not call every compound a molecule; sodium chloride is an ionic lattice. Application: Molecular structure determines smell, color, solubility, medicine action and material behavior.

one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom.

Relationship

molecule = definite group of covalently bonded atoms

Correction / limitation

Do not call every compound a molecule; sodium chloride is an ionic lattice.

Application

Molecular structure determines smell, color, solubility, medicine action and material behavior.

Interpretation and limits: Remember to multiply each atomic mass by its subscript. Application: Molecular mass is used to compare molecules and convert between mass and amount of substance.

Application: The table predicts bonding, ion formation, reactivity and material properties.

Theory

For strong acids and bases, spectator ions do not appear in the net ionic equation. The amount of acid and base determines whether excess acidity or basicity remains; mixing them does not guarantee a neutral final pH. Worked case: Mix 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L HCl with 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L NaOH. Each supplies 1.00 mmol of reactive acid or base, so they neutralize in the 1:1 net reaction H+ + OH- -> H2O. Interpretation and limits: Equal volumes do not imply equal reactive amounts when concentrations differ, and weak-acid/base salt solutions need not have pH 7. Application: Stoichiometric neutralization is used in titrations and controlled pH adjustment.

Relationship

H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)

Correction / limitation

Equal volumes do not imply equal reactive amounts when concentrations differ, and weak-acid/base salt solutions need not have pH 7.

Application

Stoichiometric neutralization is used in titrations and controlled pH adjustment.

Worked case: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e- shows magnesium being oxidized during formation of magnesium oxide. Interpretation and limits: Oxidation does not always involve oxygen. Application: Oxidation occurs in combustion, rusting, respiration, bleaching and batteries.

Concept

A redox reaction contains simultaneous oxidation and reduction.

Theory

A redox reaction contains simultaneous oxidation and reduction. Track electron loss and gain or changes in oxidation number. The oxidizing agent gains electrons, while the reducing agent loses them. Worked case: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu; zinc is oxidized and copper(II) is reduced, with two electrons transferred. Interpretation and limits: Do not label only one half of a redox reaction; oxidation and reduction always occur together. Application: Redox chemistry explains batteries, corrosion, respiration, photosynthesis and metal extraction.

Worked case

Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu; zinc is oxidized and copper(II) is reduced, with two electrons transferred.

Relationship

electrons lost = electrons gained

Correction / limitation

Do not label only one half of a redox reaction; oxidation and reduction always occur together.

Application

Redox chemistry explains batteries, corrosion, respiration, photosynthesis and metal extraction.

Concept

Dry air is a mixture dominated by nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller amounts of argon and carbon dioxide.

Theory

Dry air is a mixture dominated by nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller amounts of argon and carbon dioxide. Volume fractions describe how much of a gas mixture each component occupies at the same conditions. Water vapour varies with humidity, so dry-air percentages exclude it. Worked case: In 100 L of dry air, approximately 78 L is nitrogen and 21 L is oxygen. The remaining roughly 1 L contains mainly argon and trace gases; the components are mixed, not chemically bonded together. Interpretation and limits: Oxygen is not the most abundant gas in air; nitrogen is. Water-vapour content is not a fixed dry-air percentage. Application: Air separation supplies nitrogen for inert packaging and oxygen for industrial processes.

Worked case

In 100 L of dry air, approximately 78 L is nitrogen and 21 L is oxygen. The remaining roughly 1 L contains mainly argon and trace gases; the components are mixed, not chemically bonded together.

Relationship

gas volume fraction = component volume / total volume

Correction / limitation

Oxygen is not the most abundant gas in air; nitrogen is. Water-vapour content is not a fixed dry-air percentage.

Application

Air separation supplies nitrogen for inert packaging and oxygen for industrial processes.

Concept

Evaporation, condensation and precipitation move water between reservoirs; purification removes particular contaminants.

Theory

Evaporation, condensation and precipitation move water between reservoirs; purification removes particular contaminants. Filtration traps suspended particles but ordinarily does not remove dissolved salts. Distillation vaporizes water and condenses the vapour, leaving most nonvolatile solutes behind. Disinfection addresses microorganisms rather than salt content. Worked case: A sand-water-salt mixture passes through a filter: sand remains on the paper, but salt remains in the filtrate. Distilling the filtrate gives a much less salty condensate because dissolved salt does not vaporize with the water. Interpretation and limits: Clear filtered water is not necessarily free of dissolved chemicals or microorganisms. Application: Water treatment combines several operations because turbidity, dissolved solutes and microbial contamination require different controls.

Worked case

A sand-water-salt mixture passes through a filter: sand remains on the paper, but salt remains in the filtrate. Distilling the filtrate gives a much less salty condensate because dissolved salt does not vaporize with the water.

Relationship

filtration separates suspended solids; distillation separates by volatility

Correction / limitation

Clear filtered water is not necessarily free of dissolved chemicals or microorganisms.

Application

Water treatment combines several operations because turbidity, dissolved solutes and microbial contamination require different controls.

Concept

Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared radiation and alter the rate at which Earth loses energy to space.

Theory

Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared radiation and alter the rate at which Earth loses energy to space. Sunlight warms Earth's surface. The surface emits infrared radiation, some of which is absorbed by gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour. The atmosphere also emits radiation upward and downward; it does not simply prevent all heat from escaping. Worked case: Compare an atmosphere containing infrared-active CO2 with one without it while keeping incoming sunlight fixed. Absorption and re-emission of outgoing infrared change the energy balance, so the equilibrium surface temperature differs. Interpretation and limits: Do not describe the greenhouse effect as the ozone hole or as oxygen stopping all heat from escaping. Application: Infrared spectra and atmospheric composition help quantify the radiative effects of changing greenhouse-gas concentrations.

Worked case

Compare an atmosphere containing infrared-active CO2 with one without it while keeping incoming sunlight fixed. Absorption and re-emission of outgoing infrared change the energy balance, so the equilibrium surface temperature differs.

Relationship

absorbed solar energy = outgoing energy at thermal equilibrium

Correction / limitation

Do not describe the greenhouse effect as the ozone hole or as oxygen stopping all heat from escaping.

Application

Infrared spectra and atmospheric composition help quantify the radiative effects of changing greenhouse-gas concentrations.

Concept

Sustainable use of resources considers extraction, lifetime, recovery and waste rather than only purchase cost.

Theory

Sustainable use of resources considers extraction, lifetime, recovery and waste rather than only purchase cost. Finite mineral deposits and fossil fuels are replenished much more slowly than they are consumed. Reuse preserves an object, while recycling recovers material and may still require energy and processing. Worked case: Compare using a refillable glass container 20 times with replacing 20 single-use containers. Count washing, transport and manufacturing inputs before concluding which option has lower total environmental impact. Interpretation and limits: A recyclable label does not prove that an item is collected or recycled in practice. Application: Material-flow accounting helps plan collection systems and reduce demand for virgin resources.

Worked case

Compare using a refillable glass container 20 times with replacing 20 single-use containers. Count washing, transport and manufacturing inputs before concluding which option has lower total environmental impact.

Relationship

resource demand = virgin input + processing demand - recovered material

Correction / limitation

A recyclable label does not prove that an item is collected or recycled in practice.

Application

Material-flow accounting helps plan collection systems and reduce demand for virgin resources.

Concept

Acid-base indicators are weak acids or bases whose conjugate forms have different colours.

Theory

Acid-base indicators are weak acids or bases whose conjugate forms have different colours. Changing pH shifts the balance between the two coloured forms. Each indicator changes over a characteristic pH range. Worked case: phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution and pink in sufficiently basic solution. Interpretation and limits: An indicator does not cause neutralization and its endpoint range must suit the reaction. Application: Indicators locate titration endpoints and provide quick pH tests in laboratories and products.

HIn <-> H+ + In-; the two forms have different colours

Correction / limitation

An indicator does not cause neutralization and its endpoint range must suit the reaction.

Indicators locate titration endpoints and provide quick pH tests in laboratories and products.

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: if [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹, pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3. The solution is acidic, and diluting it tenfold ideally raises the pH by about one unit. Key check: after solving Acidic and basic substances, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

An Arrhenius acid increases H3O+ concentration in water, while an Arrhenius base increases OH- concentration. A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and a Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton.

Theory

An Arrhenius acid increases H3O+ concentration in water, while an Arrhenius base increases OH- concentration. A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and a Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton. The definition clearly explains many aqueous neutralizations but is limited to water-based systems. Each acid forms a conjugate base after donating H+, and each base forms a conjugate acid after accepting H+. Worked case: HCl forms H3O+ in water, while NaOH dissociates to provide OH-; together they form water and NaCl. Example: NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-; NH3 accepts H+ and is the base, while water donates H+ and is the acid. Interpretation and limits: A substance need not contain OH in its formula to act as a base in broader acid-base theories. Identify proton transfer, not simply the presence of H or OH in a formula. Application: The Arrhenius model explains common laboratory acids, alkalis and neutralization. This theory explains buffers, biological proton transfer and non-hydroxide bases.

Worked case

HCl forms H3O+ in water, while NaOH dissociates to provide OH-; together they form water and NaCl. Example: NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-; NH3 accepts H+ and is the base, while water donates H+ and is the acid.

Relationship

acid in water -> H3O+; base in water -> OH- acid + base <-> conjugate base + conjugate acid

Correction / limitation

A substance need not contain OH in its formula to act as a base in broader acid-base theories. Identify proton transfer, not simply the presence of H or OH in a formula.

Application

The Arrhenius model explains common laboratory acids, alkalis and neutralization. This theory explains buffers, biological proton transfer and non-hydroxide bases.

  6. The definition clearly explains many aqueous neutralizations but is limited to water-based systems.

Concept

Salts are ionic compounds produced when acid hydrogen is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.

Theory

Salts are ionic compounds produced when acid hydrogen is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. They may be prepared by neutralization, precipitation or reactions of acids with metals, oxides or carbonates. Solubility and hydrolysis determine their behavior. Worked case: H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O prepares sodium sulfate by neutralization. Interpretation and limits: Not every salt is neutral in solution, and 'salt' in chemistry includes far more than sodium chloride. Application: Salts are used in fertilizers, medicines, food, water treatment, construction and manufacturing.

Worked case

H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O prepares sodium sulfate by neutralization.

Relationship

acid + base -> salt + water

Correction / limitation

Not every salt is neutral in solution, and 'salt' in chemistry includes far more than sodium chloride.

Application

Salts are used in fertilizers, medicines, food, water treatment, construction and manufacturing.

Not every salt is neutral in solution, and 'salt' in chemistry includes far more than sodium chloride. Equal volumes do not imply equal reactive amounts when concentrations differ, and weak-acid/base salt solutions need not have pH 7.

Application

Salts are used in fertilizers, medicines, food, water treatment, construction and manufacturing. Stoichiometric neutralization is used in titrations and controlled pH adjustment.

Concept

Metals are elements that typically conduct heat and electricity and are malleable, ductile and lustrous.

Theory

Metals are elements that typically conduct heat and electricity and are malleable, ductile and lustrous. Their valence electrons are relatively mobile, and metals commonly lose electrons to form positive ions. Worked case: copper conducts electrical current and can be drawn into wire, making it useful in cables. Interpretation and limits: Not every metal is hard or solid at room temperature; mercury is liquid. Application: Metals are used in structures, wiring, transport, tools, batteries and catalysts.

Concept

A more reactive metal can displace ions of a less reactive metal from a suitable aqueous solution.

Theory

A more reactive metal can displace ions of a less reactive metal from a suitable aqueous solution. Metal reactivity concerns the tendency to lose electrons under specified conditions. An observed displacement couples metal oxidation to reduction of another metal ion. Worked case: Place zinc in copper sulfate solution: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu. Copper deposits as zinc dissolves. Copper placed in zinc sulfate does not cause the reverse displacement under ordinary conditions. Interpretation and limits: A metal does not displace every other metal merely because both conduct electricity. Application: Displacement reactions underpin cementation processes used to recover dissolved metals.

Worked case

Concept

Corrosion is unwanted electrochemical oxidation of a material by its environment.

Theory

Corrosion is unwanted electrochemical oxidation of a material by its environment. For iron rusting, anodic iron dissolution and cathodic oxygen reduction occur at different surface regions; water and ions complete the circuit. Worked case: zinc coating protects steel both as a barrier and, if scratched, by oxidizing sacrificially before iron. Interpretation and limits: Rusting requires an electrochemical pathway; oxygen alone without suitable moisture is insufficient for ordinary rust formation. Application: Corrosion science protects bridges, pipelines, vehicles, ships and electronic equipment.

Worked case

zinc coating protects steel both as a barrier and, if scratched, by oxidizing sacrificially before iron.

Relationship

anode: Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-

Correction / limitation

Rusting requires an electrochemical pathway; oxygen alone without suitable moisture is insufficient for ordinary rust formation.

Application

Corrosion science protects bridges, pipelines, vehicles, ships and electronic equipment.

Concept

Carbon allotropes have different bonding networks, while carbon-containing fuels release energy on oxidation.

Theory

Carbon allotropes have different bonding networks, while carbon-containing fuels release energy on oxidation. Diamond has a three-dimensional covalent network; graphite contains strongly bonded sheets with mobile electrons. Combustion changes chemical composition and is distinct from changing allotrope. Worked case: Graphite conducts along its sheets, whereas pure diamond is an electrical insulator under ordinary conditions. Burning carbon completely gives CO2; limited oxygen can also produce poisonous CO. Interpretation and limits: Diamond and graphite differ in structure, not in the identity of their carbon atoms. Incomplete combustion is not guaranteed to form only CO2. Application: Graphite electrodes and diamond cutting tools exploit contrasting structures; ventilation matters when burning carbon fuels.

Worked case

Graphite conducts along its sheets, whereas pure diamond is an electrical insulator under ordinary conditions. Burning carbon completely gives CO2; limited oxygen can also produce poisonous CO.

Relationship

C + O2 -> CO2

Correction / limitation

Diamond and graphite differ in structure, not in the identity of their carbon atoms. Incomplete combustion is not guaranteed to form only CO2.

Application

Graphite electrodes and diamond cutting tools exploit contrasting structures; ventilation matters when burning carbon fuels.

Concept

Solids have a fixed shape and volume and are usually difficult to compress.

Theory

Solids have a fixed shape and volume and are usually difficult to compress. Their particles are packed closely in fixed positions. The particles still vibrate, but strong attractions prevent them from flowing past one another. Worked case: a wooden block keeps its shape when moved from a desk to a box; pressing it does not noticeably reduce its volume. Interpretation and limits: Particles in a solid are not motionless; they vibrate about fixed positions. Application: Engineers select solids for buildings, tools and devices by comparing hardness, strength and flexibility.

Worked case

a wooden block keeps its shape when moved from a desk to a box; pressing it does not noticeably reduce its volume.

Relationship

closely packed particles -> fixed shape and fixed volume

Correction / limitation

Particles in a solid are not motionless; they vibrate about fixed positions.

Application

Engineers select solids for buildings, tools and devices by comparing hardness, strength and flexibility.

Concept

Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a stated amount of solvent at specified conditions.

Theory

Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a stated amount of solvent at specified conditions. It depends on solute-solvent interactions, temperature and, for gases, pressure. A saturated solution is in dynamic equilibrium with undissolved solute. Worked case: if at most 36 g NaCl dissolves in 100 g water at a temperature, adding 40 g leaves about 4 g undissolved. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse dissolving rate with solubility; stirring speeds dissolving but may not change the final maximum. Application: Solubility guides crystallization, medicines, water treatment and formulation.

Worked case

if at most 36 g NaCl dissolves in 100 g water at a temperature, adding 40 g leaves about 4 g undissolved.

Relationship

solubility = maximum dissolved solute at stated temperature and pressure

Correction / limitation

Application

Solubility guides crystallization, medicines, water treatment and formulation.

Concept

Simple separation methods exploit visible differences, particle size or response to moving air.

Theory

Simple separation methods exploit visible differences, particle size or response to moving air. Handpicking suits easily distinguished pieces, sieving separates sizes, and winnowing separates components that move differently in an air stream. No chemical reaction is required. Worked case: Remove stones from beans by handpicking, separate bran from flour using a suitable sieve, and separate light husk from heavier grain by winnowing. Changing the sieve opening changes which particles pass. Interpretation and limits: A sieve cannot remove dissolved salt from water because dissolved ions are not grains retained by the mesh. Application: Matching a separation method to particle properties is useful in food preparation and grain processing.

Worked case

Remove stones from beans by handpicking, separate bran from flour using a suitable sieve, and separate light husk from heavier grain by winnowing. Changing the sieve opening changes which particles pass.

Correction / limitation

A sieve cannot remove dissolved salt from water because dissolved ions are not grains retained by the mesh.

Application

Matching a separation method to particle properties is useful in food preparation and grain processing.

Key check: after solving Sedimentation, decantation, filtration and evaporation, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Different separation operations remove settling solids, suspended particles or solvent from mixtures.

Theory

Different separation operations remove settling solids, suspended particles or solvent from mixtures. Sedimentation lets sufficiently dense particles settle; decantation pours off a liquid layer; filtration retains suitable suspended particles; evaporation removes volatile solvent. Their products are not identical. Worked case: For muddy salt water, let heavy mud settle, decant carefully and filter residual suspended particles. The filtrate still contains dissolved salt, which can be recovered by evaporating water. Interpretation and limits: Filtration does not normally remove dissolved sodium chloride. Application: Combining physical separations helps recover useful substances from multicomponent mixtures.

Worked case

For muddy salt water, let heavy mud settle, decant carefully and filter residual suspended particles. The filtrate still contains dissolved salt, which can be recovered by evaporating water.

Relationship

suspended solid removal differs from dissolved-solute recovery

Correction / limitation

Filtration does not normally remove dissolved sodium chloride.

Application

Combining physical separations helps recover useful substances from multicomponent mixtures.

Concept

Reversibility concerns whether the initial state or substances can be restored under the stated conditions.

Theory

Reversibility concerns whether the initial state or substances can be restored under the stated conditions. Some physical changes are reversible, such as freezing and melting, while others such as breaking an object may be hard to reverse. Chemical changes may also be reversible reactions, so physical and reversible are not synonyms. Worked case: Ice melts into liquid water and can be refrozen. Burning paper forms new substances that cannot be restored to the original sheet by simply cooling the products. Interpretation and limits: Do not assume every physical change is reversible or every chemical reaction is fundamentally irreversible. Application: Recognizing practical reversibility informs material reuse and process design.

Worked case

Ice melts into liquid water and can be refrozen. Burning paper forms new substances that cannot be restored to the original sheet by simply cooling the products.

Relationship

reversibility depends on the change and the conditions used to reverse it

Correction / limitation

Do not assume every physical change is reversible or every chemical reaction is fundamentally irreversible.

Application

Recognizing practical reversibility informs material reuse and process design.

Each indicator changes over a characteristic pH range. Worked case: phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution and pink in sufficiently basic solution. Interpretation and limits: An indicator does not cause neutralization and its endpoint range must suit the reaction. Application: Indicators locate titration endpoints and provide quick pH tests in laboratories and products.

Concept

Neutralization is proton transfer between an acid and a base, often producing water and a salt in aqueous strong-acid/strong-base reactions.

Theory

Neutralization is proton transfer between an acid and a base, often producing water and a salt in aqueous strong-acid/strong-base reactions. For strong acids and bases, spectator ions do not appear in the net ionic equation. The amount of acid and base determines whether excess acidity or basicity remains; mixing them does not guarantee a neutral final pH. Worked case: Mix 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L HCl with 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L NaOH. Each supplies 1.00 mmol of reactive acid or base, so they neutralize in the 1:1 net reaction H+ + OH- -> H2O. Interpretation and limits: Equal volumes do not imply equal reactive amounts when concentrations differ, and weak-acid/base salt solutions need not have pH 7. Application: Stoichiometric neutralization is used in titrations and controlled pH adjustment.

Mix 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L HCl with 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L NaOH. Each supplies 1.00 mmol of reactive acid or base, so they neutralize in the 1:1 net reaction H+ + OH- -> H2O.

H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)

Correction / limitation

Equal volumes do not imply equal reactive amounts when concentrations differ, and weak-acid/base salt solutions need not have pH 7.

Key check: after solving Metals and non-metals around us, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Metals are elements that typically conduct heat and electricity and are malleable, ductile and lustrous. Nonmetals generally conduct poorly and, when solid, are often brittle rather than malleable.

Theory

Metals are elements that typically conduct heat and electricity and are malleable, ductile and lustrous. Nonmetals generally conduct poorly and, when solid, are often brittle rather than malleable. Their valence electrons are relatively mobile, and metals commonly lose electrons to form positive ions. They may gain or share electrons and can exist as gases, solids or one liquid at room temperature. Worked case: copper conducts electrical current and can be drawn into wire, making it useful in cables. Example: oxygen is a gaseous nonmetal essential for respiration and combustion. Interpretation and limits: Not every metal is hard or solid at room temperature; mercury is liquid. Nonmetal does not mean unimportant or always gaseous. Application: Metals are used in structures, wiring, transport, tools, batteries and catalysts. Nonmetals form water, air, fuels, fertilizers, medicines and living matter.

Correction / limitation

Not every metal is hard or solid at room temperature; mercury is liquid. Nonmetal does not mean unimportant or always gaseous.

Application

Concept

Metals differ in their reactions with oxygen, water and dilute nonoxidizing acids.

Theory

Metals differ in their reactions with oxygen, water and dilute nonoxidizing acids. Reaction observations must specify the metal and conditions. Magnesium burns in oxygen; iron rusts in moist air; some metals release hydrogen from dilute acid, whereas copper does not behave like magnesium in dilute hydrochloric acid. Worked case: Magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid gives magnesium chloride and hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. Hydrogen evolution is predicted from the metal-acid reaction, not from electrical conductivity alone. Interpretation and limits: Not every metal reacts with cold water or liberates hydrogen from every acid. Application: Metal reactivity guides material compatibility and safe selection of reaction conditions.

Concept

A liquid conducts electricity when mobile charge carriers can transport charge through it.

Theory

A liquid conducts electricity when mobile charge carriers can transport charge through it. In aqueous electrolytes, ions carry charge through the solution, while electrons move through external metal wires. A weak lamp response may reflect concentration, geometry or tester sensitivity. Worked case: An aqueous sodium chloride solution conducts because Na+ and Cl- ions are mobile. A sugar solution at comparable concentration does not form the same ionic carriers merely because sugar dissolves. Interpretation and limits: Dissolving a substance does not automatically make its solution a strong electrical conductor. Application: Conductivity measurements help distinguish ionic solutions and monitor dissolved-ion content.

An aqueous sodium chloride solution conducts because Na+ and Cl- ions are mobile. A sugar solution at comparable concentration does not form the same ionic carriers merely because sugar dissolves.

Correction / limitation

Concept

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction.

Theory

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction. The power supply pushes electrons, while ions migrate to electrodes. Deposited or released amount is proportional to charge passed. Worked case: passing 193000 C through Cu2+ solution supplies 2 mol electrons and ideally deposits 1 mol copper. Interpretation and limits: Electrode signs differ from a galvanic cell, but oxidation remains at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Application: Electrolysis is used for plating, metal refining, chemical manufacture and hydrogen production.

Correction / limitation

Electrode signs differ from a galvanic cell, but oxidation remains at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

Application

Electrolysis is used for plating, metal refining, chemical manufacture and hydrogen production.

Concept

Fibres differ in molecular composition, source and interactions with water and heat.

Theory

Fibres differ in molecular composition, source and interactions with water and heat. Cotton is rich in cellulose, while common synthetic fibres include polyesters and polyamides. Source and structure influence moisture absorption and thermal response but do not alone determine all fabric performance. Worked case: A cotton sample absorbs water into its polar cellulose-rich structure, whereas many polyester fibres absorb less water into the fibre itself. Fabric weave and finishes can also affect how quickly a drop spreads. Interpretation and limits: Natural does not automatically mean safer in every use, and synthetic does not mean waterproof. Application: Fibre selection matches comfort, durability and care requirements to molecular and fabric structure.

Concept

Thermoplastics soften on heating within a usable range, while thermosets contain networks that do not simply remelt.

Theory

Thermoplastics soften on heating within a usable range, while thermosets contain networks that do not simply remelt. Thermosets develop covalent crosslinks during curing. Excess heating may degrade either material, so softening behaviour must not be mistaken for unlimited heat stability. Worked case: Polyethylene can be reshaped by suitable heating, whereas a cured epoxy network does not melt into the same flowable material; excessive heating instead damages it. Interpretation and limits: A thermoset is not merely a thermoplastic cooled to a lower temperature. Application: Polymer architecture informs moulding methods, repair options and recycling constraints.

Concept

Coal and petroleum are complex mixtures, and petroleum refining separates useful boiling-range fractions.

Theory

Coal and petroleum are complex mixtures, and petroleum refining separates useful boiling-range fractions. Fractional distillation separates components by relative volatility. Cracking changes molecules chemically, whereas distillation mainly separates molecules already present. Worked case: In a refinery column, lighter more volatile hydrocarbons tend to be collected higher in the column than heavy fractions. A fraction is still a mixture, not one compound with a unique formula. Interpretation and limits: Distillation and cracking are not the same operation, and petrol is not a single pure substance. Application: Fraction properties guide fuel blending and petrochemical feedstock selection.

Concept

Combustion is a rapid reaction with oxygen that releases energy, often as heat and light.

Theory

Combustion is a rapid reaction with oxygen that releases energy, often as heat and light. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon forms carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen can produce carbon monoxide or soot. Worked case: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O releases energy in a clean-burning gas flame. Interpretation and limits: Combustion is not simply 'burning with a flame'; some oxidation releases energy without a visible flame. Application: Combustion powers cooking, engines and industry, while emission control reduces pollution.

Concept

Fuel performance depends on useful energy delivery as well as combustion emissions and operating conditions.

Theory

Fuel performance depends on useful energy delivery as well as combustion emissions and operating conditions. Calorific value measures energy per fuel amount, while appliance efficiency describes the fraction delivered usefully. Incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide and particulate pollutants. Worked case: Two stoves burn the same fuel, but one transfers more released heat to a pot. Its greater useful efficiency does not change the fuel's intrinsic calorific value. Interpretation and limits: A high calorific value does not guarantee clean combustion or high appliance efficiency. Application: Fuel and equipment comparisons should include useful energy, emissions and ventilation requirements.

Concept

Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom.

Theory

Quantum numbers are four labels that describe the state of an electron in an atom. The principal number n identifies shell and energy, l identifies subshell shape, ml identifies orbital orientation, and ms identifies spin. Only allowed combinations describe possible electron states. Worked case: an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2. Interpretation and limits: Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n. Application: Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior.

Worked case

an electron in a 2p orbital has n = 2 and l = 1; ml can be -1, 0 or +1 and ms can be +1/2 or -1/2.

Relationship

n = 1,2,...; l = 0 to n-1; ml = -l to +l; ms = +/-1/2

Correction / limitation

Do not assign l = 2 when n = 2; allowed l values must be smaller than n.

Application

Quantum numbers organize electron configurations and help interpret spectra and periodic behavior.

An orbital is a three-dimensional probability region that can hold at most two electrons.

Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals.

Theory

Electron configuration records how an atom's electrons occupy shells, subshells and orbitals. Electrons are placed in available low-energy states while obeying Aufbau filling, Hund's rule and the Pauli principle. Valence electrons largely control chemical behavior. Atomic Structure · Aufbauexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: potassium fills 4s before 3d, giving [Ar]4s1 because 4s is lower in energy for the neutral atom at that stage. Key check: after solving Aufbau, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

The Aufbau principle states that electrons occupy lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals.

Theory

The Aufbau principle states that electrons occupy lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals. The usual filling order follows increasing n + l; when two subshells have equal n + l, the one with lower n fills first. Some transition elements have exceptions. Worked case: potassium fills 4s before 3d, giving [Ar]4s1 because 4s is lower in energy for the neutral atom at that stage. Interpretation and limits: Do not treat the diagonal filling order as exception-free, especially for chromium and copper. Application: Aufbau filling helps construct ground-state configurations and understand periodic organization.

Worked case

potassium fills 4s before 3d, giving [Ar]4s1 because 4s is lower in energy for the neutral atom at that stage.

Relationship

lower orbital energy fills first; use the n + l rule

Correction / limitation

Do not treat the diagonal filling order as exception-free, especially for chromium and copper.

Application

Aufbau filling helps construct ground-state configurations and understand periodic organization.

Concept

Hund's rule states that electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.

Theory

Hund's rule states that electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing. Spreading electrons across degenerate orbitals reduces repulsion and gives a lower-energy arrangement. Worked case: nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy the three p orbitals separately with parallel spins rather than pairing in one orbital. Interpretation and limits: Do not pair electrons in one p orbital while another orbital of the same subshell is empty. Application: Hund's rule predicts unpaired electrons and therefore helps explain magnetic behavior.

Worked case

nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy the three p orbitals separately with parallel spins rather than pairing in one orbital.

Relationship

degenerate orbitals: single occupation before pairing

Correction / limitation

Do not pair electrons in one p orbital while another orbital of the same subshell is empty.

Application

Hund's rule predicts unpaired electrons and therefore helps explain magnetic behavior.

Atomic Structure · Pauli principleexisting authored record

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: a filled 1s orbital is written with one spin-up and one spin-down electron; a third electron must enter 2s. Key check: after solving Pauli principle, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in one atom have the same four quantum numbers.

Theory

The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in one atom have the same four quantum numbers. Therefore one orbital holds at most two electrons, and those two must have opposite spins. Worked case: a filled 1s orbital is written with one spin-up and one spin-down electron; a third electron must enter 2s. Interpretation and limits: Pauli does not say electrons must remain unpaired; it restricts how paired electrons occupy one orbital. Application: The principle determines orbital capacity, configurations and the structure of the periodic table.

Worked case

a filled 1s orbital is written with one spin-up and one spin-down electron; a third electron must enter 2s.

Relationship

one orbital -> maximum 2 electrons with opposite spins

Correction / limitation

Pauli does not say electrons must remain unpaired; it restricts how paired electrons occupy one orbital.

Application

The principle determines orbital capacity, configurations and the structure of the periodic table.

Assessment prompt

Which statement describes Pauli principle in Atomic Structure?

Case walkthrough

  1. a filled 1s orbital is written with one spin-up and one spin-down electron
  2. a third electron must enter 2s.
  3. one orbital -> maximum 2 electrons with opposite spins
  4. Therefore one orbital holds at most two electrons, and those two must have opposite spins.
  5. Pauli does not say electrons must remain unpaired; it restricts how paired electrons occupy one orbital.

Concept

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

Theory

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Shared electron density attracts both nuclei. Single, double and triple bonds differ in shared pairs, length and strength. Worked case: in H2, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duet. Interpretation and limits: Sharing is not always perfectly equal; electronegativity differences can make a covalent bond polar. Application: Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids.

Relationship

Application

Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids.

Theory

Van der Waals forces are weak attractions between atoms or molecules caused by permanent or temporary dipoles. Worked case: iodine is solid at room temperature because its large electron clouds produce stronger dispersion forces than those in chlorine. Interpretation and limits: Weak individually does not mean unimportant; many attractions together can strongly affect properties. Worked case: NH3 has four electron domains but one lone pair, giving tetrahedral electron geometry and trigonal-pyramidal molecular shape. Interpretation and limits: Do not count a double bond as two domains or include lone pairs as atoms in the molecular-shape name. The model connects Lewis structures with sigma-bond geometry. Worked case: carbon in methane is described as sp3 hybridized, giving four equivalent orbitals directed tetrahedrally. Interpretation and limits: Hybridization is a bonding model, not a physical stirring of orbitals, and pi bonds use unhybridized orbitals. Gas laws describe relationships among pressure, volume, temperature and amount. Boyle's law applies at constant temperature, Charles's law at constant pressure and Avogadro's law at fixed temperature and pressure. Temperature must be absolute. Worked case: at constant temperature, compressing a gas from 2.0 L to 1.0 L doubles its pressure because P1V1 = P2V2. Interpretation and limits: Never substitute Celsius temperature directly into gas-law ratios; convert it to kelvin. Application: Gas laws guide tyres, syringes, weather balloons, breathing and gas storage.

at constant temperature, compressing a gas from 2.0 L to 1.0 L doubles its pressure because P1V1 = P2V2.

P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 for fixed amount

Never substitute Celsius temperature directly into gas-law ratios; convert it to kelvin.

Gas laws guide tyres, syringes, weather balloons, breathing and gas storage.

The ideal gas equation combines pressure, volume, amount and absolute temperature.

Ideal particles collide elastically, have negligible individual volume and exert pressure through wall collisions. Average kinetic energy depends on absolute temperature. Worked case: heating a sealed rigid container makes particles move faster and strike the walls more forcefully, raising pressure. Interpretation and limits: Equal temperature means equal average kinetic energy, not equal molecular speed for different gases. Concept

Surface tension is the energy required to increase a liquid's surface area.

Theory

Surface tension is the energy required to increase a liquid's surface area. Surface molecules experience a net inward attraction, so the surface tends to minimize area. Stronger cohesive forces generally produce higher surface tension. Worked case: small water drops become nearly spherical because a sphere has minimum surface area for its volume. Interpretation and limits: Surface tension is not a solid skin; it results from unbalanced molecular attractions at an interface. Application: Surface tension affects detergents, capillary tubes, inkjet printing and biological droplets.

Higher temperature raises vapour pressure; stronger attractions lower it. Interpretation and limits: Vapour pressure is not the same as atmospheric pressure and applies even below the boiling point.
