Concept

A buffer resists large pH changes when small amounts of acid or base are added.

Theory

A buffer resists large pH changes when small amounts of acid or base are added. It commonly contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, which consume added OH- and H3O+ respectively. Buffer capacity is limited. Worked case: an ethanoic acid/ethanoate buffer uses CH3COOH to neutralize added OH- and CH3COO- to consume added H3O+. Interpretation and limits: A buffer does not keep pH perfectly fixed and fails when too much acid or base is added. Application: Buffers stabilize blood, medicines, foods, fermentation and analytical solutions.

Concept

Salts are ionic compounds produced when acid hydrogen is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.

Theory

Salts are ionic compounds produced when acid hydrogen is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. They may be prepared by neutralization, precipitation or reactions of acids with metals, oxides or carbonates. Solubility and hydrolysis determine their behavior. Worked case: H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O prepares sodium sulfate by neutralization. Interpretation and limits: Not every salt is neutral in solution, and 'salt' in chemistry includes far more than sodium chloride. Application: Salts are used in fertilizers, medicines, food, water treatment, construction and manufacturing.

Concept

Conservation of mass and definite proportions constrain how elements combine in compounds.

Theory

Conservation of mass and definite proportions constrain how elements combine in compounds. A balanced reaction preserves each element's atoms. A pure compound contains its constituent elements in a characteristic mass ratio, although mixtures can have variable composition. Worked case: When 2 g of hydrogen reacts completely with 16 g of oxygen, 18 g of water forms in a closed system. Doubling both masses gives 36 g of water, preserving the 1:8 hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio. Interpretation and limits: Apparent mass loss from an open beaker may be escaping gas rather than destroyed matter. Application: Mass balances check reaction equations and quantify material flows through chemical plants.

Worked case

When 2 g of hydrogen reacts completely with 16 g of oxygen, 18 g of water forms in a closed system. Doubling both masses gives 36 g of water, preserving the 1:8 hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio.

Relationship

mass of reactants = mass of products in a closed system

Correction / limitation

Apparent mass loss from an open beaker may be escaping gas rather than destroyed matter.

Application

Concept

Dalton proposed that matter consists of atoms and that chemical reactions rearrange them in whole-number ratios.

Theory

Dalton proposed that matter consists of atoms and that chemical reactions rearrange them in whole-number ratios. His theory explained conservation of mass and fixed composition. We now know atoms are divisible and isotopes of one element can have different masses. Worked case: water forms with hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a fixed ratio, consistent with atoms combining in simple whole numbers. Interpretation and limits: Dalton's claim that atoms are indivisible is historically important but not part of the modern model. Application: Dalton's ideas provide the foundation for formulas, equations and stoichiometry.

Correction / limitation

Concept

The atomic idea developed from philosophical proposals into an evidence-based scientific model. A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds.

Theory

The atomic idea developed from philosophical proposals into an evidence-based scientific model. A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds. Democritus suggested indivisible particles, but later experiments by Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr and others revealed atoms, electrons, nuclei and quantized behavior. Molecules may contain one element, such as O2, or several elements, such as H2O. Ionic compounds form formula units rather than separate molecules. Worked case: cathode-ray experiments showed that all atoms contain the same negatively charged particle, the electron. Example: one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom. Interpretation and limits: No single scientist discovered the complete modern atom at once. Do not call every compound a molecule; sodium chloride is an ionic lattice. Application: Atomic models explain materials, electricity, spectra, medicines and nuclear energy. Molecular structure determines smell, color, solubility, medicine action and material behavior.

Worked case

cathode-ray experiments showed that all atoms contain the same negatively charged particle, the electron. Example: one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom.

Relationship

new evidence -> revised atomic model molecule = definite group of covalently bonded atoms

Correction / limitation

No single scientist discovered the complete modern atom at once. Do not call every compound a molecule; sodium chloride is an ionic lattice.

Application

Atomic models explain materials, electricity, spectra, medicines and nuclear energy. Molecular structure determines smell, color, solubility, medicine action and material behavior.

Worked example focus: write the relationship, define variables, substitute units and interpret the trend. Example: 18.0 g of H₂O ÷ 18.0 g mol⁻¹ = 1.00 mol H₂O. Concept

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Avogadro's number is the number of specified particles in one mole: exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Theory

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Avogadro's number is the number of specified particles in one mole: exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole contains Avogadro's number of specified entities. Molar mass converts between amount in moles and measured mass. It links the microscopic count of atoms, molecules or ions to laboratory-scale amounts. Worked case: 18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: 0.50 mol of oxygen molecules contains 0.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ O₂ molecules. Interpretation and limits: Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Always state the entity being counted; one mole of O atoms differs from one mole of O2 molecules. Application: Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. The constant connects measured masses with particle counts in reactions and materials.

Worked case

18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: 0.50 mol of oxygen molecules contains 0.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ O₂ molecules.

Relationship

moles = mass / molar mass number of particles = moles × Avogadro constant

Correction / limitation

Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Always state the entity being counted; one mole of O atoms differs from one mole of O2 molecules.

Application

Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. The constant connects measured masses with particle counts in reactions and materials.

Concept

The Bohr model places electrons in fixed, quantized energy levels around the nucleus. Valency is an atom's combining capacity, often related to electrons lost, gained or shared.

Theory

The Bohr model places electrons in fixed, quantized energy levels around the nucleus. Valency is an atom's combining capacity, often related to electrons lost, gained or shared. An electron absorbs energy to move higher and emits a photon when it returns to a lower level. The model explains hydrogen's line spectrum well. For simple main-group compounds, valency helps predict how many bonds an atom forms or the charge of its common ion. Worked case: an excited hydrogen electron dropping to a lower level releases light with energy equal to the difference between the levels. Example: magnesium has valency 2 and chlorine has valency 1, giving MgCl2 so the combining capacities balance. Interpretation and limits: Bohr paths are a useful school model, not literal planetary orbits for all atoms. Valency is not always identical to oxidation state, especially for elements with variable behavior. Application: Energy-level ideas help explain flame colors, spectra and electronic transitions. Valency helps learners write formulas and understand common bonding patterns.

Worked case

an excited hydrogen electron dropping to a lower level releases light with energy equal to the difference between the levels. Example: magnesium has valency 2 and chlorine has valency 1, giving MgCl2 so the combining capacities balance.

Relationship

photon energy = higher level energy - lower level energy total positive combining capacity = total negative combining capacity

Correction / limitation

Bohr paths are a useful school model, not literal planetary orbits for all atoms. Valency is not always identical to oxidation state, especially for elements with variable behavior.

Application

Concept

Molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. Formula mass is the sum of atomic masses in one formula unit of a substance.

Theory

Molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. Formula mass is the sum of atomic masses in one formula unit of a substance. The molecular formula tells how many of each atom to include. Relative molecular mass is dimensionless; molecular mass is often expressed in unified atomic mass units. The term is especially useful for ionic compounds, which do not exist as separate molecules. Worked case: H2O has molecular mass 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016 u. Example: NaCl has formula mass 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44 u per formula unit. Interpretation and limits: Remember to multiply each atomic mass by its subscript. Do not describe an ionic lattice such as NaCl as having a molecular mass. Application: Molecular mass is used to compare molecules and convert between mass and amount of substance. Formula mass supports calculations for salts, minerals and ionic materials.

Correction / limitation

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.

Theory

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. One mole contains Avogadro's number of specified entities. Molar mass converts between amount in moles and measured mass. The molecular formula tells how many of each atom to include. Relative molecular mass is dimensionless; molecular mass is often expressed in unified atomic mass units. Worked case: 18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: H2O has molecular mass 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016 u. Interpretation and limits: Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Remember to multiply each atomic mass by its subscript. Application: Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. Molecular mass is used to compare molecules and convert between mass and amount of substance.

Worked case

18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: H2O has molecular mass 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016 u.

Relationship

moles = mass / molar mass molecular mass = sum of atomic masses in the molecular formula

Correction / limitation

Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Remember to multiply each atomic mass by its subscript.

Application

Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. Molecular mass is used to compare molecules and convert between mass and amount of substance.

Concept

Mass percentage states what fraction of a compound's mass comes from one element.

Theory

Mass percentage states what fraction of a compound's mass comes from one element. Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript, add the contributions to obtain formula mass, and divide the selected element's contribution by the total. Percentages for all elements sum to 100 within rounding. Worked case: Using H = 1 and O = 16, water has formula mass 18. Hydrogen contributes 2/18 x 100 = 11.1%, while oxygen contributes 16/18 x 100 = 88.9%. Interpretation and limits: Use the mass of all atoms of the element, not just one atom when its subscript exceeds one. Application: Elemental-analysis percentages help infer empirical formulae and assess sample composition.

Worked case

Using H = 1 and O = 16, water has formula mass 18. Hydrogen contributes 2/18 x 100 = 11.1%, while oxygen contributes 16/18 x 100 = 88.9%.

Relationship

element mass percent = element mass contribution / formula mass x 100

Correction / limitation

Use the mass of all atoms of the element, not just one atom when its subscript exceeds one.

Application

Elemental-analysis percentages help infer empirical formulae and assess sample composition.

Concept

The limiting reagent is the reactant consumed first and therefore sets the maximum product amount.

Theory

The limiting reagent is the reactant consumed first and therefore sets the maximum product amount. Compare each reactant in moles relative to its balanced coefficient. The other reactant is present in excess. Worked case: for 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, 3 mol H2 needs 1.5 mol O2; if only 1 mol O2 is available, O2 is limiting. Interpretation and limits: Do not choose the reactant with the smaller mass without converting to moles and using coefficients. Application: Limiting-reagent control reduces waste and predicts output in manufacturing and synthesis.

Worked case

for 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, 3 mol H2 needs 1.5 mol O2; if only 1 mol O2 is available, O2 is limiting.

Relationship

smallest value of moles/coefficient identifies the limiting reagent

Correction / limitation

Do not choose the reactant with the smaller mass without converting to moles and using coefficients.

Application

Limiting-reagent control reduces waste and predicts output in manufacturing and synthesis.

Concept

The activity series orders metals by their tendency to undergo oxidation in common displacement reactions.

Theory

The activity series orders metals by their tendency to undergo oxidation in common displacement reactions. Relative position predicts whether a metal can reduce another metal ion. Reaction rate, surface films and solution conditions can affect what is observed, so the series is not a universal speed ranking. Worked case: Iron added to copper sulfate deposits copper: Fe + Cu2+ -> Fe2+ + Cu. Silver added to iron sulfate does not displace iron because silver is less readily oxidized in this comparison. Interpretation and limits: Do not infer that an unreactive-looking aluminium surface means aluminium is intrinsically less active; its oxide film can passivate it. Application: The series guides sacrificial-anode selection and elementary metal-displacement predictions.

Worked case

Iron added to copper sulfate deposits copper: Fe + Cu2+ -> Fe2+ + Cu. Silver added to iron sulfate does not displace iron because silver is less readily oxidized in this comparison.

Relationship

more active metal + less active metal ion -> displacement

Correction / limitation

Do not infer that an unreactive-looking aluminium surface means aluminium is intrinsically less active; its oxide film can passivate it.

Application

The series guides sacrificial-anode selection and elementary metal-displacement predictions.

Concept

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element in a compound.

Theory

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element in a compound. The reactivity series predicts whether the replacement will occur and electron transfer is often involved. Worked case: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu because zinc is more reactive than copper. Interpretation and limits: A less reactive metal cannot normally displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution. Application: Displacement reactions are used in metal extraction, batteries and reactivity tests.

Worked case

Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu because zinc is more reactive than copper.

A + BC -> AC + B

Correction / limitation

A less reactive metal cannot normally displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution.

Displacement reactions are used in metal extraction, batteries and reactivity tests.

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Zinc loses two electrons and is oxidized; copper(II) gains those electrons and is reduced. The electron count lost and gained is equal. Key check: after solving Oxidation and reduction, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Oxidation is loss of electrons; at an introductory level it can also be recognized as gain of oxygen. Reduction is gain of electrons; it may also appear as removal of oxygen from a substance.

Theory

Oxidation is loss of electrons; at an introductory level it can also be recognized as gain of oxygen. Reduction is gain of electrons; it may also appear as removal of oxygen from a substance. Oxidation and reduction happen together because electrons lost by one species must be gained by another. A reducing process lowers the oxidation state of a species and must be paired with oxidation elsewhere. Worked case: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e- shows magnesium being oxidized during formation of magnesium oxide. Example: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu shows copper(II) ions being reduced to copper metal. Interpretation and limits: Oxidation does not always involve oxygen. Reduction does not mean making a substance physically smaller. Application: Oxidation occurs in combustion, rusting, respiration, bleaching and batteries. Reduction is central to metal extraction, electroplating, batteries and biological energy transfer.

Worked case

Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e- shows magnesium being oxidized during formation of magnesium oxide. Example: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu shows copper(II) ions being reduced to copper metal.

Relationship

oxidation = loss of electrons reduction = gain of electrons

Correction / limitation

Oxidation does not always involve oxygen. Reduction does not mean making a substance physically smaller.

Application

Oxidation occurs in combustion, rusting, respiration, bleaching and batteries. Reduction is central to metal extraction, electroplating, batteries and biological energy transfer.

Concept

Corrosion is unwanted electrochemical oxidation of a material by its environment. Oxidation of carbon compounds commonly adds oxygen, removes hydrogen or raises the oxidation state of carbon.

Theory

Corrosion is unwanted electrochemical oxidation of a material by its environment. Oxidation of carbon compounds commonly adds oxygen, removes hydrogen or raises the oxidation state of carbon. For iron rusting, anodic iron dissolution and cathodic oxygen reduction occur at different surface regions; water and ions complete the circuit. Alkaline KMnO4 or acidified K2Cr2O7 oxidises ethanol first to ethanal and then ethanoic acid. Combustion is more extensive oxidation to CO2 and water when oxygen is sufficient. Worked case: zinc coating protects steel both as a barrier and, if scratched, by oxidizing sacrificially before iron. Example: Warming ethanol with an oxidising agent changes it toward ethanoic acid; the product has acidic properties unlike the starting alcohol. Interpretation and limits: Rusting requires an electrochemical pathway; oxygen alone without suitable moisture is insufficient for ordinary rust formation. Do not assume adding visible oxygen gas is the only oxidation pathway; oxidising agents transfer oxygen or remove hydrogen chemically. Application: Corrosion science protects bridges, pipelines, vehicles, ships and electronic equipment. Controlled oxidation produces acids, aldehydes and industrial intermediates, while uncontrolled oxidation affects fuels and food spoilage.

Worked case

zinc coating protects steel both as a barrier and, if scratched, by oxidizing sacrificially before iron. Example: Warming ethanol with an oxidising agent changes it toward ethanoic acid; the product has acidic properties unlike the starting alcohol.

Relationship

anode: Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e- CH3CH2OH + 2[O] -> CH3COOH + H2O

Correction / limitation

Rusting requires an electrochemical pathway; oxygen alone without suitable moisture is insufficient for ordinary rust formation. Do not assume adding visible oxygen gas is the only oxidation pathway; oxidising agents transfer oxygen or remove hydrogen chemically.

Application

Corrosion science protects bridges, pipelines, vehicles, ships and electronic equipment. Controlled oxidation produces acids, aldehydes and industrial intermediates, while uncontrolled oxidation affects fuels and food spoilage.

Concept

Exothermic reactions transfer heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings.

Theory

Exothermic reactions transfer heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings. In an exothermic process the surroundings warm and products have lower enthalpy than reactants; in an endothermic process the surroundings cool and products have higher enthalpy. Activation energy is still required to begin either type. Worked case: Combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat, is exothermic. Thermal decomposition of CaCO3 requires heat and is endothermic. Interpretation and limits: A reaction that needs ignition is not necessarily endothermic; combustion needs activation energy but releases more energy overall. Application: Heat classification explains fuels, respiration, cold packs, thermal decomposition and energy-efficient industrial reactions.

Worked case

Combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat, is exothermic. Thermal decomposition of CaCO3 requires heat and is endothermic.

Relationship

exothermic: reactants -> products + heat; endothermic: reactants + heat -> products

Correction / limitation

A reaction that needs ignition is not necessarily endothermic; combustion needs activation energy but releases more energy overall.

Application

Heat classification explains fuels, respiration, cold packs, thermal decomposition and energy-efficient industrial reactions.

Concept

A metal's natural occurrence depends partly on its reactivity and the stability of its compounds.

Theory

A metal's natural occurrence depends partly on its reactivity and the stability of its compounds. Very reactive metals usually occur as compounds, while some less reactive metals can occur in native form. A mineral becomes an ore when extraction is economically and technically worthwhile. Worked case: Sodium is found in salts rather than as lumps of native sodium. Gold can occur as native metal. Bauxite is an important aluminium ore, but not every aluminium-containing rock is an economical ore. Interpretation and limits: Mineral and ore are not interchangeable terms, and native occurrence does not imply unlimited abundance. Application: Ore assessment connects chemical composition with extraction route, energy demand and recoverable metal content.

Worked case

Sodium is found in salts rather than as lumps of native sodium. Gold can occur as native metal. Bauxite is an important aluminium ore, but not every aluminium-containing rock is an economical ore.

Relationship

ore = mineral deposit suitable for economical extraction

Correction / limitation

Mineral and ore are not interchangeable terms, and native occurrence does not imply unlimited abundance.

Application

Ore assessment connects chemical composition with extraction route, energy demand and recoverable metal content.

Concept

Ore concentration increases the fraction of useful mineral before chemical extraction.

Theory

Ore concentration increases the fraction of useful mineral before chemical extraction. Separation methods exploit differences such as density, magnetic behaviour or surface wettability. The chosen process must match the mineral rather than merely the metal's name. Worked case: In froth flotation of a suitable sulfide ore, treated mineral particles attach to air bubbles and enter the froth, while much of the wetted gangue remains in the slurry. Interpretation and limits: Flotation does not reduce metal ions to metal; concentration and reduction are different stages. Application: Concentration reduces the mass of gangue that must be transported, heated or chemically treated.

Worked case

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Application

Concentration reduces the mass of gangue that must be transported, heated or chemically treated.

Concept

A metal's position in the reactivity series determines whether it is extracted by electrolysis, chemical reduction or heating of its ore.

Theory

A metal's position in the reactivity series determines whether it is extracted by electrolysis, chemical reduction or heating of its ore. Highly reactive K-Ca-Na-Mg-Al metals require electrolysis of molten compounds. Middle metals such as Zn, Fe, Pb and Cu are commonly obtained after converting ores to oxides and reducing with carbon/CO or aluminium. Low-reactivity metals may occur native or be recovered by heating. Worked case: ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis. Interpretation and limits: Do not propose carbon reduction for sodium or aluminium oxides; these metals are more reactive than carbon. Application: Selecting extraction routes balances chemical feasibility, energy demand, ore composition, pollution control and recycling.

Worked case

ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis.

Relationship

high activity -> electrolysis; middle -> roasting/calcination then reduction; low -> heating or native occurrence

Correction / limitation

Do not propose carbon reduction for sodium or aluminium oxides; these metals are more reactive than carbon.

Application

Selecting extraction routes balances chemical feasibility, energy demand, ore composition, pollution control and recycling.

Concept

An alloy is a metallic material containing more than one element and designed for useful properties.

Theory

An alloy is a metallic material containing more than one element and designed for useful properties. Substitutional atoms replace host atoms; small interstitial atoms can occupy spaces in a metallic lattice. These changes can alter strength, corrosion behaviour and electrical conductivity. Worked case: Compare pure iron with a low-carbon steel. A small carbon content changes the microstructure and mechanical response; steel is not simply iron coated with carbon. Brass contains copper and zinc. Interpretation and limits: An alloy need not be a compound with a fixed formula, and not every alloy is a single solid phase. Application: Steel structures, brass fittings and corrosion-resistant alloys are selected by matching composition and processing to service conditions.

Worked case

Compare pure iron with a low-carbon steel. A small carbon content changes the microstructure and mechanical response; steel is not simply iron coated with carbon. Brass contains copper and zinc.

Relationship

composition + microstructure -> alloy properties

Correction / limitation

An alloy need not be a compound with a fixed formula, and not every alloy is a single solid phase.

Application

Steel structures, brass fittings and corrosion-resistant alloys are selected by matching composition and processing to service conditions.

Concept

Metal recycling recovers useful metal from scrap through sorting, separation and reprocessing.

Theory

Metal recycling recovers useful metal from scrap through sorting, separation and reprocessing. Recycling can avoid some primary ore processing but still uses energy. Contamination and alloy mixing can limit the quality of recovered material. Worked case: A mixed stream of aluminium beverage cans and steel cans is first separated using differences including magnetism. Aluminium scrap is then prepared for remelting; steel contamination must not be treated as part of the desired aluminium alloy. Interpretation and limits: Recycling is not energy-free, and mixing incompatible alloys can reduce the value of the recovered metal. Application: Closed-loop scrap collection helps preserve alloy quality and reduce primary metal demand.

Worked case

A mixed stream of aluminium beverage cans and steel cans is first separated using differences including magnetism. Aluminium scrap is then prepared for remelting; steel contamination must not be treated as part of the desired aluminium alloy.

Relationship

recoverable metal = scrap mass x metal fraction x recovery yield

Correction / limitation

Recycling is not energy-free, and mixing incompatible alloys can reduce the value of the recovered metal.

Application

Closed-loop scrap collection helps preserve alloy quality and reduce primary metal demand.

The domains point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles close to 109.5°. The symmetric molecule is non-polar overall. Key check: after solving Covalent bonding in carbon, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Electron-dot structures show valence electrons and the pairs transferred or shared during compound formation.

Theory

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Electron-dot structures show valence electrons and the pairs transferred or shared during compound formation. Shared electron density attracts both nuclei. Single, double and triple bonds differ in shared pairs, length and strength. Write the correct number of valence dots around each element symbol. For covalent molecules, place shared pairs between bonded atoms and lone pairs on the appropriate atoms. For ionic compounds, show bracketed ions with charges after electron transfer. Worked case: in H2, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duet. Example: In H2O, oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen and retains two lone pairs. For NaCl, show [Na]+ and [Cl]- with chlorine's complete octet. Interpretation and limits: Sharing is not always perfectly equal; electronegativity differences can make a covalent bond polar. Do not draw core electrons or omit ionic charges; electron-dot structures focus on valence electrons and must conserve the total electron count. Application: Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids. Dot structures provide a bridge from valency and formulas to bonding, shape and chemical reactivity.

Worked case

in H2, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duet. Example: In H2O, oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen and retains two lone pairs. For NaCl, show [Na]+ and [Cl]- with chlorine's complete octet.

Relationship

bond order: single < double < triple one shared pair = one covalent bond; bracket plus charge = ion

Correction / limitation

Sharing is not always perfectly equal; electronegativity differences can make a covalent bond polar. Do not draw core electrons or omit ionic charges; electron-dot structures focus on valence electrons and must conserve the total electron count.

Application

Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids. Dot structures provide a bridge from valency and formulas to bonding, shape and chemical reactivity.

Which statement describes Covalent bonding in carbon in Carbon Compounds?

Case walkthrough

  1. in H2, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duet.
  2. Example: In H2O, oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen and retains two lone pairs.
  3. For NaCl, show [Na]+ and [Cl]- with chlorine's complete octet.
  4. bond order: single < double < triple one shared pair = one covalent bond; bracket plus charge = ion
  5. Shared electron density attracts both nuclei.
  6. Single, double and triple bonds differ in shared pairs, length and strength.

Concept

A homologous series contains compounds with the same functional group and a common general formula, with successive members differing by CH2.

Theory

A homologous series contains compounds with the same functional group and a common general formula, with successive members differing by CH2. Similar functional groups produce related reaction patterns. Physical properties such as boiling point often vary progressively with chain length, but structural isomers can complicate simple comparisons. Worked case: Methanol CH3OH and ethanol C2H5OH are consecutive members of the monohydric alcohol series. Their formulas differ by CH2, corresponding to about 14 g/mol, and both contain an OH group. Interpretation and limits: Compounds are not homologues merely because their formulas contain carbon; the functional group and series must match. Application: Homologous trends help compare solvents and predict changes in volatility across a related family.

The solution is acidic, and diluting it tenfold ideally raises the pH by about one unit. Key check: after solving Ethanol and ethanoic acid, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides.

Theory

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides. Alkenes hydrate to alcohols; aldehydes and ketones reduce to primary and secondary alcohols. Primary alcohol oxidation gives aldehydes then acids, secondary gives ketones, while tertiary alcohols resist mild oxidation. Concentrated acid causes dehydration, and carboxylic acids give esters reversibly. Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes and hydrolysis of nitriles produce acids. Resonance stabilises carboxylate ions. Acids react with bicarbonate releasing CO2, esterify alcohols reversibly, and decarboxylate as sodium salts with soda lime. Electron-withdrawing substituents increase acidity. Worked case: CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O -> CH3COOH. With ethanoic acid and acid catalyst it forms ethyl ethanoate and water. Example: CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O. CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O with H+ and heat. Interpretation and limits: Do not state that all alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids; the product depends on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary. Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst. Application: Alcohol reactions support solvents, fuels, antiseptics, fragrances, polymers and pharmaceutical synthesis. Carboxylic-acid derivatives occur in medicines, polymers, food preservatives, fats, soaps and fragrances.

Relationship

RCH2OH + [O] -> RCHO -> RCOOH; ROH + R'COOH <=> R'COOR + H2O RCOOH + ROH <=> RCOOR + H2O; RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3

Correction / limitation

Do not state that all alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids; the product depends on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary. Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst.

Application

Alcohol reactions support solvents, fuels, antiseptics, fragrances, polymers and pharmaceutical synthesis. Carboxylic-acid derivatives occur in medicines, polymers, food preservatives, fats, soaps and fragrances.

Key check: after solving Soaps and detergents, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles. Synthetic detergents clean effectively in hard water because their calcium and magnesium salts remain much more soluble than soap scum.

Theory

Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles. Synthetic detergents clean effectively in hard water because their calcium and magnesium salts remain much more soluble than soap scum. Above a suitable concentration in water, tails cluster inward around oily dirt while charged heads face outward. Agitation breaks grease into suspended droplets that can be rinsed away. Soap carboxylate ions react with Ca2+ or Mg2+ to form insoluble scum, wasting soap and reducing lather. Sulfonate or sulfate detergent heads generally avoid this precipitation, though detergent biodegradability and phosphate pollution must be considered. Worked case: When oily cloth is washed with soap, micelles encapsulate oil and keep droplets dispersed instead of redepositing them on the fabric. Example: Soap lathers poorly in hard water until Ca2+/Mg2+ are removed, while a suitable detergent continues forming micelles and cleaning. Interpretation and limits: Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material. Do not claim every detergent is environmentally harmless merely because it works in hard water; composition and biodegradability matter. Application: Micelles enable washing, emulsification and formulation of cleaners and personal-care products. Detergents support domestic and industrial cleaning, while formulation choices affect wastewater and aquatic ecosystems.

hydrophobic tails -> grease core; hydrophilic COO- heads -> water 2RCOO- + Ca2+ -> (RCOO)2Ca(s) scum

Correction / limitation

Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material. Do not claim every detergent is environmentally harmless merely because it works in hard water; composition and biodegradability matter.

Application

Concept

A liquid has fixed volume but no fixed shape because its particles remain close while moving past one another. Gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.

Theory

A liquid has fixed volume but no fixed shape because its particles remain close while moving past one another. Gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume. Intermolecular attractions give liquids measurable viscosity, surface tension and vapour pressure. Gas particles are far apart, move rapidly in random directions and have weak attractions, so a gas fills its container and is easily compressed. Worked case: water flows to match a container but remains nearly incompressible because its molecules are close together. Example: perfume molecules spread through a room by diffusion, showing that gas particles move and mix. Interpretation and limits: Liquids are not particles with no attraction; their particles are close and interact strongly enough to maintain volume. A gas does not have zero mass; its low density simply makes its mass less obvious. Application: Liquid properties matter in fuels, lubricants, medicines, coatings and fluid transport. Gas behavior is used in breathing equipment, tyres, refrigeration and weather forecasting.

Worked case

water flows to match a container but remains nearly incompressible because its molecules are close together. Example: perfume molecules spread through a room by diffusion, showing that gas particles move and mix.

Relationship

liquid properties depend on intermolecular forces and temperature far-apart fast particles -> diffusion + high compressibility

Correction / limitation

Liquids are not particles with no attraction; their particles are close and interact strongly enough to maintain volume. A gas does not have zero mass; its low density simply makes its mass less obvious.

Application

Liquid properties matter in fuels, lubricants, medicines, coatings and fluid transport. Gas behavior is used in breathing equipment, tyres, refrigeration and weather forecasting.

  4. Intermolecular attractions give liquids measurable viscosity, surface tension and vapour pressure.
  5. Gas particles are far apart, move rapidly in random directions and have weak attractions, so a gas fills its container and is easily compressed.
  6. Liquids are not particles with no attraction; their particles are close and interact strongly enough to maintain volume. A gas does not have zero mass; its low density simply makes its mass less obvious.
Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Sublimation and latent heatexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield. Key check: after solving Sublimation and latent heat, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour from non-subliming solids. Heat is energy transferred solely because of a temperature difference.

Theory

Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour from non-subliming solids. Heat is energy transferred solely because of a temperature difference. Heat the mixture gently under an inverted funnel or cold surface. The sublimable component forms vapour and deposits as solid on the cooler surface, while the nonvolatile component remains. Suitable examples include ammonium chloride, camphor or naphthalene mixed with sand or salt. Heat flows spontaneously from hotter to colder regions. In chemistry, q is positive when the system absorbs heat and negative when it releases heat. Worked case: On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish. Example: if a reaction transfers 5.0 kJ to a water bath, qsystem = -5.0 kJ and qsurroundings = +5.0 kJ. Interpretation and limits: Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions. Heat is energy in transit, not a substance stored inside a body; internal energy is the state property. Application: Sublimation is used to purify volatile solids and illustrates particle motion during direct solid-gas changes. Heat-transfer calculations guide reactors, refrigeration, climate control and material processing.

On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish. Example: if a reaction transfers 5.0 kJ to a water bath, qsystem = -5.0 kJ and qsurroundings = +5.0 kJ.

Relationship

solid --heat--> vapour --cooling--> solid deposit qsystem = -qsurroundings in an insulated calorimeter

Correction / limitation

Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions. Heat is energy in transit, not a substance stored inside a body; internal energy is the state property.

Application

Sublimation is used to purify volatile solids and illustrates particle motion during direct solid-gas changes. Heat-transfer calculations guide reactors, refrigeration, climate control and material processing.

  4. Heat the mixture gently under an inverted funnel or cold surface.

Concept

Solutions can be classified by physical state, solvent-solute combination and degree of saturation. A colloid contains dispersed particles intermediate in size between a true solution and a suspension.

Theory

Solutions can be classified by physical state, solvent-solute combination and degree of saturation. A colloid contains dispersed particles intermediate in size between a true solution and a suspension. They may be gaseous, liquid or solid and may be unsaturated, saturated or supersaturated. A true solution is homogeneous at the particle scale. Colloidal particles remain distributed through Brownian motion and surface charge and scatter light in the Tyndall effect. Worked case: air is a gas solution, salt water is a solid-in-liquid solution and brass is a solid solution. Example: milk is a colloidal dispersion whose droplets scatter a beam of light even though they do not rapidly settle. Interpretation and limits: A solution does not have to be a liquid, and a suspension is not a true homogeneous solution. A colloid may look homogeneous to the eye but is heterogeneous at the microscopic scale. Application: Classifying solutions helps select preparation, storage and separation methods. Colloids occur in foods, medicines, paints, smoke control and nanomaterial processing.

Worked case

air is a gas solution, salt water is a solid-in-liquid solution and brass is a solid solution. Example: milk is a colloidal dispersion whose droplets scatter a beam of light even though they do not rapidly settle.

Relationship

solution = solvent + one or more solutes dispersed phase + dispersion medium -> colloid

Correction / limitation

A solution does not have to be a liquid, and a suspension is not a true homogeneous solution. A colloid may look homogeneous to the eye but is heterogeneous at the microscopic scale.

Application

Classifying solutions helps select preparation, storage and separation methods. Colloids occur in foods, medicines, paints, smoke control and nanomaterial processing.

Previous worked example

Concept

The Tyndall effect is visible light scattering by dispersed particles and can distinguish some colloids from true solutions.

Theory

The Tyndall effect is visible light scattering by dispersed particles and can distinguish some colloids from true solutions. Scattering depends on particle size, refractive-index contrast and concentration. A visible light path is not a direct quantitative concentration reading without calibration and controlled conditions. Worked case: A narrow light beam is visible through a suitable milk-water colloid but not similarly through a clean sodium chloride true solution. Both mixtures can appear uniformly mixed to the unaided eye. Interpretation and limits: A transparent appearance does not prove that a sample is a pure substance, and scattering alone does not identify the solute. Application: Light scattering helps characterize dispersions and distinguish forms of mixtures.

Worked case

A narrow light beam is visible through a suitable milk-water colloid but not similarly through a clean sodium chloride true solution. Both mixtures can appear uniformly mixed to the unaided eye.

Relationship

colloidal particles scatter light more strongly than molecularly dispersed solutes

Correction / limitation

A transparent appearance does not prove that a sample is a pure substance, and scattering alone does not identify the solute.

Application

Light scattering helps characterize dispersions and distinguish forms of mixtures.

Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Separating mixtures in class 9explicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: identify the chemical species, write the balanced relationship, predict the measurable change, and compare the prediction with evidence such as color, pH, mass, spectrum, reaction rate or product yield. Key check: after solving Separating mixtures in class 9, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Centrifugation speeds separation by spinning a mixture so denser suspended particles move outward and settle faster. Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances because they travel differently with a solvent over paper. Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour from non-subliming solids.

Theory

Centrifugation speeds separation by spinning a mixture so denser suspended particles move outward and settle faster. Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances because they travel differently with a solvent over paper. Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour from non-subliming solids. Opposing tubes must have equal masses and be placed symmetrically. After spinning at the specified speed and time, the dense sediment is the pellet and the liquid above it is the supernatant. Centrifugation helps when particles are too small or slow to settle by gravity alone. Place a small sample spot on a pencil baseline above the solvent. The solvent rises by capillary action; components repeatedly partition between the mobile solvent and stationary water/paper environment. Mark the solvent front immediately and compare spots using Rf under identical conditions. Heat the mixture gently under an inverted funnel or cold surface. The sublimable component forms vapour and deposits as solid on the cooler surface, while the nonvolatile component remains. Suitable examples include ammonium chloride, camphor or naphthalene mixed with sand or salt. Worked case: A milk separator uses spinning to divide components of different density; a laboratory centrifuge can separate fine chalk from water into pellet and supernatant. Example: If an ink dye travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm, Rf = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60. Example: On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish. Interpretation and limits: Never run a centrifuge with unbalanced tubes, an unsecured lid or cracked containers; imbalance can damage the rotor and injure users. Do not draw the baseline in ink or immerse the sample spot in solvent; either action contaminates or washes away the starting sample. Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions. Application: Centrifugation is used in dairies, clinical blood processing, wastewater treatment and laboratory sample preparation. Chromatography separates inks, food colours, plant pigments and components used in forensic or quality-control comparisons. Sublimation is used to purify volatile solids and illustrates particle motion during direct solid-gas changes.

Worked case

A milk separator uses spinning to divide components of different density; a laboratory centrifuge can separate fine chalk from water into pellet and supernatant. Example: If an ink dye travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm, Rf = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60. Example: On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish.

Relationship

greater density difference and rotation -> faster sedimentation Rf = distance travelled by solute / distance travelled by solvent front; 0 <= Rf <= 1 solid --heat--> vapour --cooling--> solid deposit

Correction / limitation

Never run a centrifuge with unbalanced tubes, an unsecured lid or cracked containers; imbalance can damage the rotor and injure users. Do not draw the baseline in ink or immerse the sample spot in solvent; either action contaminates or washes away the starting sample. Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions.

Application

Centrifugation is used in dairies, clinical blood processing, wastewater treatment and laboratory sample preparation. Chromatography separates inks, food colours, plant pigments and components used in forensic or quality-control comparisons. Sublimation is used to purify volatile solids and illustrates particle motion during direct solid-gas changes.

Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Crystallisation of dissolved solidsexisting authored record

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: Copper sulfate containing insoluble dirt is dissolved in hot water and filtered. Blue crystals form on slow cooling while much of the soluble impurity stays in solution. Key check: after solving Crystallisation of dissolved solids, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Crystallisation purifies a dissolved solid by forming ordered crystals from a hot concentrated solution as it cools.

Theory

Crystallisation purifies a dissolved solid by forming ordered crystals from a hot concentrated solution as it cools. Choose a solvent in which the solute is much more soluble when hot than cold. Dissolve the impure solid in minimum hot solvent, hot-filter insoluble impurities, concentrate if needed, cool without disturbance, filter the crystals, wash with a little cold solvent and dry. Soluble impurities largely remain in the mother liquor. Worked case: Copper sulfate containing insoluble dirt is dissolved in hot water and filtered. Blue crystals form on slow cooling while much of the soluble impurity stays in solution. Interpretation and limits: Do not evaporate all the solvent to dryness: rapid complete evaporation can trap impurities and gives poorer crystals. Application: Crystallisation purifies salt, sugar, pharmaceuticals and laboratory reagents while offering better purity than evaporation alone.

Worked case

Copper sulfate containing insoluble dirt is dissolved in hot water and filtered. Blue crystals form on slow cooling while much of the soluble impurity stays in solution.

Relationship

hot saturated solution -> cooling -> crystals + mother liquor

Correction / limitation

Do not evaporate all the solvent to dryness: rapid complete evaporation can trap impurities and gives poorer crystals.

Application

Crystallisation purifies salt, sugar, pharmaceuticals and laboratory reagents while offering better purity than evaporation alone.

Concept

Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from a nonvolatile solute or from another liquid with a sufficiently different boiling point.

Theory

Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from a nonvolatile solute or from another liquid with a sufficiently different boiling point. Heat the mixture safely, allow the more volatile component to vaporise, cool the vapour in a condenser and collect the distillate. A thermometer measures vapour temperature near the condenser entrance. Anti-bumping measures and an open receiving path prevent sudden boiling and pressure buildup. Worked case: Distilling salt water produces liquid water as distillate while dissolved salt remains in the flask; filtration could not remove that dissolved salt. Interpretation and limits: Do not seal a distillation apparatus or heat a flask to complete dryness, and do not confuse distillation with simple evaporation because the solvent is recovered. Application: Distillation supports water purification, solvent recovery and preparation of distilled laboratory water.

Worked case

Distilling salt water produces liquid water as distillate while dissolved salt remains in the flask; filtration could not remove that dissolved salt.

Relationship

liquid mixture --heating--> vapour --condensation--> distillate

Correction / limitation

Do not seal a distillation apparatus or heat a flask to complete dryness, and do not confuse distillation with simple evaporation because the solvent is recovered.

Application

Distillation supports water purification, solvent recovery and preparation of distilled laboratory water.

Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Paper chromatographyexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: If an ink dye travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm, Rf = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60. Key check: after solving Paper chromatography, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances because they travel differently with a solvent over paper.

Theory

Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances because they travel differently with a solvent over paper. Place a small sample spot on a pencil baseline above the solvent. The solvent rises by capillary action; components repeatedly partition between the mobile solvent and stationary water/paper environment. Mark the solvent front immediately and compare spots using Rf under identical conditions. Worked case: If an ink dye travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm, Rf = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60. Interpretation and limits: Do not draw the baseline in ink or immerse the sample spot in solvent; either action contaminates or washes away the starting sample. Application: Chromatography separates inks, food colours, plant pigments and components used in forensic or quality-control comparisons.

Worked case

If an ink dye travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm, Rf = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60.

Relationship

Rf = distance travelled by solute / distance travelled by solvent front; 0 <= Rf <= 1

Correction / limitation

Do not draw the baseline in ink or immerse the sample spot in solvent; either action contaminates or washes away the starting sample.

Application

Chromatography separates inks, food colours, plant pigments and components used in forensic or quality-control comparisons.

Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Sublimation as a separation methodexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish. Key check: after solving Sublimation as a separation method, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour from non-subliming solids.

Theory

Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour from non-subliming solids. Heat the mixture gently under an inverted funnel or cold surface. The sublimable component forms vapour and deposits as solid on the cooler surface, while the nonvolatile component remains. Suitable examples include ammonium chloride, camphor or naphthalene mixed with sand or salt. Worked case: On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish. Interpretation and limits: Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions. Application: Sublimation is used to purify volatile solids and illustrates particle motion during direct solid-gas changes.

Worked case

On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish.

Relationship

solid --heat--> vapour --cooling--> solid deposit

Correction / limitation

Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions.

Application

Sublimation is used to purify volatile solids and illustrates particle motion during direct solid-gas changes.

Assessment prompt

Case walkthrough

  2. solid --heat--> vapour --cooling--> solid deposit
  3. Heat the mixture gently under an inverted funnel or cold surface.
  4. The sublimable component forms vapour and deposits as solid on the cooler surface, while the nonvolatile component remains.
  5. Suitable examples include ammonium chloride, camphor or naphthalene mixed with sand or salt.
  6. Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions.
Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Centrifugation of mixturesexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: A milk separator uses spinning to divide components of different density; a laboratory centrifuge can separate fine chalk from water into pellet and supernatant. Key check: after solving Centrifugation of mixtures, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Centrifugation speeds separation by spinning a mixture so denser suspended particles move outward and settle faster.

Theory

Centrifugation speeds separation by spinning a mixture so denser suspended particles move outward and settle faster. Opposing tubes must have equal masses and be placed symmetrically. After spinning at the specified speed and time, the dense sediment is the pellet and the liquid above it is the supernatant. Centrifugation helps when particles are too small or slow to settle by gravity alone. Worked case: A milk separator uses spinning to divide components of different density; a laboratory centrifuge can separate fine chalk from water into pellet and supernatant. Interpretation and limits: Never run a centrifuge with unbalanced tubes, an unsecured lid or cracked containers; imbalance can damage the rotor and injure users. Application: Centrifugation is used in dairies, clinical blood processing, wastewater treatment and laboratory sample preparation.

Worked case

A milk separator uses spinning to divide components of different density; a laboratory centrifuge can separate fine chalk from water into pellet and supernatant.

Relationship

greater density difference and rotation -> faster sedimentation

Correction / limitation

Never run a centrifuge with unbalanced tubes, an unsecured lid or cracked containers; imbalance can damage the rotor and injure users.

Application

Centrifugation is used in dairies, clinical blood processing, wastewater treatment and laboratory sample preparation.

Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Coagulation of colloidsexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: Alum added during water treatment forms flocs that trap fine suspended dirt; the larger flocs settle more readily than individual colloidal particles. Key check: after solving Coagulation of colloids, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Coagulation makes tiny colloidal particles combine into larger aggregates that can settle or be filtered.

Theory

Coagulation makes tiny colloidal particles combine into larger aggregates that can settle or be filtered. Colloid particles often carry like charges that keep them dispersed. Adding a suitable electrolyte, heating, mixing oppositely charged sols or controlled stirring can reduce this stabilisation. In water treatment, coagulant produces flocs that capture suspended material before settling and filtration. Worked case: Alum added during water treatment forms flocs that trap fine suspended dirt; the larger flocs settle more readily than individual colloidal particles. Interpretation and limits: Do not describe coagulation as dissolving dirt or as filtration itself; it changes particle aggregation so later settling and filtration work better. Application: Coagulation clarifies drinking water, treats wastewater and supports food and materials processing.

Worked case

Alum added during water treatment forms flocs that trap fine suspended dirt; the larger flocs settle more readily than individual colloidal particles.

Relationship

destabilised colloid particles -> flocs -> settling or filtration

Correction / limitation

Do not describe coagulation as dissolving dirt or as filtration itself; it changes particle aggregation so later settling and filtration work better.

Application

Coagulation clarifies drinking water, treats wastewater and supports food and materials processing.

Concept

Concentration states how much solute is present in a specified amount of solution.

Theory

Concentration states how much solute is present in a specified amount of solution. Class 9 calculations use mass-by-mass percentage, mass-by-volume percentage and volume-by-volume percentage. Identify whether the denominator is mass or volume of the complete solution, use compatible units and include the percent sign. The mass of solution equals solute plus solvent mass. Worked case: A solution made from 10 g salt and 90 g water has total mass 100 g, so mass percentage = 10/100 x100 = 10%. Interpretation and limits: Do not divide by solvent amount when the definition asks for solution amount, and do not mix grams with kilograms or millilitres with litres without conversion. Application: Concentration calculations guide medicines, beverages, cleaning solutions, agriculture and laboratory preparation.

A solution made from 10 g salt and 90 g water has total mass 100 g, so mass percentage = 10/100 x100 = 10%.

Relationship

mass % = mass solute/mass solution x100; mass-volume % = mass solute/volume solution x100; volume % = volume solute/volume solution x100

Correction / limitation

Do not divide by solvent amount when the definition asks for solution amount, and do not mix grams with kilograms or millilitres with litres without conversion.

Application

Concentration calculations guide medicines, beverages, cleaning solutions, agriculture and laboratory preparation.

Class 9 Matter and Mixtures · Solubility curves and graphsexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: If 80 g solute dissolves in 100 g water at 80 °C but only 30 g at 20 °C, ideal cooling can produce 50 g crystals. Key check: after solving Solubility curves and graphs, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

A solubility curve shows the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in a fixed mass of solvent at different temperatures.

Theory

A solubility curve shows the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in a fixed mass of solvent at different temperatures. Read temperature on the horizontal axis and solubility—often grams solute per 100 g water—on the vertical axis. A point below the curve is unsaturated, on the curve saturated and above the curve represents excess solute or a supersaturated condition if temporarily maintained. The difference between hot and cold solubility predicts crystallisation yield. Worked case: If 80 g solute dissolves in 100 g water at 80 °C but only 30 g at 20 °C, ideal cooling can produce 50 g crystals. Interpretation and limits: Do not assume every solid becomes more soluble at the same rate with temperature; read the specific curve and its axis units. Application: Solubility graphs help design crystallisation, compare substances and predict whether a solution is saturated.

Worked case

If 80 g solute dissolves in 100 g water at 80 °C but only 30 g at 20 °C, ideal cooling can produce 50 g crystals.

Relationship

crystals expected = solute dissolved hot - solute remaining dissolved cold

Correction / limitation

Do not assume every solid becomes more soluble at the same rate with temperature; read the specific curve and its axis units.

Application

Solubility graphs help design crystallisation, compare substances and predict whether a solution is saturated.

Key check: after solving Laws of chemical combination, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Conservation of mass and definite proportions constrain how elements combine in compounds.

Theory

Conservation of mass and definite proportions constrain how elements combine in compounds. A balanced reaction preserves each element's atoms. A pure compound contains its constituent elements in a characteristic mass ratio, although mixtures can have variable composition. Worked case: When 2 g of hydrogen reacts completely with 16 g of oxygen, 18 g of water forms in a closed system. Doubling both masses gives 36 g of water, preserving the 1:8 hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio. Interpretation and limits: Apparent mass loss from an open beaker may be escaping gas rather than destroyed matter. Application: Mass balances check reaction equations and quantify material flows through chemical plants.

Worked case

When 2 g of hydrogen reacts completely with 16 g of oxygen, 18 g of water forms in a closed system. Doubling both masses gives 36 g of water, preserving the 1:8 hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio.

Relationship

mass of reactants = mass of products in a closed system

Correction / limitation

Apparent mass loss from an open beaker may be escaping gas rather than destroyed matter.

Application

Mass balances check reaction equations and quantify material flows through chemical plants.

Concept

Dalton proposed that matter consists of atoms and that chemical reactions rearrange them in whole-number ratios.

Theory

Dalton proposed that matter consists of atoms and that chemical reactions rearrange them in whole-number ratios. His theory explained conservation of mass and fixed composition. We now know atoms are divisible and isotopes of one element can have different masses. Worked case: water forms with hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a fixed ratio, consistent with atoms combining in simple whole numbers. Interpretation and limits: Dalton's claim that atoms are indivisible is historically important but not part of the modern model. Application: Dalton's ideas provide the foundation for formulas, equations and stoichiometry.

Correction / limitation

Dalton's claim that atoms are indivisible is historically important but not part of the modern model.

Class 9 Atoms and Formulae · Atomic mass and molecular massexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: 18.0 g of H₂O ÷ 18.0 g mol⁻¹ = 1.00 mol H₂O. This represents about 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, producing 1.00 mol H₂O requires 1.00 mol H₂ and 0.50 mol O₂. Key check: after solving Atomic mass and molecular mass, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus.

Theory

Molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus. The molecular formula tells how many of each atom to include. Relative molecular mass is dimensionless; molecular mass is often expressed in unified atomic mass units. It is a whole number written A. Electrons contribute so little mass that they are not counted in the mass number. Worked case: H2O has molecular mass 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016 u. Example: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23. Interpretation and limits: Remember to multiply each atomic mass by its subscript. Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table. Application: Molecular mass is used to compare molecules and convert between mass and amount of substance. Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers.

Worked case

H2O has molecular mass 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016 u. Example: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23.

Relationship

molecular mass = sum of atomic masses in the molecular formula A = Z + N

Correction / limitation

Remember to multiply each atomic mass by its subscript. Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table.

Application

Molecular mass is used to compare molecules and convert between mass and amount of substance. Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers.

Concept

Valency is an atom's combining capacity, often related to electrons lost, gained or shared. A chemical formula uses element symbols and subscripts to show a substance's composition.

Theory

Valency is an atom's combining capacity, often related to electrons lost, gained or shared. A chemical formula uses element symbols and subscripts to show a substance's composition. For simple main-group compounds, valency helps predict how many bonds an atom forms or the charge of its common ion. Subscripts tell the relative number of atoms or ions; coefficients count whole particles and must not be confused with subscripts. Worked case: magnesium has valency 2 and chlorine has valency 1, giving MgCl2 so the combining capacities balance. Example: Al3+ and O2- combine in the smallest neutral ratio to give Al2O3. Interpretation and limits: Valency is not always identical to oxidation state, especially for elements with variable behavior. Do not change subscripts to balance a reaction; that would change the substances. Application: Valency helps learners write formulas and understand common bonding patterns. Formulas provide a compact language for labels, equations, recipes and safety information.

Worked case

magnesium has valency 2 and chlorine has valency 1, giving MgCl2 so the combining capacities balance. Example: Al3+ and O2- combine in the smallest neutral ratio to give Al2O3.

Correction / limitation

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: 18.0 g of H₂O ÷ 18.0 g mol⁻¹ = 1.00 mol H₂O. This represents about 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, producing 1.00 mol H₂O requires 1.00 mol H₂ and 0.50 mol O₂. Key check: after solving Mole concept introduction, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Avogadro's number is the number of specified particles in one mole: exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Theory

The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance. Avogadro's number is the number of specified particles in one mole: exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole contains Avogadro's number of specified entities. Molar mass converts between amount in moles and measured mass. It links the microscopic count of atoms, molecules or ions to laboratory-scale amounts. Worked case: 18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: 0.50 mol of oxygen molecules contains 0.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ O₂ molecules. Interpretation and limits: Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Always state the entity being counted; one mole of O atoms differs from one mole of O2 molecules. Application: Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. The constant connects measured masses with particle counts in reactions and materials.

Worked case

18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O. Example: 0.50 mol of oxygen molecules contains 0.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ O₂ molecules.

Relationship

moles = mass / molar mass number of particles = moles × Avogadro constant

Correction / limitation

Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles. Always state the entity being counted; one mole of O atoms differs from one mole of O2 molecules.

Application

Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions. The constant connects measured masses with particle counts in reactions and materials.

Class 9 Atoms and Formulae · Formation of ionic and covalent compoundsexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: Magnesium loses two electrons and two chlorine atoms each gain one, forming Mg2+ and 2Cl-, hence MgCl2. Two hydrogen atoms share one pair to form H2. Key check: after solving Formation of ionic and covalent compounds, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Ionic compounds form through electron transfer and electrostatic attraction, while covalent compounds form through sharing electron pairs.

Theory

Ionic compounds form through electron transfer and electrostatic attraction, while covalent compounds form through sharing electron pairs. Metals commonly lose valence electrons to form cations and non-metals gain them to form anions. Between non-metals, shared pairs allow atoms to approach stable outer-shell configurations. Charge balance determines ionic formulae; shared-pair count determines covalent structure. Worked case: Magnesium loses two electrons and two chlorine atoms each gain one, forming Mg2+ and 2Cl-, hence MgCl2. Two hydrogen atoms share one pair to form H2. Interpretation and limits: Do not describe an ionic compound as a molecule made of one ion pair; an ionic solid contains a repeating lattice of oppositely charged ions. Application: Bond type helps predict structure, conductivity, melting point, solubility and material use.

Worked case

Magnesium loses two electrons and two chlorine atoms each gain one, forming Mg2+ and 2Cl-, hence MgCl2. Two hydrogen atoms share one pair to form H2.

Relationship

ionic: Na -> Na+ + e- and Cl + e- -> Cl-; covalent: H:H

Correction / limitation

Do not describe an ionic compound as a molecule made of one ion pair; an ionic solid contains a repeating lattice of oppositely charged ions.

Application

Bond type helps predict structure, conductivity, melting point, solubility and material use.

Class 9 Atoms and Formulae · Properties of ionic versus covalent compoundsexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: Solid NaCl does not light a conductivity tester, but molten or aqueous NaCl can. Sugar solution generally does not conduct strongly because sugar remains as neutral molecules. Key check: after solving Properties of ionic versus covalent compounds, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Ionic and covalent compounds show different bulk properties because their particles and bonding structures differ.

Theory

Ionic and covalent compounds show different bulk properties because their particles and bonding structures differ. Ionic solids usually have high melting points, are brittle and conduct only when molten or dissolved because ions must move. Simple covalent substances often have lower melting/boiling points and usually do not conduct because they lack mobile charged particles. Giant covalent structures such as diamond are important exceptions. Worked case: Solid NaCl does not light a conductivity tester, but molten or aqueous NaCl can. Sugar solution generally does not conduct strongly because sugar remains as neutral molecules. Interpretation and limits: Do not claim every covalent substance has a low melting point or is insoluble in water; structure, polarity and intermolecular forces create exceptions. Application: Comparing compound properties guides material selection, electrolyte use and safe interpretation of laboratory tests.

mobile ions -> electrical conduction; fixed lattice ions -> no solid-state conduction
