Concept

A balanced chemical equation expresses atom conservation using coefficients rather than altered formulas.

Theory

A balanced chemical equation expresses atom conservation using coefficients rather than altered formulas. Subscripts define chemical identity; coefficients change the number of formula units or molecules. State symbols add physical information without changing atom counts. Worked case: Balancing hydrogen combustion gives 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Each side has four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms; changing water to H2O2 would describe a different product rather than balance the same reaction. Interpretation and limits: Do not change a compound's subscripts to make atom counts agree. Application: Balanced equations provide the basis for reaction stoichiometry and material accounting.

Concept

Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO3, prepared in the Solvay process and decomposed by heat to release carbon dioxide. Washing soda is crystalline sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O, obtained by crystallising sodium carbonate with water.

Theory

Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO3, prepared in the Solvay process and decomposed by heat to release carbon dioxide. Washing soda is crystalline sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O, obtained by crystallising sodium carbonate with water. Concentrated brine is saturated with ammonia and carbon dioxide so sparingly soluble NaHCO3 precipitates. Gentle heating releases CO2, which expands dough; the mild base also neutralises acids. Heating sodium hydrogen carbonate forms sodium carbonate, which crystallises from water as the decahydrate. Carbonate ions precipitate calcium and magnesium ions, allowing washing soda to soften hard water. Worked case: In baking powder, NaHCO3 reacts with an edible acid to release CO2. Tartaric acid helps prevent the bitter taste that excess sodium carbonate could cause. Example: In hard water, Ca2+ + CO3^2- -> CaCO3(s), removing calcium ions that otherwise interfere with soap. Interpretation and limits: Do not identify baking soda as sodium carbonate; it is sodium hydrogen carbonate and has different formula and behaviour. Do not confuse anhydrous sodium carbonate with washing-soda crystals; the named school compound contains ten waters of crystallisation. Application: Baking soda is used in baking powder, antacids and certain fire extinguishers. Washing soda is used for cleaning, water softening and manufacture of glass, soap and paper.

Worked case

In baking powder, NaHCO3 reacts with an edible acid to release CO2. Tartaric acid helps prevent the bitter taste that excess sodium carbonate could cause. Example: In hard water, Ca2+ + CO3^2- -> CaCO3(s), removing calcium ions that otherwise interfere with soap.

Correction / limitation

Do not identify baking soda as sodium carbonate; it is sodium hydrogen carbonate and has different formula and behaviour. Do not confuse anhydrous sodium carbonate with washing-soda crystals; the named school compound contains ten waters of crystallisation.

Application

Baking soda is used in baking powder, antacids and certain fire extinguishers. Washing soda is used for cleaning, water softening and manufacture of glass, soap and paper.

Concept

A metal's position in the reactivity series determines whether it is extracted by electrolysis, chemical reduction or heating of its ore. Corrosion is unwanted electrochemical oxidation of a material by its environment.

Theory

A metal's position in the reactivity series determines whether it is extracted by electrolysis, chemical reduction or heating of its ore. Corrosion is unwanted electrochemical oxidation of a material by its environment. Highly reactive K-Ca-Na-Mg-Al metals require electrolysis of molten compounds. Middle metals such as Zn, Fe, Pb and Cu are commonly obtained after converting ores to oxides and reducing with carbon/CO or aluminium. Low-reactivity metals may occur native or be recovered by heating. For iron rusting, anodic iron dissolution and cathodic oxygen reduction occur at different surface regions; water and ions complete the circuit. Worked case: ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis. Example: zinc coating protects steel both as a barrier and, if scratched, by oxidizing sacrificially before iron. Interpretation and limits: Do not propose carbon reduction for sodium or aluminium oxides; these metals are more reactive than carbon. Rusting requires an electrochemical pathway; oxygen alone without suitable moisture is insufficient for ordinary rust formation. Application: Selecting extraction routes balances chemical feasibility, energy demand, ore composition, pollution control and recycling. Corrosion science protects bridges, pipelines, vehicles, ships and electronic equipment.

Worked case

ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis. Example: zinc coating protects steel both as a barrier and, if scratched, by oxidizing sacrificially before iron.

Relationship

high activity -> electrolysis; middle -> roasting/calcination then reduction; low -> heating or native occurrence anode: Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-

Correction / limitation

Do not propose carbon reduction for sodium or aluminium oxides; these metals are more reactive than carbon. Rusting requires an electrochemical pathway; oxygen alone without suitable moisture is insufficient for ordinary rust formation.

Application

Selecting extraction routes balances chemical feasibility, energy demand, ore composition, pollution control and recycling. Corrosion science protects bridges, pipelines, vehicles, ships and electronic equipment.

The domains point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles close to 109.5°. The symmetric molecule is non-polar overall. Concept

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Hydrocarbons are classified as saturated, unsaturated, aliphatic, alicyclic or aromatic and named from parent chain, unsaturation and substituents.

Theory

A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Hydrocarbons are classified as saturated, unsaturated, aliphatic, alicyclic or aromatic and named from parent chain, unsaturation and substituents. Shared electron density attracts both nuclei. Single, double and triple bonds differ in shared pairs, length and strength. IUPAC naming prioritises the longest chain containing maximum multiple bonds and assigns the lowest valid set of locants. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute. Worked case: in H2, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duet. Example: CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 2-methylbutane after selecting the longest chain and lowest locant. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result. Interpretation and limits: Sharing is not always perfectly equal; electronegativity differences can make a covalent bond polar. Do not answer Hydrocarbon classification and nomenclature from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion. Application: Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids. Hydrocarbon classification and nomenclature supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.

Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon · Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergentsexplicit topic alias
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: if [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹, pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3. The solution is acidic, and diluting it tenfold ideally raises the pH by about one unit. Key check: after solving Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides. Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles.

Theory

Alcohols are prepared by hydration or reduction and react through the O-H bond and C-O bond in oxidation, dehydration, esterification and substitution. Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides. Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles. Alkenes hydrate to alcohols; aldehydes and ketones reduce to primary and secondary alcohols. Primary alcohol oxidation gives aldehydes then acids, secondary gives ketones, while tertiary alcohols resist mild oxidation. Concentrated acid causes dehydration, and carboxylic acids give esters reversibly. Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes and hydrolysis of nitriles produce acids. Resonance stabilises carboxylate ions. Acids react with bicarbonate releasing CO2, esterify alcohols reversibly, and decarboxylate as sodium salts with soda lime. Electron-withdrawing substituents increase acidity. Above a suitable concentration in water, tails cluster inward around oily dirt while charged heads face outward. Agitation breaks grease into suspended droplets that can be rinsed away. Worked case: CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O -> CH3COOH. With ethanoic acid and acid catalyst it forms ethyl ethanoate and water. Example: CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O. CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O with H+ and heat. Example: When oily cloth is washed with soap, micelles encapsulate oil and keep droplets dispersed instead of redepositing them on the fabric. Interpretation and limits: Do not state that all alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids; the product depends on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary. Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst. Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material. Application: Alcohol reactions support solvents, fuels, antiseptics, fragrances, polymers and pharmaceutical synthesis. Carboxylic-acid derivatives occur in medicines, polymers, food preservatives, fats, soaps and fragrances. Micelles enable washing, emulsification and formulation of cleaners and personal-care products.

Worked case

CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O -> CH3COOH. With ethanoic acid and acid catalyst it forms ethyl ethanoate and water. Example: CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O. CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O with H+ and heat. Example: When oily cloth is washed with soap, micelles encapsulate oil and keep droplets dispersed instead of redepositing them on the fabric.

Relationship

RCH2OH + [O] -> RCHO -> RCOOH; ROH + R'COOH <=> R'COOR + H2O RCOOH + ROH <=> RCOOR + H2O; RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3 hydrophobic tails -> grease core; hydrophilic COO- heads -> water

Correction / limitation

Do not state that all alcohols oxidise to carboxylic acids; the product depends on whether the alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary. Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst. Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material.

Application

Alcohol reactions support solvents, fuels, antiseptics, fragrances, polymers and pharmaceutical synthesis. Carboxylic-acid derivatives occur in medicines, polymers, food preservatives, fats, soaps and fragrances. Micelles enable washing, emulsification and formulation of cleaners and personal-care products.

Concept

A balanced chemical equation contains equal numbers of every type of atom on the reactant and product sides.

Theory

A balanced chemical equation contains equal numbers of every type of atom on the reactant and product sides. Write correct formulae first, count atoms, adjust whole-number coefficients and reduce them to the smallest ratio. Coefficients multiply complete formula units; subscripts belong to substance identities and must not be altered during balancing. Worked case: For Al + O2 -> Al2O3, balance aluminium and oxygen to obtain 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3, then verify four Al and six O atoms on each side. Interpretation and limits: Never change a subscript such as H2O into H2O2 to balance atoms; that changes water into a different substance. Application: Balanced equations support quantitative reaction calculations, manufacturing yields and pollution accounting.

Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon · Endothermic and exothermic reactionsexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: Combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat, is exothermic. Thermal decomposition of CaCO3 requires heat and is endothermic. Key check: after solving Endothermic and exothermic reactions, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Exothermic reactions transfer heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings.

Theory

Exothermic reactions transfer heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings. In an exothermic process the surroundings warm and products have lower enthalpy than reactants; in an endothermic process the surroundings cool and products have higher enthalpy. Activation energy is still required to begin either type. Worked case: Combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat, is exothermic. Thermal decomposition of CaCO3 requires heat and is endothermic. Interpretation and limits: A reaction that needs ignition is not necessarily endothermic; combustion needs activation energy but releases more energy overall. Application: Heat classification explains fuels, respiration, cold packs, thermal decomposition and energy-efficient industrial reactions.

Worked case

Combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat, is exothermic. Thermal decomposition of CaCO3 requires heat and is endothermic.

Relationship

exothermic: reactants -> products + heat; endothermic: reactants + heat -> products

Correction / limitation

A reaction that needs ignition is not necessarily endothermic; combustion needs activation energy but releases more energy overall.

Application

Heat classification explains fuels, respiration, cold packs, thermal decomposition and energy-efficient industrial reactions.

A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid when ions from aqueous solutions combine. The net ionic equation removes spectator ions and shows the species responsible for the visible solid. Concept

Sodium hydroxide is manufactured by electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride in the chlor-alkali process.

Theory

Sodium hydroxide is manufactured by electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride in the chlor-alkali process. At the anode chloride ions form chlorine; at the cathode water forms hydrogen and hydroxide ions. Sodium ions remain with hydroxide in solution. Chlorine and hydrogen must be kept separated because their mixture is hazardous. Worked case: Electrolysis produces NaOH solution together with chlorine for disinfectants/PVC and hydrogen for fuels or chemical synthesis. Interpretation and limits: Do not say sodium metal is deposited from brine; water is reduced preferentially at the cathode under these aqueous conditions. Application: Sodium hydroxide is used in soaps, paper, detergents, rayon, degreasing and neutralisation, with strict corrosive-chemical controls.

Worked case

Electrolysis produces NaOH solution together with chlorine for disinfectants/PVC and hydrogen for fuels or chemical synthesis.

Correction / limitation

Do not say sodium metal is deposited from brine; water is reduced preferentially at the cathode under these aqueous conditions.

Application

Sodium hydroxide is used in soaps, paper, detergents, rayon, degreasing and neutralisation, with strict corrosive-chemical controls.

Theory

Bleaching powder is produced by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime and is commonly represented as calcium oxychloride, CaOCl2. The product releases oxidising chlorine species in moist conditions, accounting for bleaching and disinfection. Dry reactants, controlled chlorine exposure and safe storage are important because acids can liberate toxic chlorine gas. Worked case: Chlorine from the chlor-alkali process reacts with slaked lime to make bleaching powder used to disinfect drinking water and bleach cotton or paper pulp. Interpretation and limits: Do not mix bleaching powder with acids or ammonia-containing cleaners; dangerous chlorine or chloramine gases may form. Application: Bleaching powder supports water sanitation, textile processing and oxidising treatments.

Chlorine from the chlor-alkali process reacts with slaked lime to make bleaching powder used to disinfect drinking water and bleach cotton or paper pulp.

Correction / limitation

Do not mix bleaching powder with acids or ammonia-containing cleaners; dangerous chlorine or chloramine gases may form.

Bleaching powder supports water sanitation, textile processing and oxidising treatments.

Concept

Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO3, prepared in the Solvay process and decomposed by heat to release carbon dioxide.

Theory

Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO3, prepared in the Solvay process and decomposed by heat to release carbon dioxide. Concentrated brine is saturated with ammonia and carbon dioxide so sparingly soluble NaHCO3 precipitates. Gentle heating releases CO2, which expands dough; the mild base also neutralises acids. Worked case: In baking powder, NaHCO3 reacts with an edible acid to release CO2. Tartaric acid helps prevent the bitter taste that excess sodium carbonate could cause. Interpretation and limits: Do not identify baking soda as sodium carbonate; it is sodium hydrogen carbonate and has different formula and behaviour. Application: Baking soda is used in baking powder, antacids and certain fire extinguishers.

Worked case

In baking powder, NaHCO3 reacts with an edible acid to release CO2. Tartaric acid helps prevent the bitter taste that excess sodium carbonate could cause.

Relationship

NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NH4Cl + NaHCO3; 2NaHCO3 --heat--> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O

Correction / limitation

Do not identify baking soda as sodium carbonate; it is sodium hydrogen carbonate and has different formula and behaviour.

Application

Baking soda is used in baking powder, antacids and certain fire extinguishers.

Washing soda is crystalline sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O, obtained by crystallising sodium carbonate with water.

Theory

Washing soda is crystalline sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O, obtained by crystallising sodium carbonate with water. Heating sodium hydrogen carbonate forms sodium carbonate, which crystallises from water as the decahydrate. Carbonate ions precipitate calcium and magnesium ions, allowing washing soda to soften hard water. Worked case: In hard water, Ca2+ + CO3^2- -> CaCO3(s), removing calcium ions that otherwise interfere with soap. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse anhydrous sodium carbonate with washing-soda crystals; the named school compound contains ten waters of crystallisation. Application: Washing soda is used for cleaning, water softening and manufacture of glass, soap and paper.

In hard water, Ca2+ + CO3^2- -> CaCO3(s), removing calcium ions that otherwise interfere with soap.

Correction / limitation

Do not confuse anhydrous sodium carbonate with washing-soda crystals; the named school compound contains ten waters of crystallisation.

Application

Washing soda is used for cleaning, water softening and manufacture of glass, soap and paper.

Concept

Plaster of Paris is calcium sulfate hemihydrate, CaSO4·1/2H2O, made by carefully heating gypsum.

Theory

Plaster of Paris is calcium sulfate hemihydrate, CaSO4·1/2H2O, made by carefully heating gypsum. Partial dehydration of gypsum near 373 K gives a powder that rehydrates and sets into hard gypsum when mixed with water. Excessive heating produces anhydrous calcium sulfate that sets poorly. Worked case: A wet plaster bandage can be shaped around an injured limb; hydration and crystal interlocking make it harden into a supportive cast. Interpretation and limits: Do not call Plaster of Paris calcium carbonate or ignore the half-water notation; it is a sulfate hemihydrate. Application: Plaster of Paris is used in casts, moulds, statues, false ceilings and decorative surfaces.

Worked case

A wet plaster bandage can be shaped around an injured limb; hydration and crystal interlocking make it harden into a supportive cast.

CaSO4·2H2O --373 K--> CaSO4·1/2H2O + 3/2H2O; CaSO4·1/2H2O + 3/2H2O -> CaSO4·2H2O

Correction / limitation

Do not call Plaster of Paris calcium carbonate or ignore the half-water notation; it is a sulfate hemihydrate.

Application

Plaster of Paris is used in casts, moulds, statues, false ceilings and decorative surfaces.

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Example: ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis. Key check: after solving Metal extraction by reactivity series, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

A metal's position in the reactivity series determines whether it is extracted by electrolysis, chemical reduction or heating of its ore.

Theory

A metal's position in the reactivity series determines whether it is extracted by electrolysis, chemical reduction or heating of its ore. Highly reactive K-Ca-Na-Mg-Al metals require electrolysis of molten compounds. Middle metals such as Zn, Fe, Pb and Cu are commonly obtained after converting ores to oxides and reducing with carbon/CO or aluminium. Low-reactivity metals may occur native or be recovered by heating. Worked case: ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis. Interpretation and limits: Do not propose carbon reduction for sodium or aluminium oxides; these metals are more reactive than carbon. Application: Selecting extraction routes balances chemical feasibility, energy demand, ore composition, pollution control and recycling.

Worked case

ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis.

Relationship

high activity -> electrolysis; middle -> roasting/calcination then reduction; low -> heating or native occurrence

Correction / limitation

Do not propose carbon reduction for sodium or aluminium oxides; these metals are more reactive than carbon.

Application

Selecting extraction routes balances chemical feasibility, energy demand, ore composition, pollution control and recycling.

Concept

A functional group is an atom or group that gives an organic compound its characteristic reactions and naming suffix or prefix.

Theory

A functional group is an atom or group that gives an organic compound its characteristic reactions and naming suffix or prefix. Class 10 groups include halo (-X), alcohol (-OH), aldehyde (-CHO), ketone (>C=O) and carboxylic acid (-COOH). The carbon skeleton determines the parent name, while the principal group determines suffix and numbering. Worked case: CH3CH2OH is an alcohol, CH3CHO an aldehyde, CH3COCH3 a ketone and CH3COOH a carboxylic acid. Interpretation and limits: Do not identify every oxygen-containing compound as an alcohol; locate the exact bonding pattern of the functional group. Application: Functional groups organise fuels, solvents, flavours, medicines, polymers and biological molecules into predictable reaction families.

Worked case

CH3CH2OH is an alcohol, CH3CHO an aldehyde, CH3COCH3 a ketone and CH3COOH a carboxylic acid.

Relationship

-OH alcohol; -CHO aldehyde; >C=O ketone; -COOH carboxylic acid; -Cl/-Br halo

Correction / limitation

Do not identify every oxygen-containing compound as an alcohol; locate the exact bonding pattern of the functional group.

Application

Functional groups organise fuels, solvents, flavours, medicines, polymers and biological molecules into predictable reaction families.

IUPAC names encode the longest parent chain, carbon-carbon bond type, substituents, functional group and their positions.

Theory

IUPAC names encode the longest parent chain, carbon-carbon bond type, substituents, functional group and their positions. Choose the longest chain containing the principal functional group and multiple bond, number for the lowest relevant locants, name substituents alphabetically and apply the correct suffix. Worked case: CH3CH(CH3)CH2OH is 2-methylpropan-1-ol: the OH-containing three-carbon chain is numbered from the OH end. Interpretation and limits: Do not always choose the visually straight chain or number from the nearest alkyl branch when a principal functional group is present. Do not always choose the visually straight chain or number from the nearest alkyl branch when a principal functional group is present.

Addition reactions consume a carbon-carbon double or triple bond as atoms add across the multiple bond.

Addition reactions consume a carbon-carbon double or triple bond as atoms add across the multiple bond. Worked case: Ethene decolourises bromine solution as Br atoms add across C=C to form 1,2-dibromoethane. Interpretation and limits: Do not classify hydrogenation as substitution; no atom is replaced and the pi bond is consumed as new sigma bonds form. Concept

In substitution, one atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another without changing the carbon skeleton's saturation.

Theory

In substitution, one atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another without changing the carbon skeleton's saturation. Saturated hydrocarbons react with chlorine or bromine in sunlight through a chain process. Further substitution can continue, so controlling reagent ratio and light exposure affects the product mixture. Worked case: One hydrogen in methane is replaced by chlorine to give chloromethane; excess chlorine may produce more highly chlorinated products. Interpretation and limits: Do not write ultraviolet light as a reactant or expect one perfectly pure product when several equivalent or nonequivalent hydrogens can be replaced. Application: Substitution produces useful halo compounds that serve as solvents and chemical intermediates, with environmental and toxicity controls.

CH4 + Cl2 --sunlight--> CH3Cl + HCl

Correction / limitation

Do not write ultraviolet light as a reactant or expect one perfectly pure product when several equivalent or nonequivalent hydrogens can be replaced.

Substitution produces useful halo compounds that serve as solvents and chemical intermediates, with environmental and toxicity controls.

Theory

Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles. Worked case: When oily cloth is washed with soap, micelles encapsulate oil and keep droplets dispersed instead of redepositing them on the fabric. Interpretation and limits: Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material. Application: Micelles enable washing, emulsification and formulation of cleaners and personal-care products.

Concept

Synthetic detergents clean effectively in hard water because their calcium and magnesium salts remain much more soluble than soap scum.

Theory

Synthetic detergents clean effectively in hard water because their calcium and magnesium salts remain much more soluble than soap scum. Soap carboxylate ions react with Ca2+ or Mg2+ to form insoluble scum, wasting soap and reducing lather. Sulfonate or sulfate detergent heads generally avoid this precipitation, though detergent biodegradability and phosphate pollution must be considered. Worked case: Soap lathers poorly in hard water until Ca2+/Mg2+ are removed, while a suitable detergent continues forming micelles and cleaning. Interpretation and limits: Do not claim every detergent is environmentally harmless merely because it works in hard water; composition and biodegradability matter. Application: Detergents support domestic and industrial cleaning, while formulation choices affect wastewater and aquatic ecosystems.

Worked case

Correction / limitation

Do not claim every detergent is environmentally harmless merely because it works in hard water; composition and biodegradability matter.

Concept

The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of atomic number.

Theory

The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of atomic number. The long-form table has seven periods and eighteen groups; position follows valence-shell electronic configuration. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute. Concept

Periodic trends are predictable changes in properties across periods and down groups.

Theory

Periodic trends are predictable changes in properties across periods and down groups. Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group; metallic character shows the opposite broad pattern. Worked case: sodium is larger and more metallic than chlorine because both are in Period 3 but sodium lies farther left. Interpretation and limits: Trends have exceptions and should not be treated as unbreakable rules. Application: Trends help predict bonding, reactivity, ion formation and properties of unfamiliar elements.

Concept

Electric current through an electrolyte can drive chemical changes at electrodes.

Theory

Electric current through an electrolyte can drive chemical changes at electrodes. Ions move in solution and electrons move through the external circuit. Electrode products depend on the ions, solvent, electrode material and conditions rather than on conductivity alone. Worked case: In suitable copper sulfate electroplating conditions, Cu2+ gains electrons at the cathode and deposits copper. A colour change, gas evolution or deposit can reveal chemical effects, but the particular product requires the actual system. Interpretation and limits: Do not assume that every electrolyte gives the same gases or deposits at its electrodes. Application: Electroplating uses electrical charge to form controlled surface coatings.

Worked case

In suitable copper sulfate electroplating conditions, Cu2+ gains electrons at the cathode and deposits copper. A colour change, gas evolution or deposit can reveal chemical effects, but the particular product requires the actual system.

Relationship

Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu at a copper-plating cathode

Correction / limitation

Do not assume that every electrolyte gives the same gases or deposits at its electrodes.

Application

Electroplating uses electrical charge to form controlled surface coatings.

Key check: after solving Electrolysis and electrode products, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction.

Theory

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction. The power supply pushes electrons, while ions migrate to electrodes. Deposited or released amount is proportional to charge passed. Worked case: passing 193000 C through Cu2+ solution supplies 2 mol electrons and ideally deposits 1 mol copper. Interpretation and limits: Electrode signs differ from a galvanic cell, but oxidation remains at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Application: Electrolysis is used for plating, metal refining, chemical manufacture and hydrogen production.

Worked case

passing 193000 C through Cu2+ solution supplies 2 mol electrons and ideally deposits 1 mol copper.

Relationship

Q = It; moles electrons = Q/F

Correction / limitation

Electrode signs differ from a galvanic cell, but oxidation remains at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

Application

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Concept

Döbereiner grouped selected elements into triads with similar properties, where the middle atomic mass was approximately the average of the other two.

Theory

Döbereiner grouped selected elements into triads with similar properties, where the middle atomic mass was approximately the average of the other two. The idea connected numerical mass patterns with chemical similarity but worked for only a few known groups, so it could not classify all elements. Worked case: For Li, Na and K, (6.9 + 39.1)/2 = 23.0, close to sodium's atomic mass, and all three show related alkali-metal chemistry. Interpretation and limits: Do not force any three consecutive elements into a triad; similarity of properties is an essential condition. Application: Triads illustrate how early evidence led scientists toward the idea of periodic recurrence.

For Li, Na and K, (6.9 + 39.1)/2 = 23.0, close to sodium's atomic mass, and all three show related alkali-metal chemistry.

middle mass approximately = (first mass + third mass)/2

Correction / limitation

Do not force any three consecutive elements into a triad; similarity of properties is an essential condition.

Application

Concept

Newlands arranged known elements by increasing atomic mass and proposed that every eighth element repeated similar properties.

Theory

Newlands arranged known elements by increasing atomic mass and proposed that every eighth element repeated similar properties. The octave pattern worked mainly up to calcium, assumed too few undiscovered elements and sometimes placed unlike elements together or two elements in one slot. Worked case: Lithium and sodium appeared in corresponding octave positions and showed similar reactivity, but the pattern broke down for heavier elements. Interpretation and limits: Do not present the law of octaves as universally valid; its limitations are part of the required explanation. Application: Newlands' work was an important attempt to recognise periodic repetition before the modern atomic-number basis was known.

Periodic Classification and Electrolysis · Mendeleev's periodic classificationexisting authored record
Previous worked example

Worked example focus: claim, evidence, calculation or model, then chemical meaning. Key check: after solving Mendeleev's periodic classification, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

Mendeleev arranged elements mainly by increasing atomic mass while keeping elements with similar chemical properties in the same groups.

Theory

Mendeleev arranged elements mainly by increasing atomic mass while keeping elements with similar chemical properties in the same groups. He compared formulas of oxides and hydrides, left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties. Limitations included hydrogen's position, isotopes and anomalous mass order such as cobalt/nickel or tellurium/iodine. Worked case: Mendeleev's eka-aluminium predictions closely matched gallium's later measured mass, density and compound formulas, supporting his table. Interpretation and limits: Do not say Mendeleev blindly followed mass order; he sometimes prioritised chemical similarity, revealing both insight and the need for atomic number. Application: Mendeleev's table enabled prediction and organised chemical evidence, forming the bridge to the modern periodic table.

Worked case

Mendeleev's eka-aluminium predictions closely matched gallium's later measured mass, density and compound formulas, supporting his table.

Correction / limitation

Concept

Dilution lowers concentration by adding solvent without changing the amount of solute.

Theory

Dilution lowers concentration by adding solvent without changing the amount of solute. For the same solute before and after dilution, initial moles equal final moles. Worked case: 25.0 mL of 2.0 M stock diluted to 100.0 mL gives M2 = 2.0 x 25.0/100.0 = 0.50 M. Interpretation and limits: Adding solvent changes concentration and volume but not moles of the original solute. Application: Dilution prepares standards, medicines, cleaners and safe laboratory reagents.

Concept

Gas tests use characteristic reactions or physical responses to distinguish proposed gases.

Theory

Gas tests use characteristic reactions or physical responses to distinguish proposed gases. A test must be performed safely and interpreted with the gas source and possible interferences. Testing by smell or direct inhalation is inappropriate. Worked case: Carbon dioxide can turn limewater cloudy by forming calcium carbonate. Hydrogen gives a characteristic small pop in a properly supervised ignition test, while oxygen supports relighting a glowing splint under suitable conditions. Interpretation and limits: Do not treat every colourless gas as oxygen or inhale a gas to identify it. Application: Gas identification links reaction observations with balanced chemical changes.

CO2 + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCO3 + H2O

Correction / limitation

Concept

Acid-base indicators are weak acids or bases whose conjugate forms have different colours. Changing pH shifts the balance between the two coloured forms. Interpretation and limits: An indicator does not cause neutralization and its endpoint range must suit the reaction. Key check: after solving Precipitation observations, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid when ions from aqueous solutions combine.

Theory

A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid when ions from aqueous solutions combine. Double-displacement reactions exchange ions, but a reaction is driven only when a precipitate, gas or weakly ionised product forms. The net ionic equation removes spectator ions and shows the species responsible for the visible solid. Worked case: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s)↓ + 2KNO3(aq) gives a yellow lead-iodide precipitate. Interpretation and limits: Do not call every double-displacement mixture a precipitation reaction; first check whether an insoluble product actually forms. Application: Precipitation is used in ion identification, water treatment, pigment preparation and removal of contaminants.

Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s)↓ + 2KNO3(aq) gives a yellow lead-iodide precipitate.

Correction / limitation

Do not call every double-displacement mixture a precipitation reaction; first check whether an insoluble product actually forms.

Concept

A measurement record includes value, units, conditions and an uncertainty appropriate to the method.

A measurement record includes value, units, conditions and an uncertainty appropriate to the method. Repeated readings characterize random variation but do not automatically remove systematic bias. Laboratory safety combines hazard recognition, risk reduction, correct technique, emergency readiness and responsible waste handling. Read labels and instructions before starting; wear eye protection and suitable clothing; tie back hair; use small quantities; label containers; never taste chemicals or pipette by mouth; waft only when instructed; add acid to water; keep flames away from flammables; report spills, breakage and exposure immediately. Dispose of each material through the instructed waste route. Worked case: When diluting concentrated acid under teacher supervision, add acid slowly to water with stirring and cooling because dilution releases heat; adding water to concentrated acid can cause splashing. Application: Safe handling prevents injuries, contamination and environmental harm while making experimental evidence more reliable.

Theory

Integrated rate laws relate reactant concentration to time for a specified kinetic model. A first-order process gives a straight line when ln concentration is plotted against time. Worked case: For a first-order reactant that falls from 0.100 M to 0.050 M in 20.0 s, k = ln(2)/20.0 = 0.0347 s^-1. After another 20.0 s the model predicts 0.025 M. Concept

Theory

The steady-state approximation treats an intermediate's formation and consumption rates as nearly equal over an appropriate time interval. The intermediate concentration can remain small even when material flows rapidly through it. This approximation differs from equilibrium: individual forward and reverse elementary steps need not balance. Worked case: For A -> I and I -> P with rates k1[A] and k2[I], setting d[I]/dt approximately zero gives [I] approximately k1[A]/k2. Product formation then proceeds at approximately k1[A]. Application: The approximation converts multistep mechanisms into testable rate expressions.

Concept

Transition-state theory relates reaction rates to the free-energy barrier between reactants and an activated configuration.

Theory

Transition-state theory relates reaction rates to the free-energy barrier between reactants and an activated configuration. The activated configuration lies near a dividing surface along the reaction coordinate. Activation free energy includes enthalpic and entropic contributions and is distinct from overall reaction free energy. Worked case: At the same temperature and prefactor, lowering an activation free-energy barrier by RT ln(10) increases the predicted rate constant tenfold. A favourable product free energy alone does not specify the reaction speed. Interpretation and limits: An exergonic reaction need not be fast; barrier height and overall free-energy change describe different questions. Application: Activation parameters help interpret temperature-dependent rates and catalytic acceleration.

Worked case

At the same temperature and prefactor, lowering an activation free-energy barrier by RT ln(10) increases the predicted rate constant tenfold. A favourable product free energy alone does not specify the reaction speed.

Relationship

k = (kB T/h) exp(-Delta G double-dagger/RT)

Correction / limitation

An exergonic reaction need not be fast; barrier height and overall free-energy change describe different questions.

Application

Activation parameters help interpret temperature-dependent rates and catalytic acceleration.

Photochemical rates depend on light absorption and excited-state reaction and decay pathways. Incident photon flux differs from absorbed photon flux. Excited molecules may react, fluoresce, undergo intersystem crossing or relax without reaction, so light intensity alone cannot predict product formation. Worked case: If a sample absorbs 2.0 micromoles of photons per second and forms 0.50 micromoles of product per second, the product quantum yield is 0.25 under those conditions. Interpretation and limits: Use absorbed rather than incident photons when calculating a quantum yield. Application: Actinometry and controlled illumination allow comparison of photochemical reaction efficiencies.

If a sample absorbs 2.0 micromoles of photons per second and forms 0.50 micromoles of product per second, the product quantum yield is 0.25 under those conditions.

Relationship

product formation rate = quantum yield x absorbed photon rate

Correction / limitation

Use absorbed rather than incident photons when calculating a quantum yield.

Application

Actinometry and controlled illumination allow comparison of photochemical reaction efficiencies.

Concept

Quantum observables are represented by operators acting on wavefunctions.

Theory

Quantum observables are represented by operators acting on wavefunctions. A normalized wavefunction yields probabilities through its squared modulus. An eigenfunction of an operator has a definite corresponding measurement value, while a general superposition need not. Worked case: For an energy eigenfunction psi_n, applying the Hamiltonian returns E_n psi_n. Multiplying a normalized wavefunction by a constant phase changes neither its probability density nor observable predictions. Interpretation and limits: A wavefunction amplitude can be negative or complex; probability density cannot be negative. Application: Operator methods determine allowed energies and expectation values in molecular quantum models.

Worked case

For an energy eigenfunction psi_n, applying the Hamiltonian returns E_n psi_n. Multiplying a normalized wavefunction by a constant phase changes neither its probability density nor observable predictions.

Relationship

H psi_n = E_n psi_n; integral abs(psi)^2 d tau = 1

Correction / limitation

A wavefunction amplitude can be negative or complex; probability density cannot be negative.

Application

Operator methods determine allowed energies and expectation values in molecular quantum models.

  3. H psi_n = E_n psi_n; integral abs(psi)^2 d tau = 1
  4. A normalized wavefunction yields probabilities through its squared modulus.
  5. An eigenfunction of an operator has a definite corresponding measurement value, while a general superposition need not.
  6. A wavefunction amplitude can be negative or complex; probability density cannot be negative.

Concept

An ideal particle confined by infinite walls has discrete translational energy levels.

Theory

An ideal particle confined by infinite walls has discrete translational energy levels. Boundary conditions require the wavefunction to vanish at the walls. The model has a nonzero ground-state energy and increasingly separated levels, and its limitations matter for real conjugated molecules. Worked case: For an electron in a one-dimensional box, doubling box length reduces every energy level to one quarter because E_n is proportional to 1/L^2. The ground state uses n = 1, not n = 0. Interpretation and limits: Do not allow n = 0 as a stationary state of the infinite-well model. Application: The model introduces quantization and gives a first approximation to delocalized-electron excitation trends.

Worked case

For an electron in a one-dimensional box, doubling box length reduces every energy level to one quarter because E_n is proportional to 1/L^2. The ground state uses n = 1, not n = 0.

Relationship

E_n = n^2 h^2/(8mL^2), n = 1,2,3,...

Correction / limitation

Do not allow n = 0 as a stationary state of the infinite-well model.

Application

The model introduces quantization and gives a first approximation to delocalized-electron excitation trends.

  3. E_n = n^2 h^2/(8mL^2), n = 1,2,3,...
  4. Boundary conditions require the wavefunction to vanish at the walls.
  5. The model has a nonzero ground-state energy and increasingly separated levels, and its limitations matter for real conjugated molecules.
  6. Do not allow n = 0 as a stationary state of the infinite-well model.

Concept

The rigid-rotor model quantizes molecular rotational energy while treating bond lengths as fixed.

Theory

The rigid-rotor model quantizes molecular rotational energy while treating bond lengths as fixed. For a diatomic molecule, rotational spacing depends on the moment of inertia, which depends on reduced mass and bond length. Pure rotational electric-dipole spectra require a permanent dipole. Worked case: Replacing H with D in a polar diatomic molecule increases reduced mass and the moment of inertia. The rotational constant decreases, so adjacent rotational lines become more closely spaced in the rigid-rotor approximation. Interpretation and limits: A homonuclear diatomic molecule does not gain a permanent dipole merely because it rotates. Application: Rotational spectra provide precise information about molecular moments of inertia and bond lengths.

Worked case

Replacing H with D in a polar diatomic molecule increases reduced mass and the moment of inertia. The rotational constant decreases, so adjacent rotational lines become more closely spaced in the rigid-rotor approximation.

Relationship

E_J = hbar^2 J(J+1)/(2I)

Correction / limitation

A homonuclear diatomic molecule does not gain a permanent dipole merely because it rotates.

Application

Rotational spectra provide precise information about molecular moments of inertia and bond lengths.

  2. The rotational constant decreases, so adjacent rotational lines become more closely spaced in the rigid-rotor approximation.
  3. E_J = hbar^2 J(J+1)/(2I)
  4. For a diatomic molecule, rotational spacing depends on the moment of inertia, which depends on reduced mass and bond length.
  5. Pure rotational electric-dipole spectra require a permanent dipole.
  6. A homonuclear diatomic molecule does not gain a permanent dipole merely because it rotates.

Concept

The harmonic oscillator models vibration near a potential-energy minimum using a quadratic restoring potential.

Theory

The harmonic oscillator models vibration near a potential-energy minimum using a quadratic restoring potential. Its energy levels are equally spaced and include zero-point energy. Real molecular vibrations become anharmonic at larger displacement, and vibrational IR activity also requires changing dipole moment. Worked case: If a bond's force constant stays fixed while reduced mass increases by a factor of four, the harmonic frequency falls by a factor of two. Isotopic substitution therefore shifts vibrational bands without changing the element's bonding framework. Interpretation and limits: The harmonic ground state does not have zero vibrational energy. Application: Isotope shifts and normal-mode frequencies help assign molecular vibrations.

Worked case

If a bond's force constant stays fixed while reduced mass increases by a factor of four, the harmonic frequency falls by a factor of two. Isotopic substitution therefore shifts vibrational bands without changing the element's bonding framework.

Relationship

nu = (1/2pi) sqrt(k/mu)

Correction / limitation

The harmonic ground state does not have zero vibrational energy.

Application

Isotope shifts and normal-mode frequencies help assign molecular vibrations.

  2. Isotopic substitution therefore shifts vibrational bands without changing the element's bonding framework.
  3. nu = (1/2pi) sqrt(k/mu)
  4. Its energy levels are equally spaced and include zero-point energy.
  5. Real molecular vibrations become anharmonic at larger displacement, and vibrational IR activity also requires changing dipole moment.
  6. The harmonic ground state does not have zero vibrational energy.

Concept

The hydrogenic atom provides exact one-electron orbital solutions for a Coulomb potential.

Theory

The hydrogenic atom provides exact one-electron orbital solutions for a Coulomb potential. Energy depends on principal quantum number in the nonrelativistic ideal model, while angular and radial factors determine orbital probability distributions. Many-electron atoms introduce electron-electron interactions absent from this model. Worked case: A hydrogen electron moving from n = 3 to n = 2 emits a photon corresponding to the energy difference between those levels. The orbital is a probability amplitude, not a small planet travelling along a fixed circular path. Interpretation and limits: Do not transfer the simple hydrogen energy formula unchanged to neutral many-electron atoms. Application: Hydrogen spectra test quantized energy differences and provide a starting point for orbital theory.

Worked case

A hydrogen electron moving from n = 3 to n = 2 emits a photon corresponding to the energy difference between those levels. The orbital is a probability amplitude, not a small planet travelling along a fixed circular path.

Relationship

E_n = -13.6 eV/n^2 for hydrogen

Correction / limitation

Do not transfer the simple hydrogen energy formula unchanged to neutral many-electron atoms.

Application

Hydrogen spectra test quantized energy differences and provide a starting point for orbital theory.

Concept

Rotational spectroscopy measures transitions between quantized molecular rotational states.

Theory

Rotational spectroscopy measures transitions between quantized molecular rotational states. For a simple linear rigid rotor, allowed electric-dipole transitions have Delta J = plus or minus one and require a permanent dipole. Centrifugal distortion causes departures from ideal equal line spacing. Worked case: CO has a permanent dipole and displays a pure rotational spectrum. N2 lacks a permanent dipole and does not show the corresponding ordinary electric-dipole rotational spectrum, even though N2 molecules rotate. Interpretation and limits: Absence of a pure rotational electric-dipole spectrum does not mean a molecule has no rotational motion. Application: Microwave spectra identify gas-phase molecules and constrain molecular geometry.

Worked case

CO has a permanent dipole and displays a pure rotational spectrum. N2 lacks a permanent dipole and does not show the corresponding ordinary electric-dipole rotational spectrum, even though N2 molecules rotate.

Relationship

rigid linear rotor line spacing approximately 2B

Correction / limitation

Absence of a pure rotational electric-dipole spectrum does not mean a molecule has no rotational motion.

Application

Microwave spectra identify gas-phase molecules and constrain molecular geometry.

  3. rigid linear rotor line spacing approximately 2B
  4. For a simple linear rigid rotor, allowed electric-dipole transitions have Delta J = plus or minus one and require a permanent dipole.
  5. Centrifugal distortion causes departures from ideal equal line spacing.
  6. Absence of a pure rotational electric-dipole spectrum does not mean a molecule has no rotational motion.

Worked example focus: define analyte, choose calibration, calculate with units, then report uncertainty. Example: Beer–Lambert law gives A = εbc. Concept

Infrared and Raman selection rules probe different changes during a molecular vibration.

Theory

Infrared and Raman selection rules probe different changes during a molecular vibration. IR activity requires a changing dipole moment; Raman activity requires a changing polarizability. These are response properties, not simply labels for bond polarity. Worked case: The symmetric stretch of CO2 is Raman-active but IR-inactive in the ideal centrosymmetric molecule. Its asymmetric stretch changes the dipole moment and is IR-active. Interpretation and limits: A vibration's IR inactivity does not imply that it cannot be observed by another spectroscopic method. Application: Combining IR and Raman spectra provides complementary vibrational assignments.

Worked case

The symmetric stretch of CO2 is Raman-active but IR-inactive in the ideal centrosymmetric molecule. Its asymmetric stretch changes the dipole moment and is IR-active.

Relationship

IR: changing dipole; Raman: changing polarizability

Correction / limitation

A vibration's IR inactivity does not imply that it cannot be observed by another spectroscopic method.

Application

Combining IR and Raman spectra provides complementary vibrational assignments.

  3. IR: changing dipole; Raman: changing polarizability
  4. IR activity requires a changing dipole moment
  5. Raman activity requires a changing polarizability.
  6. These are response properties, not simply labels for bond polarity.

Concept

UV-visible spectroscopy measures electronic absorption and can quantify concentration under suitable conditions.

Theory

UV-visible spectroscopy measures electronic absorption and can quantify concentration under suitable conditions. Absorbance depends on concentration, path length and wavelength-dependent molar absorptivity. Chemical equilibria, scattering and high-concentration effects can invalidate a simple linear calibration. Worked case: At a selected wavelength, epsilon = 10000 L mol^-1 cm^-1 and a 1.00 cm path give A = 0.500 for c = 5.00 x 10^-5 mol/L. Doubling path length doubles absorbance only if the same absorbing species and linear conditions apply. Interpretation and limits: Absorbance is not the percentage transmitted, and a calibration must specify wavelength and chemical conditions. Application: Electronic absorption supports colorimetric assays and investigation of chromophores.

Correction / limitation

Concept

NMR spectroscopy probes nuclear spin environments and couplings in an applied magnetic field.

Theory

NMR spectroscopy probes nuclear spin environments and couplings in an applied magnetic field. Chemical shift reflects electronic shielding relative to a reference, while scalar coupling can provide connectivity information. Peak integration estimates relative proton numbers under appropriate acquisition conditions. Worked case: An idealized first-order ethanol proton spectrum shows a methyl triplet coupled to two neighbouring methylene protons and a methylene quartet coupled to three methyl protons. The OH signal may behave differently because exchange affects coupling. Interpretation and limits: Do not apply n+1 splitting mechanically when exchange, equivalent nuclei or strong coupling invalidate the first-order assumptions. Application: NMR patterns and correlations help determine molecular connectivity and assess purity.

Worked case

An idealized first-order ethanol proton spectrum shows a methyl triplet coupled to two neighbouring methylene protons and a methylene quartet coupled to three methyl protons. The OH signal may behave differently because exchange affects coupling.

Relationship

chemical shift delta is reported in ppm relative to a reference

Correction / limitation

Do not apply n+1 splitting mechanically when exchange, equivalent nuclei or strong coupling invalidate the first-order assumptions.

Application

NMR patterns and correlations help determine molecular connectivity and assess purity.

Concept

Activity expresses a species' effective thermodynamic concentration relative to a defined standard state.

Theory

Activity expresses a species' effective thermodynamic concentration relative to a defined standard state. In nonideal solutions, activity differs from concentration through an activity coefficient. Equilibrium constants written thermodynamically use activities rather than unqualified molar concentrations. Worked case: For an ion on a concentration standard state, c/c-standard = 0.010 and gamma = 0.80 give activity a = 0.0080. Replacing a by 0.010 would neglect the specified nonideality. Interpretation and limits: Activity is dimensionless, and an individual-ion activity coefficient requires a convention rather than direct independent measurement. Application: Activity corrections improve equilibrium and electrochemical calculations in ionic media.

Worked case

For an ion on a concentration standard state, c/c-standard = 0.010 and gamma = 0.80 give activity a = 0.0080. Replacing a by 0.010 would neglect the specified nonideality.

Relationship

a_i = gamma_i c_i/c-standard

Correction / limitation

Activity is dimensionless, and an individual-ion activity coefficient requires a convention rather than direct independent measurement.

Application

Activity corrections improve equilibrium and electrochemical calculations in ionic media.

Concept

Debye–Hückel theory estimates ionic activity-coefficient behaviour from electrostatic interactions in dilute solution.

Theory

Debye–Hückel theory estimates ionic activity-coefficient behaviour from electrostatic interactions in dilute solution. The limiting law depends on ionic charge and ionic strength and applies as ionic strength approaches zero. Concentrated electrolytes require more suitable models. Worked case: Two 0.010 mol/L 1:1 electrolytes each contribute ionic strength 0.010 mol/L if fully dissociated and considered separately. A 2:1 electrolyte at the same formula concentration produces a different ionic strength because charges enter squared. Interpretation and limits: Equal salt concentrations do not imply equal ionic strengths for salts with different stoichiometries and charges. Application: Dilute-solution activity estimates help interpret equilibrium constants and electrolyte behaviour.

Worked case

Two 0.010 mol/L 1:1 electrolytes each contribute ionic strength 0.010 mol/L if fully dissociated and considered separately. A 2:1 electrolyte at the same formula concentration produces a different ionic strength because charges enter squared.

Relationship

I = 0.5 sum(c_i z_i^2)

Correction / limitation

Equal salt concentrations do not imply equal ionic strengths for salts with different stoichiometries and charges.

Application

Dilute-solution activity estimates help interpret equilibrium constants and electrolyte behaviour.

Concept

Electrode kinetics describes how electron-transfer rates respond to overpotential and interfacial conditions.

Theory

Electrode kinetics describes how electron-transfer rates respond to overpotential and interfacial conditions. The equilibrium potential indicates thermodynamic balance, while exchange current and transfer coefficients characterize kinetic response. Mass transport can limit current even when interfacial electron transfer is fast. Worked case: Two electrodes can have the same equilibrium potential but different exchange-current densities. At a specified small overpotential, the electrode with larger exchange current typically gives a larger kinetic current. Interpretation and limits: A favourable equilibrium cell voltage does not by itself establish a fast electrode reaction. Application: Kinetic measurements guide electrode and electrocatalyst selection.

Worked case

Two electrodes can have the same equilibrium potential but different exchange-current densities. At a specified small overpotential, the electrode with larger exchange current typically gives a larger kinetic current.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

A favourable equilibrium cell voltage does not by itself establish a fast electrode reaction.

Application

Kinetic measurements guide electrode and electrocatalyst selection.

Concept

Voltammetry records current as electrode potential is varied, revealing electrochemical reactions and transport behaviour.

Theory

Voltammetry records current as electrode potential is varied, revealing electrochemical reactions and transport behaviour. Peak or wave position relates to the redox process, while current depends on concentration, diffusion and experimental waveform. Background and supporting electrolyte conditions matter. Worked case: In cyclic voltammetry of a suitable reversible dissolved redox couple, peak current scales with the square root of scan rate. A surface-confined redox species can instead show peak current proportional to scan rate. Interpretation and limits: Do not interpret every peak-height change solely as a concentration change; scan rate and transport also affect it. Application: Voltammetric signatures distinguish dissolved and surface-associated electrochemical processes.

Correction / limitation

Do not interpret every peak-height change solely as a concentration change; scan rate and transport also affect it.

Application

Key check: after solving Fuel cells and batteries, explain why at least two wrong approaches fail.

Concept

A fuel cell generates electricity continuously while fuel and oxidant are supplied. Batteries store chemical free energy in coupled electrode reactions and deliver it as electrical work.

Theory

A fuel cell generates electricity continuously while fuel and oxidant are supplied. Batteries store chemical free energy in coupled electrode reactions and deliver it as electrical work. Unlike a battery, reactants are stored externally. Hydrogen fuel cells combine hydrogen and oxygen electrochemically to produce water, electricity and heat. Worked case: the overall hydrogen fuel-cell reaction is 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O while electrons pass through the load. Example: Lithium-ion capacity is estimated from reversible electron transfer per mass of active material. Interpretation and limits: Fuel cells are not pollution-free by definition; total impact depends on fuel production and system materials. Electrons flow through the external circuit; ions carry charge through the electrolyte rather than the same electrons crossing both pathways. Application: Fuel cells provide power for vehicles, backup systems and distributed generation. Separated oxidation and reduction half-reactions store and deliver electrical energy while ion transport maintains charge balance.

chemical fuel + oxidant -> electrical work + products specific capacity = charge / active-material mass

Correction / limitation

Fuel cells are not pollution-free by definition; total impact depends on fuel production and system materials. Electrons flow through the external circuit; ions carry charge through the electrolyte rather than the same electrons crossing both pathways.

Concept

Electron-deficient compounds cannot always be described using only localized two-centre two-electron bonds and octets.

Theory

Electron-deficient compounds cannot always be described using only localized two-centre two-electron bonds and octets. Multicentre bonding allows several atoms to share an electron pair. Electron counting must include the entire bonding framework rather than forcing unsupported localized bonds. Worked case: Diborane B2H6 contains four terminal B-H bonds and two bridging hydrogen atoms. The B-H-B bridges are described by three-centre two-electron bonding, not two ordinary independent B-H single bonds for each bridge. Interpretation and limits: An octet shortfall does not justify drawing extra electron pairs that the formula does not supply. Application: Multicentre bonding explains structures of boranes and other electron-deficient clusters.

Worked case

Diborane B2H6 contains four terminal B-H bonds and two bridging hydrogen atoms. The B-H-B bridges are described by three-centre two-electron bonding, not two ordinary independent B-H single bonds for each bridge.

Relationship

three-centre two-electron bonding shares one pair over three atoms

Correction / limitation

An octet shortfall does not justify drawing extra electron pairs that the formula does not supply.

Application

Multicentre bonding explains structures of boranes and other electron-deficient clusters.

Concept

Boranes and carboranes form cage and cluster structures supported by delocalized skeletal bonding.

Theory

Boranes and carboranes form cage and cluster structures supported by delocalized skeletal bonding. Electron-counting schemes classify idealized skeletal frameworks such as closo and nido. Carbon substitution changes skeletal electron contributions, so formula charge must be included. Worked case: A closo cluster with n skeletal vertices requires 2n+2 skeletal electrons in the Wade framework. A six-vertex closo cage therefore corresponds to 14 skeletal electrons after appropriate exo-bond accounting. Interpretation and limits: Total valence-electron count and skeletal-electron count are not interchangeable without subtracting exo-bond contributions. Application: Cluster counting supports comparison of borane and carborane cage structures.

Concept

Silicates contain silicon-oxygen inorganic frameworks, while silicones contain siloxane backbones with organic substituents.

Theory

Silicates contain silicon-oxygen inorganic frameworks, while silicones contain siloxane backbones with organic substituents. SiO4 tetrahedra can share oxygen atoms to form chains, sheets or frameworks. Silicones contain repeated Si-O-Si linkages with carbon-containing side groups and are not elemental silicon. Worked case: Quartz has a three-dimensional Si-O framework. Polydimethylsiloxane instead contains a repeating -Si(CH3)2-O- chain, giving a flexible polymer rather than the rigid quartz network. Interpretation and limits: Silicon, silica and silicone name different materials and cannot be used interchangeably. Application: Framework silicates are structural minerals, whereas silicone polymers serve in sealants, elastomers and surface treatments.

Worked case

Quartz has a three-dimensional Si-O framework. Polydimethylsiloxane instead contains a repeating -Si(CH3)2-O- chain, giving a flexible polymer rather than the rigid quartz network.

Correction / limitation

Application

Concept

Phosphazenes contain alternating phosphorus and nitrogen atoms in rings or chains, with substituents attached to phosphorus.

Theory

Phosphazenes contain alternating phosphorus and nitrogen atoms in rings or chains, with substituents attached to phosphorus. Changing substituents can strongly alter solubility, flexibility and chemical stability. Bonding is delocalized and should not be reduced to a literal sequence of isolated classical double bonds. Worked case: Replacing chloride substituents on hexachlorocyclotriphosphazene with alkoxy groups changes the ring's chemical functionality while retaining the alternating P-N skeleton. Interpretation and limits: Do not confuse a phosphazene P-N backbone with the Si-O backbone of a silicone. Application: Substituent-tunable phosphazenes provide routes to specialized inorganic-organic materials.

Worked case

Concept

Heavier noble gases can form stable compounds under appropriate chemical conditions.

Theory

Heavier noble gases can form stable compounds under appropriate chemical conditions. Xenon fluorides illustrate how a closed-shell atom can participate in bonding with strongly electronegative partners. Molecular shape follows the arrangement of bonding and nonbonding electron domains. Worked case: XeF4 has four Xe-F bonds and two lone pairs in an approximately octahedral electron-domain arrangement, producing a square-planar molecular geometry. Interpretation and limits: Do not identify electron-domain geometry as molecular geometry when lone pairs are present. Application: Xenon compounds test bonding models beyond a simplistic statement that noble gases never react.

Concept

Ligand field theory describes metal-ligand electronic structure using orbital interactions as well as symmetry and electron repulsion.

Theory

Ligand field theory describes metal-ligand electronic structure using orbital interactions as well as symmetry and electron repulsion. Unlike a purely electrostatic crystal-field picture, ligand-field treatments can include covalent mixing, sigma donation and pi effects. Spectra and magnetic data constrain the description. Worked case: A pi-acceptor ligand such as CO can increase relevant orbital energy separations through metal-ligand interactions. The resulting low-spin preference cannot be justified by treating every ligand as an identical point charge. Interpretation and limits: Do not equate ligand field theory with a model that excludes all covalent orbital interaction. Application: Ligand-field reasoning connects spectra, spin states and bonding trends across coordination compounds.

Worked case

A pi-acceptor ligand such as CO can increase relevant orbital energy separations through metal-ligand interactions. The resulting low-spin preference cannot be justified by treating every ligand as an identical point charge.

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Do not equate ligand field theory with a model that excludes all covalent orbital interaction.

Application

Ligand-field reasoning connects spectra, spin states and bonding trends across coordination compounds.

Concept

Transition-metal electronic spectra can contain ligand-field transitions and charge-transfer transitions.

Theory

Transition-metal electronic spectra can contain ligand-field transitions and charge-transfer transitions. d-d transition energies depend on geometry and ligand field. Intensities depend on selection rules and coupling, so absorption intensity cannot be inferred from oxidation state alone. Worked case: For an octahedral d1 ion, promoting the electron from t2g to eg requires the ligand-field splitting energy in the simple crystal-field model. Replacing ligands can shift the absorption and the observed colour. Interpretation and limits: The colour seen is not generally the same as the wavelength most strongly absorbed. Application: Electronic spectra help compare ligand fields and electronic structures of metal complexes.

Concept

Magnetochemistry relates magnetic response to spin populations, orbital contributions and interactions between centres.

Theory

Magnetochemistry relates magnetic response to spin populations, orbital contributions and interactions between centres. Temperature dependence can distinguish independent-spin behaviour from magnetic coupling. A spin-only moment is an approximation and is not equally reliable for every metal and geometry. Worked case: Two metal centres each containing an unpaired electron can couple antiferromagnetically, producing a low-spin ground state. Counting local unpaired electrons without considering coupling can overestimate the measured response. Interpretation and limits: A low molecular magnetic moment does not prove that every isolated metal centre has all electrons paired. Application: Temperature-dependent susceptibility probes exchange coupling and spin-state changes in coordination materials.

Worked case

Correction / limitation

Application

Worked example focus: mark electron-rich/electron-poor sites, follow arrows, then check the product. Example: in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, six CN⁻ ligands contribute −6 overall. Concept

Ligand substitution exchanges coordinated ligands through pathways that differ in bond-making and bond-breaking order.

Theory

Ligand substitution exchanges coordinated ligands through pathways that differ in bond-making and bond-breaking order. Associative pathways involve substantial incoming-ligand bonding before outgoing-ligand loss; dissociative pathways involve substantial outgoing-ligand separation first. Rate-law evidence must be interpreted with speciation and solvent effects. Worked case: For a limiting associative substitution, increasing entering-ligand concentration can increase rate. A limiting dissociative rate may be approximately independent of entering-ligand concentration while depending on the original complex concentration. Interpretation and limits: A fast substitution reaction is not automatically associative; mechanism requires kinetic and structural evidence. Application: Mechanistic classification helps predict how ligand identity and concentration affect complex reactivity.

Worked case

For a limiting associative substitution, increasing entering-ligand concentration can increase rate. A limiting dissociative rate may be approximately independent of entering-ligand concentration while depending on the original complex concentration.

Relationship

A: bond-making advanced; D: bond-breaking advanced

Correction / limitation

A fast substitution reaction is not automatically associative; mechanism requires kinetic and structural evidence.

Application

Mechanistic classification helps predict how ligand identity and concentration affect complex reactivity.

Concept

Electron-transfer reactions alter oxidation states without necessarily exchanging ligands or breaking the molecular framework.

Theory

Electron-transfer reactions alter oxidation states without necessarily exchanging ligands or breaking the molecular framework. Inner-sphere pathways use a bridging ligand or related bond-connected route; outer-sphere transfer occurs without creating such a bridge between the reacting coordination spheres. Worked case: An electron can transfer between two metal complexes while both retain their ligand sets. Observing oxidation-state change alone therefore does not prove ligand transfer or a bridging intermediate. Interpretation and limits: Do not classify a metal-centred redox reaction as ligand substitution solely because its charge changes. Application: Electron-transfer mechanisms connect coordination chemistry with electrochemistry and biological redox processes.

Worked case

Relationship

Correction / limitation

Application

Electron-transfer mechanisms connect coordination chemistry with electrochemistry and biological redox processes.

Concept

The 18-electron rule is a useful electron-counting guideline for many low-valent organometallic complexes.

Theory

The 18-electron rule is a useful electron-counting guideline for many low-valent organometallic complexes. Count the metal's d electrons and ligand donation using one consistent ionic or covalent convention. Important stable exceptions exist, particularly for some square-planar d8 and electron-deficient complexes. Worked case: In the neutral counting scheme, Ni(CO)4 has 10 electrons from nickel and eight from four neutral two-electron CO ligands, giving 18 electrons overall. Interpretation and limits: Do not mix ionic and neutral counting conventions within one electron count. Application: Electron counting helps compare plausible organometallic structures and identify sites for ligand association.

Worked case

In the neutral counting scheme, Ni(CO)4 has 10 electrons from nickel and eight from four neutral two-electron CO ligands, giving 18 electrons overall.

Relationship

metal valence contribution + ligand contributions = valence electron count

Correction / limitation

Do not mix ionic and neutral counting conventions within one electron count.

Application

Electron counting helps compare plausible organometallic structures and identify sites for ligand association.

Concept

Metal carbonyl bonding combines CO-to-metal sigma donation with metal-to-CO pi back-donation.

Theory

Metal carbonyl bonding combines CO-to-metal sigma donation with metal-to-CO pi back-donation. Back-donation populates CO antibonding orbitals and generally weakens the internal C-O bond. Infrared stretching frequencies can therefore report changes in the metal's electron density. Worked case: Relative to a less electron-rich analogue, stronger back-donation in an electron-rich metal carbonyl often lowers the CO stretching frequency because the C-O bond is weakened. Interpretation and limits: CO coordination does not universally strengthen the internal C-O bond; back-donation changes its bond order. Application: Carbonyl infrared spectra help diagnose electron density and bonding in organometallic complexes.

Worked case

Relationship

Correction / limitation

CO coordination does not universally strengthen the internal C-O bond; back-donation changes its bond order.

Application

Carbonyl infrared spectra help diagnose electron density and bonding in organometallic complexes.
